children.translated_text: "But in this way, when the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) qualified by the <s>sādhya</s> (provable) is being predicated, from the understanding of the mere connection of the <s>sādhya</s> alone, there would be the exclusion of other properties. And then, when it is stated 'sound is impermanent,' due to the restrictive determination 'it is only impermanent,' properties like having the character of thunder and so forth would also not belong to it. And thus, since even the <s>hetu</s> (reason) would be rejected, the establishment of the <s>sādhya</s> itself would be hard to obtain. And if there is no restrictive determination, it might also be permanent — so the undesired is also established. Now, how can one thing be both permanent and impermanent — thus the rejection of the opponent follows by implication." True, and precisely for that reason, when the restrictive determination is being made for the purpose of excluding the contrary, the exclusion of the other also follows. Hence he says — 'restriction.' The restriction is posited only with reference to the intended property to be proved, not with respect to even non-contradictory other properties. Therefore, when 'possessing fire' is being proved, only the mere absence of fire is excluded, not any other property. Just as when it is said 'the cloth is white,' only the exclusion of its contrary — its absence — occurs, not of non-contradictory properties like fineness and the rest. And here 'the meaning that is not proximate' is stated — what is the purpose of that? If it means that inference brings into its scope only a meaning not previously apprehended — that is not so. For at the very time of knowing the connection, the connection of fire etc. with whatever possesses smoke etc. is already apprehended. Otherwise, the invariable determination would not have been ascertained. Nor should it be said that here some additional spatial-temporal connection is [intended]. For the spatial etc. connection of smoke is manifest, not of fire. Since the connection with the entire range of locations marked by smoke is already settled at the time of apprehending the connection. For this very reason, some have explained the term <s>asannikṛṣṭa</s> ('not proximate') as serving to exclude the misconception that inference is memory. For memory mostly arises as an impression elicited by proximate apprehension — it operates through [the recognition] 'that.' But inference is not like this. Therefore, this is not memory. "But even without such elicitation, memory does arise — as in cases of sudden recollection." Not so. Because of the absence of a cause for apprehension, in such cases, knowledge that operates in the form of an experience is accepted as memory. For it is not possible that the sense-organs, which operate through contact, could be the cause of the appearance of silver etc. that are not proximate. But the cause of memory — the <s>bhāvanā</s> (dispositional impression) produced by prior experience — does exist, so it is accepted as memory alone, devoid of the apprehension of that [present object]. But this inferential cognition, arising by the force of a present cause such as the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark), operates in the form of an experience, and cannot be removed from that status because of its very nature. And experience is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) for us. Therefore, inference is called a <s>pramāṇa</s>. "If so, then let this very thing be the purpose of the word <s>asannikṛṣṭa</s>." No — because in the absence of a result (<s>phala</s>), there would follow the deficiency of not being a <s>pramāṇa</s>. A <s>pramāṇa</s> has as its result the additional ascertainment. But if mere ascertainment were the result, it would also follow for memory — for memory too arises as nothing but the ascertainment of its own object. "The view may be that for us, a <s>pramāṇa</s> is independent. And memory depends on prior apprehension. Therefore it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>." That is not so — because the same would follow for inferential knowledge. For that too is dependent on the perception of a part (the mark) and other things. "Memory depends on the apprehension of its own object — this [inference] does not." Not so — because there is such dependence here too. For inferential knowledge too depends on prior knowledge of fire. For one who has not apprehended fire, whose connection is not known, the thought 'there is fire here' does not arise. Nor is it a royal decree that apprehension is necessarily a <s>pramāṇa</s> — because the same would follow for erroneous cognition too. Inverted apprehension is also apprehension. And it is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And that such does exist has already been stated by us in classifying cognitions into true and false. Moreover, by the <s>Sūtrakāra</s> (author of the <s>Sūtras</s>), in formulating the rule 'in a meaning not [previously] apprehended' —
having been grasped in its true form, and also contrariwise —

children.text: pramitasya pramāṇe hi nāpekṣā jāyate puna' // Msv_5,4.56 //
children.translated_text: for regarding what has been already validly known, no expectation for a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) arises again.
Regarding what has been ascertained in its true form, a further <s>pramāṇa</s> is fruitless;

children.text:
sarvamanupalabdhārthaviṣayameva pramāṇamiti sūtritam /
etadapi tadvyākhyānāvasare varṇitameva /
ato vyākhyeyamasannikṛṣṭārthagrahaṇamata āha--- asannikṛṣṭeti /
asyārtha'--- dvedhā hi sannikṛṣṭaṃ bhavati tadrūpapramitaṃ viparītanirūpitaṃ vā /

children.translated_text: With the desire to exclude both, this statement about what is not proximate is made.
What then is the refutation of that? Hence he says — 'of what has been validly known.'
For a <s>pramāṇa</s> is sought for the ascertainment of what has not been validly known, for the sake of practical activity, not out of a compulsive interest.

children.text: sa ca sakṛtpramāṇavyāpārādeva siddha iti na pramāṇāntarāpekṣeti ||55,56||
children.translated_text: And that [ascertainment] is accomplished by a single operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> — so there is no need for another <s>pramāṇa</s>.

it has been stated in the <s>Sūtra</s> that all <s>pramāṇas</s> pertain only to meanings not [previously] apprehended. This too has been explained at the occasion of explaining that [<s>Sūtra</s>]. Therefore, what is to be explained is the grasping of what is not proximate — hence he says: 'not proximate.' The meaning is: The proximate is twofold — either validly known in its true form, or determined through its contrary.

children.text:
kiṃ puna' pramitasya pramāṇāntarāpekṣā na jāyeta /
ata āha---tādrūpyeṇeti /
varṇitamidaṃ ---dvedhā hi pramitaṃ bhavati tādrūpyeṇa vaiparītyeneti /
tatra tāvat tādrūpyaparicchede na paraṃ pramāṇaṃ phalavat /
pūrvapiracchedādeva tadarthasiddhe' /
vaiparītyaparicchede tu pramāṇāntaramanavakāśameveti tadubhayanirākaraṇārthamasannikṛṣṭagrahaṇamarthavat /
nanvevamapramāṇamevānumānaṃ
sannikṛṣṭaviṣayatvādityuktameva /
na /
adhikāraviṣayatvāt /
yadyapi pūrvāvagato dharma' smṛtiviṣaya' /
dharmī ca giriranubhavasiddha', tathāpi viśiṣṭamanumānena viṣayīkrayata iti varṇitamasakṛt /
nanvagniviśiṣṭo 'pi sambandhasamaya eva saṃvidita' /
evaṃ hyanena vyāptigrahaṇakāle 'vagataṃ dhūmavanmātramagnimaditi /
tadasya dhūmavanmātra evāpekṣā /
vidite tu tasminnagnimattā pramitapūrvaivānubhūyate /
satyam /
kintu dhūmavānagnimattayā pritapūrvo 'pi samapratyanumānena pratyabhijñāyate /
pratyabhijñānaṃ cedaṃ pramāṇameva pratyakṣapratyabhijñānavat /
pūrvaṃ hi dhūmavattvopalakṣitena rūpeṇāgnimattayā deśo nirjñāta' /
samapratyayamasāvagnimāniti viśeṣato 'numānena pratyabhijñāyata iti kimanupapannam /
avaśyaṃ caivamabhyupagantavyam, anyathā kathamagnimāniti viditvā vyavahārāya ghaṭate /
eṣa hi paktukāmo 'gnimattāmanumāyāgnaye dhāvatīti paśyāma' /
children.translated_text: But why should no need for another <s>pramāṇa</s> arise regarding what has been validly known? Hence he says — 'in its true form.' This has been explained: the validly known is twofold — in its true form or contrariwise. Of these, first, in the case of ascertainment in its true form, a further <s>pramāṇa</s> has no result. Because the purpose of that is already accomplished by the prior ascertainment. And in the case of ascertainment through the contrary, there is no scope for another <s>pramāṇa</s> at all. Therefore, the word 'not proximate' serves to exclude both — and is thus meaningful. "But then, inference would not be a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all, because its object is proximate" — this has already been stated. No — because its object is additional. Although the property apprehended previously is the object of memory, and the <s>dharmin</s> (the mountain) is established through experience, nevertheless the qualified entity is made the object by inference — this has been stated repeatedly. "But the one qualified by fire is also known at the very time of apprehending the connection. For he understood at the time of grasping the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) that 'whatever merely possesses smoke possesses fire.' Therefore his expectation concerns only what merely possesses smoke. And when that is known, the possession of fire is experienced as already validly known." True. But the one previously known as possessing fire through possessing smoke is now re-cognized through inference at the present time. And this re-cognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>) is itself a <s>pramāṇa</s>, just like perceptual re-cognition. For previously, the location was known through the form marked by possessing smoke as possessing fire. Now, at the present time, it is re-cognized specifically through inference as 'this one possesses fire' — so what is unjustified? And this must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, how could one, having known 'it possesses fire,' engage in practical activity? For we see that one who desires to cook, having inferred the possession of fire, runs toward the fire.
But for what has been ascertained through the contrary, there is no scope for another [<s>pramāṇa</s>].

children.text: mūle tasya hyanutpanne pūrveṇa viṣayo hṛta' /
children.translated_text: For when the root of that [contrary determination] has not arisen, its object has already been taken by the prior [<s>pramāṇa</s>];
and of the set of six — perception and the rest — the objects are not determined [as contrary].
By that same [prior <s>pramāṇa</s>], sublation of the subsequent would occur, because of the impossibility of conceptual construction and the like.

children.text: agrāhyatā tu śabdāde' pratyakṣeṇa viridhyate // Msv_5,4.59 //
children.translated_text: But the non-graspability of sound and the like by perception is contradicted.

children.text:
tat kasya heto', na yadi pūrvānubhavādadya viśeṣa', avāgamat khalvayaṃ dhūmavānagnimāniti, na cāgnaye dhāvatīti /
kathamanāśrayapratipanne 'gnau vyavaharatīti cet /
na /
prāgapi dhūmavadāśrayatvanāvagamāt /
parvatamadhunā pratyakṣeṇa viśeṣato 'vagamyāgnye vyavaharatīti cet /
kimasyāgnyarthina' parvatapratyakṣeṇa /
tadayamagnimattayā bodha eva pūrvabodhād vilakṣaṇo 'bhyupagantavya' /
yatkṛto vyavahāraviśeṣa ityagṛhītaviṣayatvādanumānaṃ pramāṇamiti vaktavyam /

children.translated_text: This is what has been stated by the word 'not proximate' (<s>asannikṛṣṭa</s>).

children.text: ye tu smṛtyāśaṅkānirākaraṇama' saya prayojanamāhu', teṣāṃ bādhitaviṣayamapyanumānamāpadyeta /
children.translated_text: But those who say that the purpose of this is the exclusion of the suspicion of memory — for them, even inference whose object has been sublated would follow.
For the exclusion of that [memory] is not found to have been accomplished by any other component in the text of the definition.
Therefore, the word 'not proximate' alone serves the purpose of excluding both kinds of proximate meaning — and this is the correct interpretation.

For what reason, then, if there is no difference from prior experience? He did indeed apprehend 'this one possessing smoke possesses fire' — but he does not then run toward the fire. How does he engage in practical activity with fire when it has not been ascertained with respect to a substrate? No — because even previously, the substrate-nature of the smoke-possessor was not apprehended. "He now apprehends the mountain specifically through perception and engages with fire" — but what use is the perception of the mountain to one who seeks fire? Therefore, this cognition of possession-of-fire must be accepted as different from the prior cognition — being that on account of which there is a specific practical activity. And therefore, since its object is not previously grasped, inference is to be called a <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text:
vaiparītyaparicchinne paramanavakāśamityuktam /
tatra kāraṇamāha--- mūla iti /
vyāptismaraṇādi hyanumānasya mūlam, tadyāvaduttaraṃ tattadvyāpāravyagratayā vilambate tāvacchīghrabhāvinā pūrveṇa viṣayāpahārād viprakṛṣṭasādhanasyotpattireva nirudhyata ityanantarameva vakṣyata iti kathaṃ punaranumānaṃ bādhyate /
tadapi hi pramāṇaṃ kathaṃ pramāṇāntareṇa bādhituṃ śakyate /
bādhe vā na kvacidāśvāso bhavet /
ābhāso bādhyata iti cet, kathamābhāsatvam /
yadi bādhādevetarāśrayaṃ tarhyastu vā jyeṣṭhapramāṇena pratyakṣeṇānumānabādha' /
natu tato 'pi jaghanyairaparairbādhyate, tat kasya heto' ata āha---pratyakṣāderiti syādantena /
ayamabhiprāya'---na pramāṇaṃ nāma kvacit bādhyate /
avadhāraṇātmakaṃ hyevaitaditi jñānaṃ pramāṇam /
tad yatra kasyacidarthasya kenacidātmanāvadhāraṇaṃ bhavati tatra tenotpannasyotpatsyamānasya vā jñānasya bādho 'bhidhīyeta /
taddvividho hi bādha' prāptabādhaścāpratāptabādhaśceti /
prāptabādho hi yathā--- śuktikārajatajñāne /
tatra hi pūrvopamardanenaivottaramātmānaṃ labhata iti tat tasya bādhakam /
uttaraṃ ca deśādibhede 'pyabādhitaṃ svabhāvataśca pramāṇaṃ pūrvamābhāsīkaroti /
tadevaṃ prāptabādhe tāvad yenottareṇārtho 'vadhārita' /
trividhamapyaprāmāṇyamavadhāritapadena vyudasyati /
na hyajñāta' sandigdho viparyasto vārtho 'vadhārito
bhavatīti trividhimapyaprāmāṇyaṃ yasya nāstītyuktaṃ bhavati /
tadevamātmanā jñānena pūrvamābhāsīkṛtamiti tatrābhāsa eva bādhyata iti nātiprasaṅga' /
aprāptabādhe tu yāvat kliṣṭasādhanamanumānaṃ svagocare sāmānyaśāstraṃ vā kvacid viśeṣaviṣaye pravartitumārabhate tāvat pratyakṣeṇānumānena vā siddhasarvāṅgakenāgamena vā viśeṣaviṣayeṇa śīghrajanmanā yenaivārtho 'vadhārito
bhavati tenaivottarasyotpattipratibandhalakṣaṇo bādho bhavati /
na hi balavatā śīghrabhāvinā pramāṇena niruddhamukhamutpattumarhati /
tadevamaprāptabādhe paramanutpannameva prāptisambhāvanayā tu bādhyata ityucyate śrutyeva liṅgamiti na kvacit pramāṇabādha' /
yattu jaghanyena mukhyabādho na yukta iti /
tanna /
na hi pratyakṣādīnāṃ viniyogapramāṇānāmiva pāradairbalyaniyama' /
yadeva tu śīghrabhāvi pūrvopamardena vātmānaṃ labhate tadeva bādhakamabhidadhmahe /
itarañca bādhyamata eva tenaiva tasya bādhaṃ brūma' /
prāptabādha iva pratyakṣasya tenaivānumānena ca siddhāṅgakena sādhyāṅgakasya viśeṣaśāstreṇa sāmānyaśāstrasya /
ata' sarvapramāṇāviruddhameva pakṣamabhidhāsyāma' /
na cānāśvāsa' /
ābhāsabādhāt /
svata' pramāṇena cāvadhāraṇātmanā jñānenetarābhāsīkaraṇāt /
tadidamavadhāritapadenoktamiti /
nanu ca balavatāpi nāvaśyaṃ durbalaṃ bādhyate /
asati hi sambhave bādha' sambhavati /
ato viṣayavyavasthāyā vikalpena samuccayena vobhayamupapādayiṣyate vinātyantikabodhāśrayaṇena (?), ata āha---vikalpāderiti /
nātroktā vikalpādaya' sambhavanti /
na tāvatparasparaviruddhaṃ rūpadvayamekatra samuccīyate /
na hi śrāvaṇo 'śrāvaṇaśca
nityonityaśceti sambhavati /
na ca vikalpa' /
vidhiniṣedhaviṣayatvāt tasya siddhe vastunyasambhavāt /
na ca viṣayavyavasthā, varṇātmanāmeva nityānityatvasādhanāt /
ato 'sambhavādeva bādhamabhidadhmaha iti /
evamupapādito bādha udāharaṇairdarśayitavya' /
tatra pratyakṣabādhameva tāvad darśayati agrāhyateti /
imaṃ tu pratyakṣabādhaṃ na budhyāmahe /
svagocaraviparītārthaṃ hi pramāṇaṃ
children.translated_text: It was said that when the opposite is ascertained, there is no room for the other. He states the reason—'root.' For the remembrance of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) and such is the root of inference, and so long as the subsequent [cognition] is delayed due to the preoccupation with the operation of each [step], the earlier [cognition], being swifter, seizes the object, and the very arising of the inference whose means of proof are remote is obstructed—this will be stated immediately after. But how then is inference sublated? For that too is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge); how can a <s>pramāṇa</s> be sublated by another <s>pramāṇa</s>? Or if sublation [is possible], there would be no confidence anywhere. If [you say] it is a semblance (<s>ābhāsa</s>) that is sublated—how [do you establish] its being a semblance? If that is only from sublation itself, there would be mutual dependence. Then let it be that inference is sublated by the superior <s>pramāṇa</s>, namely perception. But it is not sublated by other inferior [means]—for what reason? Hence he says—'from perception and such,' up to the end [of the section]. The purport is this: no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever is actually sublated. For knowledge that has the nature of determinate ascertainment is [what constitutes] a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Where some object has been determinately ascertained through some [cognition] in some form, there it would be said that the cognition that has arisen or will arise is sublated. For sublation is of two kinds: sublation-already-reached and sublation-not-yet-reached. Sublation-already-reached is, for example, in the case of shell-silver cognition. For there, the subsequent [cognition] obtains itself only through the destruction of the prior, and so it is the sublator of the former. And the subsequent, being uncontradicted even when there is difference in place and the like, being intrinsically a <s>pramāṇa</s>, renders the prior a mere semblance. Thus, in the case of sublation-already-reached, the subsequent [cognition] by which the object has been ascertained—by the word 'ascertained' he dispels all three forms of non-validity. For an object that is unknown, doubtful, or erroneously known is not 'ascertained'—thus it is stated that none of the three forms of non-validity belongs to it. Thus, since it has been rendered a semblance by the subsequent cognition itself, only the semblance is sublated therein—so there is no over-extension. In the case of sublation-not-yet-reached, however, so long as inference—whose means of proof are laborious—or a general scripture begins to operate in some particular domain, a perception, or an inference with all its components established, or a scripture dealing with a particular subject, being of swifter birth, by which the object has already been ascertained—by that very [cognition], the sublation, characterized by the obstruction of the arising of the subsequent, occurs. For what has had its mouth obstructed by a powerful and swifter <s>pramāṇa</s> cannot arise. Thus, in sublation-not-yet-reached, the other has not even arisen, but through the possibility of its arising, it is said to be sublated—as 'scripture alone [is superior to] inferential mark'—so nowhere is there sublation of a [genuine] <s>pramāṇa</s>. As for the [objection] that sublation by an inferior [means of knowledge] of a superior one is not proper—that is not so. For there is no fixed rule of relative strength among perception and the like, as there is among the means of knowledge for ritual application. Rather, whatever is of swifter birth or obtains itself through the destruction of the prior—that alone we call the sublator. And the other is the sublated, precisely because we declare its sublation by that [swifter one]. In the case of sublation-already-reached, [the sublation is] of perception by that very [subsequent perception], and of inference with established components; [and] of a general scripture by a particular scripture dealing with a specific subject. Therefore, we shall state a thesis that is not contradicted by any <s>pramāṇa</s>. Nor is there lack of confidence, because what is sublated is only the semblance. And because the cognition that has the nature of ascertainment, being intrinsically a <s>pramāṇa</s>, renders the other a semblance—this is stated by the word 'ascertained.' But even by a stronger [means], a weaker is not necessarily sublated. For sublation occurs [only] when there is impossibility [of both being true]. Therefore, through the alternative of either domain-distinction or combination, both will be justified without resorting to an absolute resolution (?). Hence he says—'alternative and so on.' The alternatives and such stated here are not possible. To begin with, two mutually contradictory forms are not combined in a single [entity]. For 'auditory and non-auditory,' 'permanent and impermanent'—such [a combination] is impossible. Nor is there an alternative, because [the alternative] applies to what is to be enjoined or prohibited, and is impossible for an established entity. Nor is there domain-distinction, because the very letters themselves are what the proofs of permanence and impermanence are about. Therefore, it is precisely because of impossibility that we declare sublation.
Their non-auditoryness and the like is contradicted by inference;
for auditoryness is not apprehended by perception.
That [auditoryness] is known through co-presence and co-absence in the deaf and others;
the contradiction with scripture would be threefold, according to the division of thesis and such.

children.text:
pratyakṣeṇa bādhyata iti yuktam /
na cagrāhyatā pratyakṣaviṣayā grāhyagrahaṇasambandhaviṣayatvāttala' /
tasya ca pratyakṣagocaratvāt /
śabdo hi pratyakṣa' na grāhyatā /
ata eva hyaśrāvaṇatāpakṣo 'pi na pratyakṣeṇa virudhyata iti vakṣyate /
atrocyate /
satyam,
nendriyaviṣayo grāhyatā, grāhyastu tadviṣaya' /
tadiha grāhyapalāpasyaiva pratyakṣavirodho darśita' /
nirālambanānumānasyeti yāvat /
pratyayastvagrāhyaparadādupapannastasyaivābhāvamabhidhatte /

children.translated_text: And what is the existence of the apprehensible other than its being?
For this is the non-apprehensibility of a hare's horn—that it does not exist.
Due to the very absence of that, both the designation and the cognition of non-apprehensibility [arise] with respect to it.

children.text: tadanena prakāreṇa śabdābhāvapakṣasyaiva pratyakṣavirodha upadiṣṭa iti na kiñcidanupapannamiti ||58,59||
children.translated_text: Thus, in this manner, the contradiction with perception has been indicated precisely for the thesis of the non-existence of sound—so nothing is unjustified. // 58, 59 //

It is fitting that [the thesis] is sublated by perception. And non-apprehensibility is not itself an object of perception, because [perception] has as its domain the relation between the apprehensible and apprehension. And because that [relation] is an object of perception. For sound is perceptual, not apprehensibility [itself]. For precisely this reason, it will also be stated that the thesis of non-auditoryness too is not contradicted by perception. To this it is replied: True, apprehensibility is not an object of the senses; but the apprehensible is an object thereof. So here, the contradiction with perception has been shown precisely for the denial of the apprehensible—that is to say, of inference without a real object (<s>nirālambana</s>). But the cognition that arises from [asserting] non-apprehensibility states the very absence of that [apprehensible].

children.text:
anumānavirodhodāharaṇamāha---teṣāmiti /
teṣāmeva śabdādīnāmaśrāvaṇatvādyanumānaviruddhaṃ yo hyaśrāṇamanityaṃ vā śabdaṃ pakṣamicchati tasyāsau śīghrabhāvinā viparyayānumānena bādhyata iti /
idaṃ tu pratyakṣavarodhamanye manyante /
tān nirokaroti--- nahīti /
śabdo hi pratyakṣa' na tacchrāvaṇatā grāhyagrāhakasambandho hi śabdasya śrāvaṇasya ca tvatalbhyāmucyate /
"kṛtaddhitasamāseṣu sambandhābhidhānaṃ tvatalbhyām"iti smṛte' /

children.translated_text: And that [relation] is not to be ascertained by perception.

children.text: api ca atīndriyaṃ śrotraṃ,kathaṃ tatsambandha' śabdasya pratyakṣo bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: Moreover, the auditory sense is beyond the senses—how then will its relation with sound be perceptual?

children.text: na hyaindriyānaindriyādhāra' sambandha' pratyakṣo bhavati vāyuvanaspatyoriva /
children.translated_text: For the relation based on a non-sensory [entity] and a sensory [entity] is not perceptual, like [the relation] of wind and trees.
Therefore, this is not a contradiction with perception. // 60 //

He states the example of contradiction with inference—'their.' The non-auditoryness and such of those very [entities] such as sound are contradicted by inference. For whoever holds the thesis that sound is non-auditory or impermanent, his [thesis] is sublated by the inference of the opposite, which is of swifter birth. But others consider this [to be] contradiction with perception. He refutes them—'for not.' For sound is perceptual, not its auditoryness. The relation between the apprehensible and the apprehender—[the auditoryness] of sound and of the auditory [sense]—is expressed by the suffixes <s>tva</s> and <s>tal</s>. As stated in the grammatical tradition: 'In compounds with <s>kṛt</s> and <s>taddhita</s> suffixes, the relation is denoted by <s>tva</s> and <s>tal</s>.'

children.text:
kiṃpramāṇikā tarhi śrāvaṇatā /
ata āha---seti /
abadhirādiṣu śabdopalabdherbadhirādiṣu cānupalabdheranvayavyatirekau dṛśyete /
tathāhi śrotropaghātamātreṇa cakṣurādimato badhirasya śabdabuddhirna dṛśyate /
śrotre ca dṛḍhe cakṣurādiṣvasambhave 'pi śabdagrahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam, ata ābhyāmanvayavyatirekābhyāmidaṃ śrāvaṇatvaṃ gamyata iti /
nanvevaṃ kathamanumānavirodha', na hyanvayavyatirekāvanumānam, tatprabhavasamatu mānasa' śrāvaṇatvavikalpa', ato mānasapratyakṣa evāyamiti kaścit bhrāmyati sa vaktavya' /
na bahirviṣayabodhe mana' svatantramiti varṇitamasakṛt /
yad yadīyānvayavyatirekāvanuvidhatte tattakāraṇakamiti sarvakāryeṣu samadhigatam, anuvidhatte ca śabdajñānaṃ śravaṇamiti tattatkāraṇakamiti /
idameva ca śabdasya śrāvaṇatvam /
yattu jñānasya śravaṇajanyatvamato 'numānamevedam /
nanvanyatrāpyanvayavyatirekānuvidhāyina' kathaṃ tatkāraṇakatvamavagantavyam, yanna mānasaṃ pratyakṣamāśrīyate, śrūyatām /
paśyāmo hi vayaṃ kumbhakāravyāpārānantaraṃ kumbhasambhavamudīkṣamāṇā' kāryakāraṇabhāvaṃ cakṣuṣaiva /
idaṃ hi kumbhasya tatkāryatvaṃ yā tadanantarasambhūti' /
sa ca kumbhastatsambhavaścobhayaṃ cākṣuṣameveti kimatra manasā /
ato yad yasmin sati bhavati, asati ca na bhavati, tattatkāraṇakamiti pratyakṣato viditavyāpteranumāmupapannameva /
evaṃ ca prayoga'--- śravaṇapramāṇaprakāśya' śabda' tasmin
satyevopalabhyamānatvāt /
yadevaṃ tattataprakāśyaṃ santamasa iva ghaṭa' pradīpaprakāśya iti /
idaṃ ca pratyakṣapūrvakārthāpattipūrvakamanumānaṃ tayā śrāvaṇatvasiddhe' /
idaṃ ca siddhasarvāgatvādaśrāvaṇatvānumānād balavat /
yāvaddhi guṇatvasyāśrāvaṇatvena vyāptirgrahītumiṣyate, tāvacchīghrajanamanā śrāvaṇatvānumānena vyāptisaṃvidaṃ pratibandhatā tasyotpattireva nirudhyate /
children.translated_text: For so long as the <s>vyāpti</s> of the property of being a quality (<s>guṇatva</s>) with non-auditoryness is sought to be grasped, in the meantime, by the inference of auditoryness, which is of swifter birth, having obstructed the cognition of <s>vyāpti</s>, the very arising of that [inference of non-auditoryness] is prevented.
In the same way, the inference of impermanence too [is sublated].

children.text: yat kṛtakatvādihetukaṃ tadapyasiddhivyabhicārādidoṣānna śīgharmupajāyata iti siddhāvayavai' śīghrajanmabhirnityatvānumānairbādhyate /
children.translated_text: That [inference] which has being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) and the like as its reason—that too, due to defects such as non-establishment and deviation, does not arise swiftly; therefore it is sublated by the inferences of permanence that are of swifter birth and have established components.

children.text: yathā deśakālādibhinnā gośabdabuddhaya' samānaviṣayā' gaurityatpadyamānatvāt sampratyutpannagośabdabuddhivad hyastanoccārito vā gośabdo 'dyāpyasti gośabdatvād, adyoccaritagośabdavadityādibhiriti ||60||
children.translated_text: Just as the cognitions of the word 'cow' at different places and times have the same object, because they occur as 'cow'—like the presently arisen cognition of the word 'cow,' the word 'cow' uttered yesterday also still exists today because of its being a cow-word, like the cow-word uttered today—and so on. // 60 //

By what means of knowledge, then, is auditoryness [established]? Hence he says—'that.' In non-deaf persons, the apprehension of sound is observed, and in the deaf and others, the non-apprehension [is observed]—thus co-presence and co-absence are seen. For example, by the mere impairment of the auditory organ, the cognition of sound is not seen in a deaf person who possesses sight and the other [senses]. And when the auditory organ is intact, even when the eye and other [senses] are absent, the apprehension of sound is observed. Therefore, through these two—co-presence and co-absence—this auditoryness is understood. But if so, how is it a contradiction with inference? For co-presence and co-absence are not [themselves] inference. Rather, the conceptual cognition of auditoryness originating from them is mental. Therefore, whoever is confused [thinking] 'this is indeed mental perception' should be told: it has been stated repeatedly that the mind is not independent in the cognition of external objects. Whatever conforms to the co-presence and co-absence of whatever—that has that as its cause; this is understood in all effects. And the cognition of sound conforms to the auditory organ—therefore that [cognition] has that [organ] as its cause. And this itself is the auditoryness of sound—namely, that the cognition [of sound] is produced by the auditory organ. Therefore, this is indeed inference. But [you might ask:] elsewhere too, where something conforms to co-presence and co-absence, how is its being caused by that to be understood without resorting to mental perception? Listen: For we see, while observing the occurrence of a pot following the activity of a potter, the cause-effect relation through the eye itself. For this pot-hood of the pot is its arising in succession to that [potter's activity]. And the pot, its arising, and both—all are objects of visual perception; so what need is there of the mind? Therefore, since the <s>vyāpti</s> is known from perception—that what exists when something is present and does not exist when it is absent is caused by that—inference is well-established. And the formulation is thus: Sound is revealed by the auditory sense as its <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it is apprehended only when that [sense] is present. If this is so, then everything of that kind [would be revealed by its respective sense], just as a pot in darkness is revealed by a lamp. And this inference, preceded by perception and based on <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), establishes auditoryness through that [presumption]. And this, having all its components established, is stronger than the inference of non-auditoryness.

children.text:
śabdavirodhaprakāramidānīṃ pratijānāti---tridheti /
pratijñāvirodhādayo hi śabdavirodhatayā prasiddhā iti te tathābhidhīyante /
na tvete śabdavirodhā' /
yatra hi kvacidarthe pratiṣṭhitena śabdena pratijñāntaraṃ bādhyate, tatra śabdavirodho bhavati /
na ca svavāgvirodhe śabdasya kvacidarthe pratiṣṭhāsti vyāhatābhidhānāt /
pūrvasañjalpavirodhe 'pi pūrvāparanyāyabalābalānusāryeva nirṇaya
children.translated_text: He now announces the manner of verbal contradiction—'threefold.' For contradiction with the thesis, and such, are well-known as verbal contradiction, and so they are so designated. But these are not [truly] verbal contradictions. For where a thesis is sublated by a word established in some meaning, there is verbal contradiction. But in the case of self-contradiction of one's own speech, the word has no establishment in any meaning, because the assertion is self-defeating. In the case of contradiction with a previous statement too, the resolution follows the relative strength of the earlier and later reasoning.
From the thesis, from a previous statement, and from common knowledge of all people—
'I shall be silent all my life'—this is sublated by the very act of uttering it.
By [declaring] all statements to be false, the very <s>dharma</s>-statement [itself] is self-defeating;

children.text: dharmyuktyāhaṃ yato jāta' sā vandhyā jananī mama // Msv_5,4.63 //
children.translated_text: 'From <s>dharma</s> and reasoning I was born; that barren woman is my mother.'

children.text:
iti na śabdavirodha' /
na hi tatra śabdapramāṇator'tha' nyāyagamyatvāt /
lokaṃ prasiddhistu na śabdo na pramāṇāntaram /
api tu pratyakṣādyantargataiveti tadviruddhapakṣapradarśanenaiva pradarśiteti na śabdavirodhe 'ntarabhāvayitumucitā /
nahyacandra' śaśīti pakṣa' śabdena virudhyate /
na hi candraśabdaśaśāṅkayo' sambandhaṃ śabdo vadati yenātadvācyapakṣasya śabdavirodho bhavati sambandhavācyatve hītaretarāśrayaṃ bhavet /
abhidhānāt sambandha' sambandhāccābhidhānamiti /

children.translated_text: Therefore, these are not verbal contradictions.

But through consideration of the relative strength of the earlier and later statements, by abandoning one and accepting the other, they are known as verbal contradiction—thus the division well-known in other systems, 'verbal contradiction is threefold,' is stated.
In the ultimate sense, however, the thesis asserting the opposite meaning of a Vedic pronouncement is to be refuted by verbal testimony [alone].
And this we shall state immediately hereafter. (61)

Thus, this is not verbal contradiction. For the meaning there is not [established] by the verbal <s>pramāṇa</s>, since it is known through reasoning. And common knowledge is not verbal testimony, nor another <s>pramāṇa</s>. Rather, it is included within perception and the like. So by merely showing the contradicting thesis, [the point] has been shown—and it should not be included within verbal contradiction. For the thesis 'the moon is not the moon' is not contradicted by verbal testimony. For verbal testimony does not state the relation between the word 'moon' and the moon, such that there would be verbal contradiction for the thesis that [the moon] is not denoted by [the word 'moon']. For if verbal testimony [stated] the relation [and the relation was stated by verbal testimony], there would be mutual dependence: the denotation from the relation, and the relation from the denotation.

children.text:
tāneva trīn prakārān darśayati---pratijñeti /

sa ca tredhā bhidyate /

na hyanuktā sadī pratijñā bhavati /
uktimātreṇa bādhāda bhavati pratijñayā bādha' /

sarvamṛṣātve hi pratijñāvacanamapi mṛṣeti netaranmṛṣā bhavet /
tadamṛṣātve hi pratijñāvacanamapi mṛṣeti dharmasaṃsargāsambhavaparāmarśāt pakṣabādha iti dharmoktivirodhābhidhānam /
pūrvatra tvaviśiṣṭamuktimātrameva maunaṃ bādhate ityuktimātreṇetyuktam /
ātmabādhanamiti /
dharmabādhanamityartha' /
dharma evāyamukta ātmānaṃ bādhata iti yāvat /
vandhyā me jananīti pakṣo dharmyuktyā bādhyate /
jananītve hyuddiṣṭamātre na
children.translated_text: He shows those very three types — 'pratijñā' (thesis). Therein, contradiction of the thesis alone is divided threefold — he says 'yāvat' with the half-verse. The meaning is this: Contradiction of the thesis is contradiction of one's own statement. And that is threefold, from the distinction of utterance, property, and property-bearer. The thesis 'I am a silent one for life' is defeated by the very act of making the thesis. For a thesis is not a thesis unless it is uttered. Since the defeat occurs by the mere act of utterance, there is defeat by the thesis [itself]. But the thesis 'all sentences are false' is defeated by the statement of the property. For if all [sentences] are false, then the statement of the thesis itself is false — hence the other [sentences] would not be false. And if that [thesis statement] is not false, the reflection on the impossibility of the combination with the property [i.e., falsehood applying to itself] constitutes the defeat of the thesis — hence this is called 'contradiction by the statement of the property.' In the former case, however, the unspecified mere utterance itself defeats the silence — hence it is called 'by mere utterance.' 'Self-defeat' means: defeat of the property — that is, this property as stated defeats itself — such is the purport. The thesis 'my mother is barren' is defeated by the statement of the property-bearer. For when the motherhood is merely stated, the barrenness does not find a locus.
The Buddhist's [thesis that] sound is not eternal is defeated by what was previously accepted;
One who denies that the moon is the denotation of the word 'candra' (moon) — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.64)
He is defeated by the cognition of 'moon' that is established among all people.
For one who, having seen the form of a cow-like <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox), seeks to prove: (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.65)
'A cow does not resemble a <s>gavaya</s>' — his defeat is from analogy.
When <s>Caitra</s>, whose non-existence was ascertained at home, is [seen] alive outside — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.66)

children.text:
vandhyātvamāspadaṃ labhate /
na ca gauṇo jananīśabda ityapi vaktavyam /
ahaṃ yato jāta iti viśeṣaṇāt /
evaṃ viśeṣite pakṣe dharmyuktivirodha ityuktaṃ bhavati /
etaccābhyupagamavādenoktam /
na tu śrutismṛtyatirekīṇi jalpākavacanāni gauṇatvādibhi' samīkartuṃ śakyante /
children.translated_text: But statements of disputants that go beyond <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> cannot be reconciled through figurative usage and the like,
Because this would lead to the elimination of all defects [i.e., no argument could ever be refuted].
For defects arise only from carelessness or ignorance.

children.text: teṣu kathañcitsamādhīyamāneṣu na kiñcid dūṣaṇaṃ nāma bhavediti ||62,63||
children.translated_text: If they could somehow be reconciled, then nothing would ever constitute a defect. (62, 63)

Nor can one say that the word 'mother' is used figuratively, because of the qualifier 'I who was born from her.' When the thesis is thus specified, the contradiction by the statement of the property-bearer has been explained. And this has been stated by way of <s>abhyupagamavāda</s> (argument from the opponent's own admission).

children.text:
pūrvasañjalpavirodhamudāharatibauddhasyeti /
anitya' śabda iti bauddhenokte kathaṃ kṣaṇikādagṛhītasambandhādarthapratyaya ityanuyuktena tenaiva yadā punarucyate nityastarhīti tadā tasya pūrvābhyupagamavirodha' /
yadyapi cātra nyāyabalābalānusārī bādhyabādhakabhāva', tathāpyevaṃvidhā pūrvāparaviruddhā pratijñaivātmānaṃ na labhata iti na nyāyāvatāramapekṣate /
sambhāvito hi pratijñāyāmartho nyāyena sādhyate /
asambhāvite tu nyāyāpekṣā nāstyeva,svarasabhaṅguratvāt /
ata' śabdavirodha evainamantarbhāvayati /

children.translated_text: For the verbal construction itself —

children.text: tādṛśa' pūrvāparaviruddha' pakṣaṃ vināśayatīti teṣāmabhiprāya iti /
children.translated_text: Such a thesis, contradictory in its prior and later parts, is what destroys [itself] — such is their view.
He gives an example of contradiction with what is established among all people — 'candra.' (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.64)

children.text: atrāpi mahājanaviparītārtha' śabdasaṃsarga' svarasādeva bhajyate na pramāṇaṃ yāvadapekṣata iti śabdabādha udāhṛta iti ||64||
children.translated_text: Here too, a verbal construction whose meaning is contrary to [what is accepted by] the great public collapses of its own accord — hence it is illustrated as a case of verbal defeat, without even awaiting a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition). (64)

He illustrates the contradiction with a previous assertion — 'bauddhaysa' (of the Buddhist). When the Buddhist asserts 'sound is impermanent,' and is then challenged 'How is the cognition of meaning [generated] from a momentary [word] whose relation [with meaning] has not been apprehended?' — when he then says 'Well then, [sound] is eternal,' there is a contradiction with his previous admission. And although here the relation of defeated and defeater follows the strength and weakness of reasoning, still, a thesis that is self-contradictory in its prior and later parts does not even attain [the status of being a thesis] — hence it does not even await entry of reasoning. For it is [only] when a meaning is feasible in the thesis that it is established by reasoning. But when [the meaning] is not feasible, there is no need for reasoning at all, since it [the thesis] collapses of its own accord. Hence this [type of contradiction] is subsumed under verbal contradiction itself.

children.text:
upamānavirodhodāharaṇamāha---jñāteti /
yena hi nagare gavākāro dṛṣṭa' samprati cāraṇye gavayākāra', taṃ prati gaurgavayasadṛśo na bhavatīti pakṣa upamānena virudhyata iti /
children.translated_text: He gives an example of contradiction by analogy — 'jñāta.' For one who has seen a cow-form in the city and now [sees] a <s>gavaya</s>-form in the forest — for him, the thesis 'a cow does not resemble a <s>gavaya</s>' is contradicted by analogy.
When non-existence is to be proved, the defeat comes from <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption);
When fire is to be proved as non-burning, or when sound [is to be proved as] non-denoting — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.67)
And when the non-existence of the sense organs [is to be proved], or when the eternality of sound is to be proved —
The defeat here is from <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) derived from what is heard, when the statement of a trustworthy person is being refuted. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.68)
One who eats by day would be refuted by reasoning [establishing that he must eat] at night.
When the cow is out of sight, [similarity is established by] analogy;
But when it is in sight, by direct perception itself.
For this very reason, the sequence 'one who has known the form of a cow-like <s>gavaya</s>' is intended [in the verse]. (65)

Now, wishing to illustrate the contradiction by <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), following the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator), he first gives an example of [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by non-existence — 'geha' (at home). (66)
Not possessing that capacity — such is the meaning.
He illustrates [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by inference — 'śabde ca' (and regarding sound), 'non-denoting.'
Since, after hearing a word, the cognition of meaning arises through the inferred activity, it is deduced that the word is the cause therein.

children.text: ata' sarvakārakāṇāṃ kriyāvinābhāvādabhidhābhidhāno vyāpāra',tadanupapattyā cārthāpattyā tacchaktisiddhiriti ||67||
children.translated_text: Therefore, since all instrumental factors are invariably concomitant with the action, the operation called denotation [is established], and from its otherwise inexplicability, the capacity [of the word to denote] is established through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption). (67)
He illustrates [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by perception — 'agnau' (in fire). 'Non-burning' means:

children.text: yadyapi pratyakṣapūrvikodāhṛtaiva tathāpi pakṣadoṣodbhāvanacchalenendriyāpalāpapakṣasyāpyayaṃ doṣa iti vivakṣatā punastadvirodho 'bhihita' /
children.translated_text: Although this has already been illustrated as [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by perception, nevertheless, under the pretext of showing the defect of the thesis, this contradiction of the thesis denying the existence of the sense organs has been stated again.

children.text: atraivādiśabdenopamānapūrvikayā virodho darśayitavya'--- yathā gavayopamitāyā gostajajñānagrāhyaśaktyapahnava iti /
children.translated_text: Here, with the word 'ādi' (and such), the contradiction by [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by analogy should be shown — for example, the denial of the capacity apprehended through the knowledge of cow-likeness that has been compared to a <s>gavaya</s>.
He illustrates the contradiction by [<s>arthāpatti</s>] preceded by <s>arthāpatti</s> — 'śabda.'

children.text: arthābhidhānānyathānupapattyā hi vācakaśaktimarthāpattyā pramāya punastadanupapattyārthapattyantareṇa śabdanityatvamavagamyata iti ||67||
children.translated_text: For the denotative capacity [of words] is first established through <s>arthāpatti</s> from the otherwise inexplicability of meaning-denotation, and then, from the otherwise inexplicability of that [capacity], the eternality of sound is ascertained through another <s>arthāpatti</s>. (67)
Similarly, the thesis denying the existence of the sense organs is also contradicted by <s>arthāpatti</s> preceded by perception — he says 'śrotra' (the auditory organ).

na hi tasyā' svarūpeṇa vrīhayo viṣayabhūtā', tadavayavāstu cūrṇībhūtā vrīhiśāstrārtha' /

tadihātadgocaratvapakṣasyopamānapūrvakānumānabādha' /
arthāpattipūrvakānumānabādhastu śrāvaṇatvapakṣe 'bhihita eva /
yatra dūrād vṛkṣābhāvaṃ viditvā tacchāyābhāvo 'numīyate tatrābhāvapūrvakānumānena chāyāsadbhāvapakṣo bādhyate /

children.translated_text: He illustrates the contradiction of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) preceded by verbal testimony — 'śrutārthāpattibādha' etc. But why is <s>arthāpatti</s> illustrated in such detail, when demonstrating its contradiction could be accomplished with even a single example? Moreover, the contradictions of the other <s>pramāṇas</s> have not been elaborated. Or else, like <s>arthāpatti</s>, the contradictions of other <s>pramāṇas</s> too should be stated in detail. True. The author of the <s>Vārttika</s> intends the contradiction as sixfold, of the six [pramāṇas] themselves divided into six — and to demonstrate this, the <s>arthāpatti</s> produced by six <s>pramāṇas</s> has been illustrated. By the same route, the elaboration regarding other <s>pramāṇas</s> too is to be shown. First, perceptual contradiction itself is divided into six (excluding the sixth) through experience, memory, inference, and so forth. The thesis 'fire is not hot' of a debater who is being scorched is contradicted by perception in its experiential mode. The same thesis, when fire is not nearby, is contradicted by perception in its memory mode — when he propounds at the time of debate 'fire is not hot,' the other reminds him: 'Do you not remember the hotness of fire previously experienced? How can you say this?' He, remembering it, then desists from the perceptual [evidence] — thus there is contradiction of perception stored in memory. The contradiction of perception by inference: where, upon an authoritative person's face, from not seeing the particular gestures [of enjoying food], the absence of the tasted bitterness etc. is claimed — from the distortion of the face, his experience of bitterness is inferred — hence the contrary thesis is contradicted by inferred perception. The contradiction of perception by verbal testimony: where someone denies something, and witnesses [say] 'this matter was seen by us' — the contradiction by the witnesses' perception is stated. And this is not contradiction by words. For they do not [merely] state the matter — but rather their seeing. Hence the determination follows their seeing. And their seeing is conveyed by them through their own words — thus this is the contradiction of perception understood through words. Analogy has as its object merely the similarity of an object known through another <s>pramāṇa</s> — hence it objectifies the similarity of what is established elsewhere. Just as, in the recognition of a sickle etc., one who has seen such action in oneself compares it to what is seen elsewhere: 'My recognition of the sickle etc. arose through perception — how else would he engage on the next day in completing the work half-done the previous day?' Here, through action, one infers a corresponding object pertaining to another, and then the similarity of one's own cognition is compared there. Although here it could be shown as merely the contradiction of perception understood through inference, nevertheless, because the similarity to one's own cognition can be shown to be established, the contradiction of perception understood through analogy is stated. The very existence of perception is measured by analogy. The contradiction of perception understood through <s>arthāpatti</s> is to be shown thus: When many thirsty people going [to fetch water], one having set out to fetch from a tank, delays — then, from the otherwise-inexplicability of that delay, his perception of water is established through <s>arthāpatti</s>. There, the contrary thesis of a waterless tank is contradicted by perception established through <s>arthāpatti</s>. But through absence, a positive perception is not cognized — hence the contradiction of perception not cognized through absence is not illustrated here. The sixfold contradiction of inference will now be examined — first, the denial of fire cognized through smoke: there is contradiction of inference preceded by perception. When hotness is inferred from the fire inferred from smoke, the contrary thesis is contradicted by inference preceded by inference. Where the thesis contrary to the rest of the <s>mantra</s> inferred from the known ritual application 'he offers to the deity' is held, there is contradiction of inference by <s>āgama</s> (scriptural tradition). When a regular ritual is being performed and rice is unavailable, and <s>nīvāra</s> (wild rice) grains similar to rice are compared through analogy, the Vedic injunction 'one sacrifices with rice' is inferred as extending to <s>nīvāra</s>. For the parts of rice, whose connection is known as being the object of that [injunction], lead to that inference. For rice is not the object of that [injunction] in its own form — rather, the parts of rice, when pulverized, are the purpose of the rice-scripture. And since those [parts] exist in <s>nīvāra</s> too, the rice-injunction, extending to <s>nīvāra</s> through analogy by the general parts of rice, is inferred. Here, the thesis that it does not extend to that is contradicted by inference preceded by analogy. The contradiction of inference preceded by <s>arthāpatti</s> has already been stated in the thesis of audibility. Where the absence of a tree is known from afar and the absence of its shade is inferred, there the thesis of the existence of shade is contradicted by inference preceded by absence. The threefold contradiction of perception and words has already been shown. Another should be demonstrated through <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>. The thesis of <s>aṣṭakā</s> rituals etc. being unrighteous is contradicted by verbal testimony of the general approval of the agent — this has been shown in the <s>smṛtyadhikaraṇa</s>. For <s>aṣṭakā</s> and such can be inferred as [righteous], like the <s>agnihotra</s>, because of having scripture as their basis and being performed by noble residents of <s>Āryāvarta</s>. The contradiction of <s>āgama</s>-based words: where, in a dispute about the subject-matter of a <s>śruti</s> found in another recension, the existence of the <s>śruti</s> is ascertained by the statement of <s>smṛti</s>-based reasons — there, the contradiction of the contrary thesis is possible through the eternal <s>āgama</s> understood through authoritative tradition. The contradiction of words preceded by analogy: when, from the <s>smṛtis</s> of <s>Manu</s> and others, some Vedic source is postulated through <s>arthāpatti</s>, and the source is compared to a similar <s>smārta</s> statement itself through analogy, the thesis of it being based on <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage) is contradicted by words preceded by analogy. The thesis of the <s>viśvajit</s> (sacrifice) being fruitless is contradicted in the established restriction of the <s>arthāpatti</s> derived from scripture — its operation, there being its absence — the thesis of the arising of obligatory duties in the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> <s>prākṛta</s> (primary rite) is contradicted. As he will say: 'Because of complete injunction, <s>soma</s> is unprecedented.' When rice is absent, the thesis of the non-acceptability of <s>nīvāra</s> is contradicted by analogy arising from perception. The contradiction of analogy preceded by inference: when the motion of the sun is inferred from its reaching different locations, and in the middle or at the end [of its course] the motion of the sun is of such a kind in successive years — there the thesis of dissimilarity of motion is contradicted by analogy preceded by inference. The thesis 'pūtīkā plants are not similar to soma' is contradicted by analogy preceded by words. For the similarity of <s>sāma</s> and <s>pūtīkā</s> is not perceptual. Nor
The contradiction of the possibility of hare's horns and such is from non-apprehension. // Msv_5,4.69 //

and of property, subject, both, and the own-nature and its specific features— // Msv_5,4.70 //

children.translated_text: The thesis that the non-existence of the maker of the <s>Vedas</s> is not similar to the absence of hare's horns is contradicted by analogy preceded by absence.
When absence is understood through the absence of both, similarity is compared through analogy.
The contradiction of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), sixfold, has already been described.
The contradiction of absence, however, we shall state immediately after. // 68 //

can be inferred. But through words alone, by demonstrating the birth of <s>pūtīkā</s> from soma-rays, the similarity of cause and effect is demonstrated through the fitness of cause and effect — thus, because the similarity of <s>pūtīkā</s> to soma in analogy, arising from the cause-and-effect relationship understood through words, is established, the contrary thesis is contradicted by analogy preceded by words. For the <s>dharmas</s> of the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> do not exist in the <s>satra</s> and <s>ahīna</s> [sacrifices] — this thesis is contradicted by analogy through analogy. For they extend to the twelve-day rite through analogy with the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>, and to the <s>satra</s> and <s>ahīna</s> through analogy with the twelve-day rite. But when the sense organs of another are compared through the similarity [to one's own] self and sense organs, there the thesis denying them is contradicted by analogy preceded by <s>arthāpatti</s>.

The [thesis] '<s>darvīhomas</s> (ladle-oblations) have a prior [oblation]' is contradicted by the absence of analogy.

children.translated_text: Similarly, when sound does not come to the location of the ear, and the ear does not go to the location of the sound — since hearing of sound is explicable merely by the arrival of vibration — if one maintains through <s>arthāpatti</s> that sound terminates in another sound, and hence sequentially the last is apprehended by the ear, that thesis is contradicted by the absence of <s>arthāpatti</s>.

children.text: abhāvābhāvastyevaṃ darśayitavya'--- yadā hi kartrabhāvena vedānāṃ doṣābhāvo 'vagato bhavati tadā doṣavatpakṣasyābhāvābhāvena bādha iti ||69||
children.translated_text: The absence of absence is to be shown thus: when the absence of defect in the <s>Vedas</s> is understood from the absence of an author, then the thesis of there being defects is contradicted by the absence of absence. // 69 //

He now illustrates the contradiction of absence — 'śaśaśṛṅga' etc. And this is the contradiction of absence by perception. When it is being considered whether the sun has reached a certain zodiacal position or not, and through astronomical calculation-inference-absence it is established that it has not reached, one who is confused says it has reached. There is the contradiction of absence by inference.

children.translated_text: Nor should one say that in frost too it is not apprehended because it is overpowered—
because of the perception of coldness, which is its opposite.
The presentation of the reason, at the occasion of stating the faults of the thesis, is merely to show its seed — this is the contradiction of the specific feature of the <s>dharma</s> by absence.

There, the contradiction of the own-nature of the <s>dharma</s> has already been described — hence, leaving that aside, he illustrates the contradiction of its specific feature — 'tṛṇādi' etc. For one who proves that frost has fire from seeing the transformation of grass and such, the contradiction of the own-nature of the <s>dharma</s> occurs through its absence. Its specific feature too — hotness — being implied by the meaning, is contradicted by coldness apprehended through perception. Nor should one say: 'Even in luminous bodies, fire is seen as non-hot — how then is the specific feature implied?' For even in luminous bodies, fire is indeed hot; but because it is overpowered, the touch is not apprehended — it never abandons its hotness, for that is its inherent nature.

children.translated_text: But the sublation of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer), though of two kinds, has been left unstated — so he gives examples of the sublation of both, with a verse and a half beginning with '<s>adharma</s>.' It is generally understood that violence is <s>adharma</s> (unrighteous). So when the enjoined <s>adharma</s>, the violence to the <s>dīkṣā</s> sacrificial animal, is restated and argued to be a minor [form of <s>adharma</s>], even then, by virtue of being enjoined, the <s>adharma</s>-nature itself is sublated, and its specific aspect too — the property of being a cause of suffering, which is implied by the meaning — is also sublated by that very fact. For nothing that is enjoined is ever a cause of suffering, since the injunction is a means solely for the fulfillment of human purpose. This is
When it is stated 'all cognitions are false,' there is sublation of both;
because the falsity of those very cognitions is proved from both their own nature and their specific aspects.
Momentariness and absolute falsity are the two specific aspects of both here;
by the phrase 'from the perception of one part,' this is refuted.
Where, regarding one or both, there is doubt, wrong understanding, or false cognition —
'fire does not burn because of its coldness'; 'sound is impermanent because of its visibility' —
in such cases as 'of sound,' there is an established false cognition regarding both.
Not through scripture is the sublation of the specific nature of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) [accomplished].

children.text: na cātra śrutyupātta eva svaviśeṣa iti codanīyam /
children.translated_text: And here one should not object that the specific aspect is itself taken up by the <s>śruti</s> (scriptural text),
because what is implied by the meaning, being minor,
is merely restated for the purpose of the injunction.
He illustrates the sublation of both by both — 'all cognitions are false' etc.

children.text: yadā hi sarvajñānāni mithyeti sādhyate tadā dharmadharmigrāhiṇorapi jñānayormithyātvāt tadviśeṣaṇagrāhiṇośca mithyātvād bhavatyubhayasyaivobhayabādha iti /
children.translated_text: For when it is argued that all cognitions are false, then, since the cognitions that grasp the <s>dharma</s> (property) and the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) are also false, and since the cognition that grasps their specific qualifications is also false, there is sublation of both by both.

children.text: ayaṃ ca dharmoktyobhayabādha iti śabdabādha eva niveśanīya iti samadhigataṃ tāvadubhayo' svarūpabādha iti ||74||
children.translated_text: And this sublation of both, stated as a sublation of the <s>dharma</s> (property), should be classified as 'verbal sublation' (<s>śabdabādha</s>) alone. Thus it has been understood so far — the sublation of the own nature of both.

children.translated_text: What then are those two specific aspects that are implied and sublated? Hence he says — 'momentariness' etc. 'Are sublated' — the connection should be shown by transposing this [verb]. And here 'from the perception of one part' is stated. And therein, the word 'perception' (<s>darśana</s>) is redundant — 'from one part' alone should be said. For it is the <s>liṅga</s> (mark) that matters, not the perception. Therefore what is to be explained is 'from the perception of one part' — hence he says 'from perception.' The meaning is: The one part (<s>ekadeśa</s>) is not a mark merely by its existence. Rather, it is its apprehension. And the word can accommodate both [readings], since the form is common to both the causative and non-causative [verbal forms]. In the case of <s>svārtha</s> (for-oneself inference): when one part is perceived, the cognition is <s>anumāna</s> — that is the meaning. In the case of <s>parārtha</s> (for-others) usage, the causative-ending word 'perception' means: the cognition that arises after having shown one part is <s>anumāna</s> — this is what is stated. Thus, the word 'perception' used there is to be explained in both senses. And by this, where regarding one part, for both the proponent and opponent, or for one of them, there is doubt, wrong cognition, or false cognition — that <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (pseudo-reason) called <s>asiddha</s> (unestablished) is refuted. For such [a reason] cannot be shown as such to the other.
When properties like being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) or being-a-quality (<s>guṇatva</s>) are stated by the opponent to a <s>Yājñika</s> (Mīmāṃsaka) —
and when one states a reason of such a kind to the opponent, then for one or the other it is unestablished.
When there is doubt about whether it is steam (<s>bāṣpa</s>) or such, for both, or for one or the other,
smoke is threefold unestablished. Thus, first, as regards its own nature,
these very same modes apply in the case of <s>āśrayāsiddha</s> (unestablished substratum).
For even when [the reason] is known in its own nature, there is no probative force in what does not possess that property;
or it is itself seen directly.
That is, it is wrong cognition — this is the meaning.
Therein he gives the example of what is falsely cognized by both — 'from coldness' etc.
Regarding the two — fire and sound — coldness and visibility are, for both proponent and opponent, falsely cognized — hence unestablished.

children.text:
anyatarāsiddhodāharaṇamāha---kṛtakatveti /
yadā vaiśiṣiko yājñikaṃ prati śabdo 'nitya' kṛtakatvāt guṇatvādveti hetuṃ prayuṅkte,tadāsau svarūpeṇa tasyāsiddho bhavati /
yadā tu svayamevaṃprakāraṃ hetuṃ paraṃ prati vadati tadā tasyāsiddhi' /
children.translated_text: But when one himself states such a type of reason to the opponent, then it is unestablished for that [opponent].
For example: 'Sound is permanent because of being-a-substance, like space.'

children.text: na hi vaiśiṣikā' śabdaṃ dravyamabhyupagacchanti guṇatvābhyupagamāt /
children.translated_text: For the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> do not accept that sound is a substance, since they accept it as a quality.
'Of such a kind' means: of the kind unestablished for the opponent — that is the meaning.

He gives an example of <s>anyatarāsiddha</s> (unestablished for one party) — 'being-produced' etc. When the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> employs the reason against the <s>Yājñika</s>: 'Sound is impermanent because of being-produced or because of being-a-quality' — that is unestablished for the latter in its own nature.

children.text:
sandigdhāsiddhamudāharati---bāṣpādītisyādantena /
yadā hi dhūmo bāṣpādibhāvena sandihyate dvābhyāmekena vā kiṃsvidayaṃ rajasāmudgamo bāṣpo vā dhūmo veti tadā dvayorapyantatarasya vā sandigdhāsiddho bhavati /
evaṃ tāvat sandehaviparyayābhāyamasiddhatodāhṛtā /

children.translated_text: But unestablished-ness due to ignorance should be shown in the case of using an unfamiliar word.
'Threefold' —
The three modes are with respect to the proponent, opponent, and both.

children.text: evaṃ tāvat svarūpato heturasiddho bhavatītyuktamityāha--- evamiti ||78||
children.translated_text: Thus it has been stated that the <s>hetu</s> (reason) is unestablished as regards its own nature — so he says 'thus.'

He gives an example of <s>sandigdhāsiddha</s> (unestablished due to doubt) — 'steam and such' etc. with a half-verse. For when smoke is doubted as being steam or such — by both or by one — 'is this rising dust or steam or smoke?' — then it is <s>sandigdhāsiddha</s> for both or for one. Thus, unestablished-ness due to doubt and false cognition has been illustrated.

The unestablished-ness of the substratum (<s>āśrayāsiddha</s>) too is divided threefold by the same factors of cognition and the like, relative to the proponent, opponent, and both — so he says 'these very same.'

children.text:
nanu svarūpāsiddhyāheturduṣyet āśrayāsiddhyā tu kastasya doṣa' ata āha---jñāte 'pīti /
ayamabhiprāya---na svarūpeṇa heturgamaka',apitu
children.translated_text: "But the <s>hetu</s> is defective through its own non-establishment; but from the non-establishment of the substratum, what fault does it have?" Hence he says — 'even when known.' The purport is: The <s>hetu</s> is not a proof-giver by its own nature alone, but rather
'Because effects are seen everywhere, the self is all-pervading' —
against a Buddhist, the substratum is unestablished; and for an ordinary person, there is doubt.
Merely because of non-establishment in speech alone, practical usage does not fail to occur;
what is known by both to be non-existent — the objection against that is considered a refutation.

children.text: itarat sādhanaṃ tu syāt vādinā yadi sādhyate // Msv_5,4.82 //
children.translated_text: But the other would be a proof, if the proponent proves it.

children.text:
pakṣadharmatayā jñāta' /
na cāprasiddhāśrayastaddharmatayā jñātuṃ śakyate /

children.translated_text: Even of coldness and visibility, it is the non-establishment as properties of the <s>pakṣa</s> that constitutes the non-probative-ness.

children.text: siddhaṃ hi svarūpeṇa jale śaityaṃ rūparūpirūpapaikārthasamavāyiṣu ca cākṣuṣatvam /
children.translated_text: For coldness is established in its own nature in water, and visibility in [entities] co-inhering in color, colorful things, and things with single-substrate inherence.

children.text: śabdā(dau) hi pakṣadharmatayā tu tayorasiddhatvamiti taddharmarūpāsiddhavacanam /
children.translated_text: But in the case of sound etc., their non-establishment as properties of the <s>pakṣa</s> is what makes the statement one of 'unestablished in the form of the property' (<s>taddharmarūpāsiddha</s>).
Therefore, even in the case of <s>āśrayāsiddha</s> (unestablished substratum), since the <s>pakṣa</s>-property is also unestablished, the non-probative-ness is justified.
[The <s>hetu</s> is probative] by being known as a property of the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis-subject). And an unestablished substratum cannot be known as possessing that property.

children.text:
tāmidānīmāśrayāsiddhimudāharati---sarvatreti asiddhāntena /
yadā hi boddhaṃ prati sarvatra kāryopalambhādātmana' sarvagatatvaṃ mīmāṃsakā' sādhayanti, tadānyatarāsiddhāśrayo heturbhavati /
bauddhasyātmanano 'siddheriti /
yastu pramāṇagatimajānāno laukika' kaścidātmani saṃśete tasminneva hetāvucyamāne sadnigdhāśrayo heturityāha--- laukikāderiti /
ātmani saṃśaya ityartha' /
ādiśabdena satīrthikānāmapi yeṣāmātmani saṃśaya' ta upādriyante /
children.translated_text: By the word 'etc.' (<s>ādi</s>), even those co-religionists who have doubt about the self are included.
Thus, <s>āśrayāsiddha</s> through doubt and false cognition has been stated.
The non-establishment of the substratum through ignorance too should be shown in the case of using an unfamiliar word.

children.text: yasya hi pakṣavacana' śabdo na prasiddhastaṃ pratyevañjātīyake hetāvucyamāne 'jñānenāśrayāsiddhiriti ||80||
children.translated_text: For one to whom the word denoting the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis-subject) is unfamiliar — when such a type of reason is stated to him, there is <s>āśrayāsiddha</s> through ignorance.

He now illustrates the <s>āśrayāsiddha</s> (unestablished substratum) — 'everywhere' etc. with a half-verse. For when the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> argue against a Buddhist: 'The self is all-pervading because effects are seen everywhere' — the substratum is unestablished for one party, since for the Buddhist, the self is not established. But for some ordinary person who does not know the ways of <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge) and doubts the self, when that very reason is stated, the substratum is doubtfully unestablished — so he says 'for an ordinary person' etc. The meaning is: there is doubt regarding the self.

children.text:
nanu yadyanyatarāsiddhyā heturduṣyati, evaṃ tarhyamūrtatvādātmā niṣkriya ityevamāderapi hetutvaṃ na syāt digambarāṇāmātmano 'mūrtatvāsiddhe' /
mūrtaṃ hi te śarīrapariṇāmamātmāne manyante /
akartṛkatvānnityo veda iti ca bauddhānāṃ tadasiddherahetu' /
śabdo 'nitya' kṛtakatvāditi mīmāṃsakānāmasiddhe' /
tadeva heturnāma na kaścit vyavatiṣṭhate /
ata āha---vāṅmātreti /
ayamartha'--nāsiddho mameti vāṅmātrāddheturasiddho bhavati /
tathā sati na kaścidanumānavyavahāra' prakalpeta /
dvābhyāṃ tu vādiprativādibhyāmasattvenā
children.translated_text: "But if the <s>hetu</s> is defective through <s>anyatarāsiddha</s> (non-establishment for one party), then the reason 'the self is incorporeal, hence inactive' and similar ones would also not be probative, since for the <s>Digambaras</s> (Jains), the incorporeality of the self is not established — for they consider the self to be a material transformation of the body. And 'the <s>Veda</s> is eternal because it has no maker' — this too would be non-probative for the Buddhists, since that [no-maker status] is not established for them. And 'sound is impermanent because of being-produced' — this is non-established for the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>. Therefore, nothing at all remains as a <s>hetu</s>." Hence he says — 'merely by speech' etc. The meaning is: The <s>hetu</s> does not become non-established merely because someone says 'it is not established for me.' Otherwise, no inferential transaction would be possible. But what is known by both — the proponent and the opponent — to be non-existent,
if the refutation or establishment [of the substratum is accomplished], then it becomes a refutation by the opponent;
and the reasons based on doubt and contrariety are also refuted here.
From the statement 'whose connection is known,' three causes of doubt —

children.text:
vadhārito 'siddhobhavati, tasyaiva tathāviṣayasyāsiddhatāvacanaṃ vādino dūṣaṇaṃ bhavati nāsiddha iti
vākpravṛttimātrāditi ||81 ||nanu kimidaṃ dvayorasiddho 'siddha iti, na hi vivadamānayorekatrārthe sampratipattirbhavati,na hi janmasahasreṇāpi bauddho vedānāmakartṛkatvamanyate, mīmāṃsako vāpi kaṇṭhagataprāṇo 'pi kṛtakatāṃ śabdasya /
tadevamādāvubhayasampratipatterabhāvānna hetubhāva'vatiṣṭhate /
ata āha---itaraditi, ayamabhiprāya'--- na dvayorasaṃpratipattirityetāvataiva sādhanadūṣaṇayoranavakḷpti' /
yadi vādinā prayuṅkte sādhane prativādinā cāsiddhatva udbhāvite vādinā tatsādhanaṃ sādhyate, tato bhavati sādhanam /
yadi tuparamārthopapattyābhidhānena prativādinā nirākriyate tatastasya dūṣaṇaṃ sidhyati /
tatpramāṇata' siddhirevātropayujyate nobhayābhyupagama' /
dvābhyāṃ yo 'sattvato jñāta ityapi pramāṇasiddhyabhiprāyeṇoktam, nābhyupagamamātrāpekṣayā /
yaddhi pramāṇena sādhyate
bādhyate vā tatra prāyeṇobhayasampratipattirdṛṣṭeti /
asattvato jñātāpekṣayetaracchabda' /
yadvādinā sattvena jñātaṃ bhavati prativādinā ca vaiparityena, tadvādinā sādhyamānaṃ sādhanaṃ bhavati /
etacca jalpanyāye sthitvoktam /
vāde tu dvayorapi sampratipattirbhavatyeveti /
na caivamanyatarāsiddhiradūṣaṇam, yāvattu vādī na sādhanaṃ sādhayati, tāvadanyatarāsiddhyā nigṛhyate, sādhite tu tasmin dūṣaṇaṃ parihṛtaṃ bhavatīti ||82 1/2||
children.translated_text: that known to be non-existent by both — the statement of its non-establishment is a refutation for the proponent and is not a mere verbal assertion. But what is known to be existent by one and contrary by the other — when the proponent proves that, it becomes a proof. This has been said adopting the standpoint of <s>jalpa</s> (sophistical debate). In <s>vāda</s> (honest discussion), there is mutual agreement by both. And this does not mean that <s>anyatarāsiddha</s> is not a defect — but rather, as long as the proponent does not prove the proof, he is defeated through <s>anyatarāsiddha</s>; but when it is proved, the defect is overcome.

children.text:
darśitaṃ tāvadasannikṛṣṭaikadeśaśabdayorvyāvartya, jñātasambandhapadasyedānī vyāvartyaṃ darśayatisandehetivacanāntena /
sandehaviparītahetvorhi na sambandho jñāto bhavati, na hi sādhāraṇa' saṃśayahetu' prameyatvaṃ nityatvena jñātasambandhamiti śakyate vaktum, ghaṭādiṣvanityatayāpi jñātasambandhatvāt nāpi kṛtakatvaṃ nityatayā, teṣvevānityatayā sambandhasavitte' /
atastajjātīyatubhayaṃ na jñātasaṃbandhamiti jñātasambandhapadena vyudasyati /
atra cāsannikṛṣṭapadāt, prabhṛti prātilobhyena vārtikakṛtā lakṣaṇagranthe viśeṣaṇopadānaphalamuktam,
children.translated_text: Having shown what is excluded by the words <s>asannikṛṣṭa</s> (not proximate) and <s>ekadeśa</s> (one part), he now shows what is excluded by the phrase <s>jñātasambandha</s> (whose connection is known) — with the half-verse beginning with 'doubt.' For when the connection is based on doubt or contrariety, it is not 'known.' For the common property of being knowable (<s>prameyatva</s>), which is a reason for doubt, cannot be said to have a known connection with permanence, since it also has a known connection with impermanence in cases like pots. Nor can being-produced have a [known connection] with permanence, since in those very cases, the connection is known with impermanence. Therefore, both of this kind are not 'of known connection' — and the phrase <s>jñātasambandha</s> excludes them. And herein, from the word <s>asannikṛṣṭa</s> (not proximate) onwards, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> has stated the purpose of including each qualifier in the definition-text, systematically.

children.text: sat sādhye tadabhāve ca dvābhyāṃ vyāvṛtta eva ca // Msv_5,4.84 //
children.translated_text: [The connection] being present in the <s>sādhya</s> (provable) and absent in its absence, and excluded by both [parties] —
two [reasons] connected with a contradictory meaning — as long as they belong to a single one-part-possessor;
properties like being knowable, impermanence, and corporeality are common to both [alternatives].

children.text:
tat kasya heto' /
pratītikramānusāreṇa /
pramātā hi prathamaṃ pakṣa pratyeti, tato hetumapekṣate,tato dṛṣṭāntavacanam ato 'satpakṣanirākaraṇārthaṃ prayuktamasannikṛṣṭapadameva tāvadupavarṇitam /
tato hetupadamekadeśadarśanāditi, tato jñātasambandhasyeti dṛṣṭāntadoṣā api sādhyahetuvikalatvādayo 'nena nirākriyante /
tadvaikalye 'pi svayaṃ sambandho jñātuṃ parasmai pratipādayituṃ śakyata iti /
kiyanta' puna' saṃśayahetava', āta āha---traya iti ||83 1/2||
children.translated_text: For what reason? Following the order of cognition. For the cognizer first cognizes the thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), then expects the reason (<s>hetu</s>), then the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>). Therefore, the term 'not proximate' (<s>asannikṛṣṭa</s>), employed for the purpose of removing the false thesis, has first been explained. Then the term for the reason — 'from the perception of one part' (<s>ekadeśadarśanāt</s>). Then 'of that whose connection is known' (<s>jñātasambandhasya</s>) — by this, defects of the example such as incompleteness of the provable and the reason are also refuted. Even when that [example] is deficient, the connection can be known by oneself and communicated to another. How many, then, are the causes of doubt? Hence he says — 'three.' // 83½ //

children.text:
tāneva trīn prakārān darśayati---sanniti /
sādhyatadabhāvayo' san sādhāraṇo 'bhidhīyate /
yathā prameyatvaṃ nityānityatvayo' /
dvābhyāṃ sādhyatadabhāvābhyāṃ vyāvṛtto 'sādhāraṇa' kṣitareva gandhavattvam /
vyāvṛtaṃ hi tat sakalasajātīyavijātīyadravyāntaraguṇakarmabhya' /
dvau viruddhārthasambandhāviti /
yau viruddhāvyabhicārīti parairabhihitau, tau cānantaramevodāhāryāviti neha vyākhyāyete iti ||84 1/2||
children.translated_text: He shows these very three types — 'existing.' That which exists in both the provable (<s>sādhya</s>) and its absence is called <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common). For example, <s>prameyatva</s> (knowability) with respect to both permanence and impermanence. That which is excluded from both the provable and its absence is called <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon) — such as earth's possession of smell (<s>gandhavatva</s>). For that is excluded from all other homogeneous and heterogeneous substances, qualities, and actions. The two connections with contradictory meanings — those which others have called <s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s> (contradictory non-deviating) — these are to be illustrated immediately after and are not explained here. // 84½ //
Therein, he first elaborates on the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common) type with examples — 'knowable.'

children.text: ete ca dharmā' sādhyatadabhāvayo' sādhāraṇā ityartha' ||85||
children.translated_text: And these properties are common to both the provable and its absence — this is the meaning. // 85 //

children.text:
keṣu puna' sādhyeṣu teṣāṃ sādhāraṇyamata āha---nityeti nityeṣvantena /
kathaṃ punarvaiṣamye yathāsaṅkhyamata āha--- dviranityateti /
anityatā svasthāne dvi' paṭhitavyā /
ato yathāsaṅkhyopapatti' /
tadayamartha'--- yordṛṣṭamiti sādhāraṇatvādannaikāntāya prabhavati /
ato naikāntarikamityucyate /
ata eva ca saṃśayahetu' /
saṃśayo hi sāmānyapratyakṣādviśeṣāpratyakṣādviśeṣasmṛteśca bhavati /
yathā sthāṇupuruṣayorārohapariṇāhasāmānyadarśanād bhedaka
children.translated_text: In which provables, then, is their commonality? Hence he says — 'permanent,' with 'among permanents' at the end. How then is the correspondence in the case of asymmetry? Hence he says — 'twice, impermanence.' 'Impermanence' (<s>anityatā</s>) should be read twice in its proper place. Thus the correspondence in order is established. The meaning is this: What is seen as 'knowable' (<s>prameyatva</s>) — being common, it serves for non-certainty; therefore it is called 'non-exclusive.' And for this very reason it is a cause of doubt. For doubt arises from the perception of a general [feature], from the non-perception of the specific [feature], and from the memory of a specific [feature]. Just as from seeing the general features of height and girth common to a stump and a person, without perceiving the differentiating
The earth would be permanent through possessing smell — this would be your <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon [reason]). // Msv_5,4.86 //
The deficiency of one component of determination is the cause of doubt in these cases;

children.text:
dharmānavadhāraṇācca viśeṣasmṛtyapekṣa' /
kiṃsvidayaṃ sthāṇurāhosvit puruṣa ityanavadhāraṇajñānātmaka' saṃśayo jāyate /
evaṃ prameyatvamapi
nityānityayo' sāmānyaṃ viditavatastadviśeṣamasmaraṇāpekṣastayorevānirdhāraṇātmaka' pratyaya' saṃśayāparanāmā jāyata iti prameyatvaṃ saṃśayahetu' /
ayaṃ ca kṛtsnobhayavyāpī saṃśayahetu' /
tathā yatnottha' śabda' anityatvādityayamapi sādhāraṇa eva /
ayatnottheṣu keṣucidvidyudādiṣu gatatvādyatnottheṣu ca sarveṣu ghaṭādiṣu vṛtte' /
tadaya sakalavipakṣavyāpatī sapakṣaikadeśagata iti veditavyam /
tathā yatnottha' śabda' anityatvāditi, yatnottheṣu sarveṣvevānityatā dṛṣṭā /
tadabhāve 'pi kvacinmeghādau dṛṣṭā, na vyomādau iti,
sakalasapakṣavyāpī vipakṣaikadeśavartī cāyaṃ sādhāraṇa ityavasātavyam /
ubhayaikadeśagatastu yathā nitay' śabda' amūrtatvāditi /
amūrtatā hi na sarvanityavyāpinī vyomādiṣu bhāvādaṇuṣu cābhāvādanityamapi na svaṃ vyāpnoti ghaṭakuḍyādiṣvabhāvāt karmādiṣu bhāvāt /
sarvatra cātra dvayavṛttitvameva heto' saṃśaye kāraṇavṛttyaṃśastu sannapi na kāraṇamityatantram /
ata eva sādhāraṇasya caturdhāvibhāgaṃ vadanti ye teṣāmasāvanupayogyeva sādhanadūṣaṇayorityupekṣayoravṛttyaṃśa' kvacidupayujyate /
aṇvāpi hi mātrayā vipakṣe vartamāno hetustyājya eva /
dūṣaṇavādino 'pi vipakṣavṛttimātraṃ vacanīyamiti kiṃ tadavāntaraviśeṣāśrayaṇena /
vārtikakāreṇāpi sarvasādhāraṇeṣu dvayavṛttitvameva saṃśayakāraṇamiti darśayitumudāharaṇaprapañco darśita', na punaścāturvidhyamabhametya /
yathāha---
"na tvekasyopayogo 'sti dūṣaṇodbhāvanaṃ prati /
