tyajyate sādhane caivaṃ sādhāraṇyād viśeṣata' ||iti 85 1/2||
children.translated_text: feature, and from the failure to determine a specific property — the doubt arises: 'Is this a stump or a person?' — this is the cognition of non-determination. So too, for one who knows <s>prameyatva</s> (knowability) as a general feature common to both permanence and impermanence, without remembering the specific difference between them, a cognition of non-determination regarding those very two, which is another name for doubt, arises — thus <s>prameyatva</s> is a cause of doubt. And this cause of doubt pervades the entirety of both sides. Similarly, the [reason] 'sound is produced by effort, therefore impermanent' — this too is merely common. Because it occurs in some effortless [things] like lightning, etc. that have perished, and in all effortful [things] like pots, etc. Thus this should be understood as pervading all the counter-examples (<s>vipakṣa</s>) while being present in only a part of the positive examples (<s>sapakṣa</s>). Likewise, 'sound is produced by effort, therefore impermanent' — impermanence is seen in all effortful [things]. But it is also seen in its absence, in some [things] like clouds, etc., and not seen in others like space, etc. — thus this is a <s>sādhāraṇa</s> that pervades all positive instances while being present in only a part of the counter-examples. One that is present in only a part of both — such as 'sound is permanent because of incorporeality' — for incorporeality does not pervade all permanent things (being present in space etc. but absent in atoms); nor does it pervade all impermanent things (being absent in pots, walls, etc. but present in actions, etc.). And in all these cases, it is precisely the occurrence in both that is the cause of doubt — the portion where it occurs is not the cause even when present — this is a matter of indifference. For this very reason, those who speak of a fourfold division of the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> — the portion where it does not occur is sometimes useful for purposes other than proof or refutation. For a reason that occurs even to the slightest degree in the counter-examples must be abandoned. And even one who is stating a refutation need only point out its occurrence in the counter-examples — what need is there to resort to its sub-varieties? The <s>Vārttikakāra</s> too, in showing that the occurrence in both is alone the cause of doubt among all <s>sādhāraṇas</s>, has presented the elaboration of examples, but has not accepted the fourfold division. As he says: 'There is no use of one [sub-type] for the purpose of raising a refutation; and in proof too, it is abandoned precisely because of commonality, due to the specific [occurrence in both].' // 85½ //

children.text:
prapañcata' sādhāraṇa', asādhāraṇamidānīṃ saṃśayahetumudāharati---nityā bhūriti /
gandho hi pṛthivyā' svāsādhāraṇo guṇa', na tāṃ vihāya nityamanityaṃ vā bhāvāntaramāśrayayatītyasādhāraṇa iti gīyata /
children.translated_text: Having elaborated on the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), he now illustrates the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon) cause of doubt — 'the earth is permanent.' For smell is an uncommon quality of earth alone; it does not reside in any other entity, permanent or impermanent, besides earth — therefore it is called uncommon.
Just as the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), having been observed, is the cause of both cognitions [i.e., doubt], // Msv_5,4.87 //
and because of the non-attainment of either of the two contradictory [conclusions],
it is accepted as the cause of doubt; and where the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon) is not present, through the absence of that — // Msv_5,4.88 //
and because of the contradiction with the non-existence of both, it is accepted as the cause of doubt.

children.text:
āha--- astvasādhāraṇaṃ gandhavattvaṃ, kathaṃ tu saṃśayahetu', yuktaṃ hi pakṣadvayāvalambī sādhāraṇo dvayoranavasthādhiyamādadhāno yatsaṃśayaheturiti, asādhāraṇastu dvābhyāṃ vyāvṛtto naikatrāpi dhiyamupajanayitumalāmiti kathamasya saṃśayahetubhāva', ata āha---niścayeti /
hetorhi niścayajanane 'nvayavyatirekāvaṅgamanyatarāpāye 'pi na niścayāya hetu' paryāpto bhavati /
tad yathā sādharaṇo 'nvayasanātho 'pi vinākṛto vyatirekeṇa na niścayāya prabhavati, evamevāsādharaṇo 'pi niścayasyaikenānvayanāmnāṅgena vilastamakurvan saṃśayahetutāṃ pratipadyata iti ||86 1/2||
children.translated_text: He says: Let the possession of smell (<s>gandhavatva</s>) be uncommon; but how is it a cause of doubt? For it is appropriate that the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), supporting both alternatives, produces the instability of cognition regarding both and thus is a cause of doubt. But the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon), being excluded from both, is unable to produce cognition regarding either — so how is it a cause of doubt? Hence he says — 'deficiency of one component.' For in generating certainty, co-presence (<s>anvaya</s>) and co-absence (<s>vyatireka</s>) are the two components of the reason. In the absence of either one, the reason is not sufficient for certainty. Just as the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), though endowed with co-presence, being devoid of co-absence, is not sufficient for certainty, so too the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon), failing in one component — namely co-presence — serves as a cause of doubt. // 86½ //

children.text:
nanūktaṃ sādhāraṇo dvayagāmī dvaye buddhiṃ janayan saṃśaye heturiti /
asādhāraṇastu na kiñcid jñāpayatīti nāsāvekāṅgavikalatāmātreṇa saṃśayaheturiti yuktamata āha---sādhāraṇaiti dvayena /
ayamabhiprāya'---sādhāraṇo 'pi nobhayatra buddhijananāt saṃśayahetu', kintu viruddhobhayapratipādanamukhena, viruddhe dyubhayasmin pratipādite tayorekatra samavāyasambhavād vyāghātādeva saṃśayo bhavati /
tañcāsādhāraṇe 'pyaviśiṣṭam, asādhāraṇo 'pi dyubhayasmād vyāvṛttestadabhāvaṃ gamayan dvayābhāvāsambhavādeva saṃśayaṃ janayati /
na hi sambhavati nityamanityaṃ ca vastu na bhavatīti, dharmadvandvaireva hi nityānityatvādibhi' sarvaṃ janagadavasthitam /
ata ubhayābhāvo virudhyate /
na cobhayabhāva', virodhādeva /
na cānyataraparigraho 'viśeṣāt /
tamimaṃ saṅkaṭamāsādya prāmāṇika' saṃśete /
ayaṃ cātrāvayavārtha'---yathā prameyatvādi' sādhāraṇo dṛṣṭa' san buddhidvayanimittaka' /
buddhidvayaṃ saṃśayenimittamasthātīti bahuvrīhi', nimittaśabdena ca buddhidvayasya nimittamātratāṃ kathayati /
sādhyatadabhāvaviṣayaṃ hi buddhidvayaṃ nimittīkṛtya viruddhaikānavāptereva sādhāraṇena saṃśayo janyate /
na hi
parasparaviruddhābhyāṃ nityānityatvābhāveka' śabdo vyāpyate, dharmibhedanibandhanohi viruddhadharmābhyāso dṛṣṭa' /
yathā nityaṃ vyoma anityaṃ kāryadravyamiti /
ato 'smāt pratītivyāghātādeva sādhāraṇena saṃśayo manyate /
sa cāyamasādhāraṇasyāpi samāna' /
so 'pi hi yatra nitye 'nitye vā nāsti tadabhāvaṃ pratipādya tanmukhena dvayasattvavirodhamāpādayan saṃśayakāraṇaṃ bhavatīti /
idaṃ cāsādhāraṇasya saṃśayahetutvaṃ nāmumanyante /
avyavasthayā hyubhayasmin manasi viparivartamāne saṃśayo bhavati /
na cāsādhāraṇena kiñcid buddhāvādhīyate, tasya kenacidanvayābhāvāt /
api ca parimiteṣveva bhāveṣu saṃśayo dṛṣṭa' /
nivṛttimukhena tu saṃśayajanane sarvato nivṛttenāsādhāraṇena sarvatomukha' saṃśayo janyeta /
na ca sarvaviṣaya' saṃśayo dṛṣṭacara' /
tasya buddhāvanārohāt /
naca kvacinnivṛttimātreṇa sarvatrābhāva' śakyate 'vagantum, yanmukhena saṃśayo bhavet /
na hyanuvṛttāvadṛṣṭāyāṃ vyāvṛtti' sidhyati /
agnāvanuvartamāno hi dhūmo dṛṣṭavyatireko 'gniniyatasvabhāvatvenāvagator'thādadṛśyamānebhyo 'vagnibhyo vyatiricyata ityavagamyate /
yastu na kenacidanvitastasya kathamanupalabdhiyogyāt sarvato vyatireka' pratīyeta /
tato nānena prakāreṇāsādhāraṇasya saṃśayahetutvam /
yadi tvasādhāraṇadharmāṇobhāvā nityānityabhāvabhājo dṛṣṭā iti kṣitimapi taddharimikāmupalabhya nityā vā syādanityā veti saṃśayo bhavatītyucyate /
evaṃ tarhyasādhāraṇadharmatvādeva bahusādhāraṇāt saṃśayo nāsādhāraṇāt, anyo hyasādhāraṇadharma' anyā ca bahusādhāraṇī tadvattā /
tad yadyasau saṃśayakāraṇaṃ jātā kiṃ jātamasādhāraṇasya /
hantaivaṃ sādhāraṇa eva saṃśayaheturabhyupagato bhavatīti siddham /
nāsādhāraṇasya saṃśayahetutvam /
anyanmatam--- anadhyavasāyaheturevāyamiti /
asti kilānadhyavasāyo nāma jñānasya prakāra' /
so 'sena janyate /
bhavati hi tādṛgadharmadṛśa' kimbhūtatasyāsya dharmo 'yamityanadhyavasitāvabhāsavratyaya' /
nacaiva prāmāṇam, aniścayātmakatvāt /
na ca saṃśaya' pakṣadvayāsaṃsparśāt /
so 'yamevaṃvidhānadhyavasāyo 'sādhāraṇena janyata iti /
na tvetada ghaṭate /
na hyanavyavasāyo nāma kaścid jñānasya prakāra', yamayaṃ janayet /
adhyavasāyābhāvo 'nadhyavasāya' /
sa ca prāgabhāvarūpatvānna janya' /
athānyamātravacano nañ abrāhmaṇādivadiṣyate tato 'dhyavasāyādanya' saṃśaya
children.translated_text: But [objection:] it was said that the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), pervading both sides, generates cognition in both and thus causes doubt. But the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon) does not establish anything — so it is not a cause of doubt merely from the deficiency of one component. Hence he says — '<s>sādhāraṇa</s>' with the two [verses]. The purport is: Even the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common) is not a cause of doubt because it generates cognition in both, but rather through the channel of indicating both contradictory [conclusions]. When both contradictory conclusions are indicated, since the coexistence of both in one [entity] is impossible, doubt arises precisely from the conflict. And this is no different in the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon). The <s>asādhāraṇa</s> too, being excluded from both, indicating the absence of that [property], generates doubt precisely through the impossibility of the non-existence of both. For it is not possible that a thing is neither permanent nor impermanent — for the entire world is constituted by pairs of properties such as permanence and impermanence. Therefore, the non-existence of both is contradictory. And the existence of both is [also contradictory], precisely because of contradiction. Nor is the acceptance of either [alone possible], due to the absence of a distinguishing factor. Having arrived at this impasse, the rational thinker doubts. And here is the meaning of the verse components: Just as the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> (common), having been observed, is the cause of both cognitions (<s>buddhidvayanimittaka</s>). 'Cause of both cognitions' is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound meaning 'that for which the two cognitions are causes' — by the word 'cause' (<s>nimitta</s>) he indicates that the two cognitions are merely causes. For having made the two cognitions regarding the provable and its absence the occasion, it is precisely from the non-attainment of either of the two contradictory [conclusions] that doubt is generated by the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>. For a single sound is not pervaded by both mutually contradictory permanence and impermanence — for the conjunction of contradictory properties is observed only with respect to different substrates. As 'space is permanent, produced substances are impermanent.' Therefore, from this very conflict of cognitions, doubt is held to arise through the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>. And this is the same for the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon). For it too, where it does not exist — in the permanent or the impermanent — indicating the absence of that, through that channel, producing the contradiction of the existence of both, becomes a cause of doubt. But this causation of doubt by the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> is not accepted [by some]. For doubt arises when both [alternatives] revolve in the mind in an unsettled manner. But the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> does not establish anything in cognition at all, since it has no co-presence with anything. Moreover, doubt is observed only with respect to a limited number of entities. But if the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> generates doubt through the channel of negation, then being excluded from everything, it would generate doubt regarding everything. And universal doubt is not observed in practice. Because it does not enter cognition. And from the mere absence [of the reason] in some [domain], the absence of everything cannot be understood as a basis for doubt. For exclusion is not established when co-presence has not been observed. For smoke, co-present with fire, when observed to be excluded, is understood to be excluded from non-fire things due to its nature being invariably connected with fire. But for that which has no co-presence with anything — how could its exclusion from everything that lacks perceptual presence be understood? Therefore, the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> is not a cause of doubt in this manner. But if it is said that entities possessing the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> property have been seen to partake of both permanence and impermanence — and so, apprehending earth too as possessing that property, the doubt 'is it permanent or impermanent?' arises — if so, then it is precisely from the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> quality of possessing that property, which is common to many, that the doubt arises, not from the <s>asādhāraṇa</s>. For the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> property is one thing, and the possession of it, which is common to many, is another. If the latter becomes the cause of doubt, what has the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> accomplished? Alas, thus the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> alone is accepted as the cause of doubt — this is established. The <s>asādhāraṇa</s> is not a cause of doubt. Another view holds: This is merely a cause of non-determination (<s>anadhyavasāya</s>). There exists, it is claimed, a type of cognition called non-determination. That is produced by this [<s>asādhāraṇa</s>]. For when one who has seen such a property [thinks] 'what kind of property is this of this thing?' — a cognition in the form of undetermined appearance arises. It is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because of its non-determinate nature. Nor is it doubt, because it does not touch either of the two alternatives. This kind of non-determination is generated by the <s>asādhāraṇa</s>. But this does not work either. For there is no type of cognition called 'non-determination' that this [<s>asādhāraṇa</s>] would generate. Non-determination is simply the absence of determination. And that, being in the nature of prior non-existence, is not something to be produced. If the negative particle is taken as meaning 'something other than,' like 'non-<s>Brāhmaṇa</s>' — then something other than determination, namely doubt,
The status of these [reasons] as causes of doubt is said to be relative to the subject matter. // Msv_5,4.89 //
The status of being a cause of ascertainment (<s>nirṇaya</s>) too is observed with respect to another object to be proved;
having obtained exclusion and co-presence, as incorporeality [proves non-activity] and such. // Msv_5,4.90 //

children.text:
eva tacchabdavācyo bhavet /
na ca taddheturasādhāraṇa iti phaṇitameva /
athādharmādivad vipaparītavacano nañ, evaṃ sati viparyavācyo 'nadhyavasāyaśabdo bhavet, na ca viparītāvagraho 'sādhāraṇena janyata iti /
yadi tu na me 'smin vastunyadhyavasāyo 'stītyadhyavasāyābhāvāvadhāraṇamevānadhyavasāya', sa tarhi pramāṇābhāvenaivādhyavasāyābhāvo 'vagamyate /
tatra hetorna vyāpāra' /
ato jijñāsāmātraheturasādhāraṇa iti samarthanīyam /
bhavati hi taddarśina' kīdṛgdharmo 'yamito dharmād bhāvo bhavediti
jijñāsā /
yadyapi cāsau śuddhadharmidarśanādapi kadācid bhavatyeva tathāpi dharmadvāreṇāpi tāvad bhavatyeveti na taddhetutvamanupapannam /
āha ca---
tenājñānamasiddhebhyo jijñāsānanyagāmina' /
sāmānyātsaṃśayo yuktastathā sa pratisādhanāt || iti /
yattvihāsādhāraṇasya saṃśayahetutvamuktaṃ tatparamatam /
jñātasambandhapadasya hi vyāvartanīyamatra darśayitumabhipretam, tat saṃśayahetutve 'pyasādhāraṇasya ghaṭata eva /
bhavatu tāvadayaṃ yasya kasyaciddhetu' /
sarvathā jñātasambandhapadena vyudasyata iti tātparyam /
śākyāstu saṃśayahetumasādhāraṇaṃ manyante, udāharanti ca śabdānityatve sādhye śrāvaṇatvam /
yathoktam---
anaikāntikamenaivanaṃ śākyā' prāyeṇa manvate /
ubhayasmānnivṛttatvādubhayatrānuvṛttivat||
children.translated_text: it would be denoted by that word. And that the reason [for doubt] is <s>asādhāraṇa</s> (uncommon) has already been stated. Alternatively, if the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>) is of contrary signification, like [the prefix in] <s>adharma</s> and the like, then in that case the word <s>anadhyavasāya</s> would denote the contrary [of ascertainment], but an erroneous apprehension is not produced by an <s>asādhāraṇa</s> [reason]. If, however, <s>anadhyavasāya</s> (non-ascertainment) means simply the determination of the absence of ascertainment, in the sense of 'I have no ascertainment regarding this entity,' then the absence of ascertainment is understood merely through the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). In that case, the <s>hetu</s> (reason) has no role. Therefore it should be maintained that the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> [reason] causes merely the desire to know (<s>jijñāsā</s>). For upon seeing it, the desire to know arises: 'What kind of property is this? From this property, what [other] entity might follow?' And although that [desire to know] sometimes arises even from the perception of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) alone, still, since it arises at least through the property, it is not unreasonable to call it the cause thereof. As [the verse] states: 'Therefore, from things that are not established, [there arises] the desire to know, which does not go elsewhere; doubt is appropriate from a common [feature], and likewise its resolution from counter-proof.' Now, what was said here—that the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> is a cause of doubt—that is the other [opponent's] view. For what is intended to be shown here is the exclusion of what pertains to the known-relation domain; and that is quite compatible even with the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> being a cause of doubt. Let this then be a cause of whatever it may be. The purport is that in all cases it is excluded by the phrase 'known-relation domain.' The <s>Śākyas</s> (Buddhists), however, consider the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> to be a cause of doubt, and they give the example: when impermanence of sound is to be proved, auditoryness [is the reason]. As stated: 'The <s>Śākyas</s> generally consider this to be <s>anaikāntika</s> (inconclusive), since it is excluded from both [the <s>sapakṣa</s> and <s>vipakṣa</s>], just as co-presence in both [would be inconclusive].'
Thus.

children.text: idaṃ ca vārttikakṛtaiva pradeśāntare svayamupanyasya yathoktadūṣaṇairdūṣi tameveti ||88||
children.translated_text: And the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> himself, having introduced this in another context, has refuted it with the objections stated there. // 88 //
Is the causation of doubt by the cited [reasons] natural or not?—he says, '<s>sandigdha</s>' (doubtful). // 89 //

children.text:
kāraṇamāha---nirṇayasyeti labdhvāntena /
kva dṛṣṭamata āha---niṣkriyeti /
amūrtatā hi nityatve sādhye nityānityavyomakarmasādhāraṇī saṃśayaheturāsīdat, saiva tu niṣkriyatve sādhye labdhvānvayavyatirekau hetutāṃ
children.translated_text: He states the reason—'of resolution,' ending with 'having obtained.' Where is this seen? Hence he says—'<s>niṣkriya</s>' (actionless). For incorporeality, when permanence is to be proved, was a cause of doubt, being common to the permanent ether and the impermanent action. But the same [incorporeality], when actionlessness is to be proved, having obtained co-presence and co-absence [with the <s>sādhya</s>], attains the status of a reason.
When existence in some part of the earth is to be proved, the property of possessing smell serves as the reason;
where the imperceptibility of wind is proved through its being formless.
Or its perceptibility [is proved] from touch—this is called <s>viruddhāvyabhicāritā</s> (contradictory non-deviation).
[This] is demonstrated.
For incorporeality is pervaded by actionlessness.
For the incorporeal ether and the self do not move about.
And the incorporeality of those possessing it, such as chariots and the like, is not observed. // 90 //

children.text:
asādhāraṇasya nirṇaye hetutvaṃ darśayati---kṣityekadeśeti /
gandhaviśeṣadarśino hi viditavyāpte' kṣityekadeśasiddhatve bhavatyānumāniko nirṇaya iti ||90 1/2||
children.translated_text: He shows that the <s>asādhāraṇa</s> serves as a reason in resolution—'existence in a part of the earth.' For one who perceives a specific smell and knows the <s>vyāpti</s>, an inferential resolution regarding the existence [of that entity] in some part of the earth is possible. // 90½ //

children.text:
dvau viruddhārthasambandhāvekadeśini saṃśaye heturityuktam /
tatrodāharaṇamāha---yatreti /
yatra hi na sākṣātkārijñānaviṣayo vāyu' arūpatvādityeka' sādhayati /
aparo 'pi sparśāt tadviparyayam /
tatrāsau viruddhāvyabhicāritā bhavatīti śākyairabhihitam /
tatra tulyabalobhayahetusannipātāt saṃśaya' /
dvayorapi sādhanayo' prasiddhāvayavatvāviśeṣāt /
arūpaṃ hyarūpisamavetamapratyakṣamiti kāṇādā manyante /
tathā ca vāyu' /
ato na pratyakṣa' /
karmasvarūpamapi rūpaikārthasamavāyāñcākṣuṣamācakṣate /
evaṃ sparśo 'pi vāyo' prasiddha eva /
prasiddhavyāptikaścāparokṣatvena /
atastulyabalatvam /
tataśca saṃśaya', viruddhayorekatropānapātāsambhavāt, samuñcayānupapatte', siddhe ca vastuni vikalpāsambhavāt bādhyabādhakabhāvasyāpi tulyakakṣyatvāt /
ato 'navasthayobhayasmin pariplavamāne bhavati saṃśaya' /
tādātmyāt /
tasya balābalaviśeṣe tvanumānavirodho varṇita eva /
yathā sarvajño 'stīti buddhavacanaṃ samyak taduktatvād kṣaṇabhaṅgādivākyavadityekenokte 'para' prabravīti buddho 'sarvajña iti madvacanaṃ samyak maduktatvāt yathā jyotiruṣṇamāpo dravā iti /
atra maduktatvamubhayorapi siddham /
buddhoktatā tu na na' prasiddhā, ato 'prasiddhāṅgakatvāt pūrva sādhanaṃ balavatā prasiddhāṅgakena bādhyate /
yattu viruddhāvyabhicārī saṃśaye heturiti śākyā vadanti /
na caikasya saṃśayahetutvam anyataraparicchedāt /
na ca samudāyābhiprāyamekavacanam /
tasya viruddhatvāvyabhicāripadānāspadatvāt /
sa hyaṃśābhyāṃ vyabhicāryeva /
dvau tu viruddhāvyabhicāriṇāviti vaktavyam /
na tvekavacanena /
yadi pratihetu
children.translated_text: It was said that two relations with contradictory meanings, residing in the same locus, are causes of doubt. He gives an example thereto—'where.' For where one person proves that wind is not an object of direct sensory knowledge, because it is formless, another also proves the opposite from touch. Therein, the <s>Śākyas</s> have stated that this is <s>viruddhāvyabhicāritā</s>. There, from the conjunction of two equally strong reasons, doubt arises, because both proofs have no difference in the establishment of their components. For the <s>Kāṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas) hold that what is formless, being inherent in formless [substances], is imperceptible. And such is wind. Therefore it is not perceptible. They also state that even action (<s>karman</s>) itself is visual, from its being co-inherent with form in a single substance. Similarly, the touch of wind is well-established. And one whose <s>vyāpti</s> is well-established [proves] through perceptibility. Therefore there is equal strength. And from that, doubt [arises], because the descent of two contradictory [reasons] in one [locus] is impossible, because combination is untenable, because in the case of an established entity an alternative is impossible, and because the relation of sublator and sublated is also on equal footing. Therefore, with both oscillating due to an infinite regress, doubt arises. [This is so] due to the identity [of the logical situation]. But when there is a difference in strength, the contradiction with inference has already been described. For example, when one says 'An omniscient being exists; this is a true <s>Buddha</s>-statement, because it was stated by him, like the statements about momentariness and so on,' another responds: 'The <s>Buddha</s> is not omniscient; my statement is correct because it was stated by me, just as "light is hot" and "water is liquid".' Here, 'being stated by me' is established for both. But 'being stated by the <s>Buddha</s>' is not established for us. Therefore, since the former proof has an unestablished component, it is sublated by the latter, which has all its components established. Now, the <s>Śākyas</s> say that the <s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s> is a cause of doubt as a single [fallacious reason]. But the causation of doubt by a single [reason] cannot be, since one of the pair is ascertained. Nor is the singular form intended to refer to the aggregate, since the aggregate has no basis for the terms 'contradictory' and 'non-deviating.' For the aggregate, through both its parts, is itself deviating. Rather, one should say 'two <s>viruddhāvyabhicārins</s>'—and not with the singular.
Some describe this as a different species; others, however,
[describe it as having] commonness through a part, or as a whole, as having non-co-presence [i.e., uncommonness].

children.text:
viruddhamarthamekaiko na vyabhicaratīti viruddhāvyabhicārītyucyate /
tadastu /
na tveka' saṃśaye heturityuktam /
ata eva vārtikakāreṇa dvau /
viruddhārthasambandhau saṃśayahetū iti dvivacanāntenaiva nāmnā saṃśayahetubhāvo darśita' /
ihāpi viruddhāvyabhicāritetyetāvadevoktam /
na tu viruddhāvyabhicārī saṃśayaheturiti /
tadatra yogyatayānayorviruddhāvyabhicāritenati vyākhyeyam /
dvau viruddhāvyabhicāriṇāviti yādaviti ||91 1/2||
children.translated_text: each one individually does not deviate from its contradictory meaning—hence it is called <s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s>. Let it be so. But it has been stated that a single one is not a cause of doubt. For precisely this reason, the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> [has used] the dual: 'two relations with contradictory meanings are causes of doubt'—showing their status as causes of doubt with the dual ending in the very name. Here too, only '<s>viruddhāvyabhicāritā</s>' has been stated, but not '<s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s> is a cause of doubt.' Therefore, this should be explained here as: 'of these two, through [their] <s>viruddhāvyabhicāritā</s>'—[thus] 'two <s>viruddhāvyabhicārins</s>,' as <s>Yādava</s> [explains]. // 91½ //

children.text:
imāṃ ca viruddhāvyabhicāritāṃ saṃśayahetuṃ sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇābhyāṃ jātyantarameke varṇayanti /
apare puna' samudāyasyāṃśābhyāṃ sādhāramapanikṣepam /
anye tu samastamidaṃ militamubhayaṃ naikatrāpyanugatamityananvayamasādhāraṇamevāsthiṣata
ityāha---keciditi /
atra ca pradeśāntare vārtikakṛtā sādhāraṇya evāsthā darśitā /

children.translated_text: As he says:
'And there is no difference of this from the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>;
for the aggregate is established in the domain of the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> through its parts.'

children.text:
iti /
na ca vācyaṃ dvayasyānanvayādasādhāraṇa evāyamiti /
yadi hyekena dvayaṃ prayujyeta tato bhavedapyevaṃ, pratyekamanvitau dṛṣṭau dvābhyāṃ prayuktau nānanvitāviti śakyate vaktum /
api cāsādhāraṇatve saṃśayahetubhāvo nopapadyeta /
tasya nirākṛtapūrvatvāt /
ata' sādhāraṇa evāyamiti /
vayaṃ tu jātyantarameva sādhīyo manyāmahe /
yathā hi na dvayamekena prayuktamiti nāsādhāraṇatvam /
evaṃ sādhāraṇatvamapi na syādeva /
kiṃ khalvatra sādhāraṇam /
ekaikasyaikaikena vyāptasyaikaikena prayogāt, aṃśata' sādhāraṇasya ca samudāyasyāprayogāt /
ata eva cātra sādhāraṇād bhedena pratihetu viruddhayo' saṃśayahetutvamuktam /
itarathā tenaiva gatatvānna pṛthagupādīyeta /
saṃśayajananaprakāro 'pi cātra bhidyata eva /
sādhāraṇo hyubhayadṛṣṭastu pratītimādadhāna' saṃśayaheturimau tvekaikaśyenobhayamupasthāpayantau saṃśayahetū iti vārtikakāreṇāpi sādhāraṇapade sthita ityuktam /
na hyu sādhāraṇa
eveti ||92 1/2||
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said 'since the pair has non-co-presence, this is <s>asādhāraṇa</s> alone.' For if a single [reason] were to employ the pair, then this might be so; but since each individually is observed as co-present, it cannot be said that the two, when employed, are non-co-present. Moreover, if it were <s>asādhāraṇa</s>, its status as a cause of doubt would not be tenable, since that has already been refuted. Therefore, it is <s>sādhāraṇa</s> alone. We, however, consider the classification as a different species to be more warranted. For just as the pair is not employed by a single [reason], so it would not be common either. What indeed is common here? Since each one individually is pervaded by each [respective <s>sādhya</s>] and is employed with each individually, and since the aggregate, which is partially common, is not employed [as a whole]. For precisely this reason, the causation of doubt has been stated here as being by counter-reasons with contradictory [meanings], distinct from the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>. Otherwise, since it would already be covered by that, it would not be separately mentioned. And the manner of generating doubt also differs here. For the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>, being seen in both, produces a cognition that is a cause of doubt; but these two, each individually presenting both, are causes of doubt—thus even the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> said 'established in the domain of the <s>sādhāraṇa</s>.' He did not say 'it is simply <s>sādhāraṇa</s>.' // 92½ //

Some describe this <s>viruddhāvyabhicāritā</s> as a cause of doubt that is a different species from the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> and <s>asādhāraṇa</s>. Others, however, classify it under the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> through the aggregate's parts. Yet others have adopted the position that this aggregate, being united, since both together do not co-occur even in one [locus], is uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>) as non-co-present—thus he says, 'some.' And the author of the <s>Vārttika</s>, in another context, has shown his preference for [classifying it under] the <s>sādhāraṇa</s> alone.

children.text: pratijñā yatra bādhyeta pūrvoktairyasya sādhanai' // Msv_5,4.93 //
children.translated_text: Where the thesis is sublated by the previously stated proofs—
the resolution should be made from the defeat of that [thesis], by the avoidance of sublation;

children.text: kvacit saṃśayahetū yau pratyekatvena lakṣitau // Msv_5,4.94 //
children.translated_text: the two that are recognized individually as causes of doubt somewhere—

children.text:
kathaṃ punarevañjātīyake viṣaye nirṇaya', ata āha---pratijñetinirṇayāntena /
pakṣabādhoktai' pratyakṣādibhi' pramāṇairyasya
sādhanavākyāvayavapratijñā bādhyate tatparājayenetarasya nirṇaya' kārya' /
yathehaiva tāvat udāharaṇe tvagindriyavyāpāreṇa vāyāvaparokṣamanubhūyamāne tenaivānubhavena parokṣatāpakṣo bādhyate /
na hi nastvagindriyabhuvastoyapratyakṣādvāyupratyakṣaṃ viśiṣyate /
na hīhānadhiṣṭhānaṃ sparśanamātramanubhayate /
api tu tadadhikaraṇaṃ dravyamapi /
na hi prabalena marutābhihanyamānasya jalaṃ vā śliṣyata' saṃvida viśiṣyate /
ato 'kṣasambandhaphalānusārāt pratyakṣo vāyuriti niścīyate /
kvaciñcāgamena viṣayāpahāro bhavati /
yathā śuci naraśira'kapālaṃ, prāṇyaṅgatvāt, śaṅkhaśuktiśakalavāditi pāśupatenokte 'nyo 'śucīti sādhayati, prāṇyudbhūtatvāduñcārādivaditi /
tatra pūrvapratijñāyā āgamena viṣayāpahārāduttareṇārthanirṇayo bhavati /
śucītaraviveke hyāgama eva śaraṇam /
tasmin paripanthini na śucitvānumānamātmānaṃ labhate /
smaranti hi---
"nāraṃ spṛṣṭavāsthi sasnehaṃ savāsā jalamāviśet" iti /
'rudro hi mahāvrataṃ cacāra sa etacchavaśīrṣamupadadhāre'ti tvarthavādamātraṃ na śavaśirodhāraṇavidhi' /
atra ca pratyakṣādīnyeva yathāsvamarthaṃ sādhayantīti sādhanapadenocyanta iti /
kathaṃ puna' pratyakṣādīnyeva pratijñābādhanāyotsahante /
teṣvapi sāmānyato darśanena bādhasya śaṅkyamānatvādata āha--- bādhavarjanāditi /
na tāvat teṣu bādho dṛśyate, kadācid bādhasambhāvanā tu na teṣāṃ prāmāṇyamutsārayīti ||93 1/2||
children.translated_text: How then does resolution [occur] in a subject of this kind? Hence he says—'thesis,' ending with 'resolution.' The thesis—that component of the proving statement—of the one whose [thesis] is sublated by the means of knowledge such as perception mentioned [earlier] in connection with the defeat of the thesis: from his defeat, the resolution in favor of the other should be made. For example, in this very illustration, when wind is directly experienced through the operation of the skin-organ, by that very experience the thesis of imperceptibility is sublated. For our perception of wind through the skin-organ does not differ from the perception of water. For here it is not merely unsupported touching that is experienced, but also the substance that is its substrate. For the cognition of one who is struck by a powerful wind or who is in contact with water does not differ [in directness]. Therefore, from conformity with the result of sense-contact, it is ascertained that wind is perceptual. And sometimes, the seizure of the domain [occurs] through scripture. For example, when a <s>Pāśupata</s> says: 'A human skull is pure, being a limb of a living being, like a conch-shell piece,' another proves it is impure: 'because it originates from a living being, like excrement and such.' There, since the domain of the first thesis is seized by scripture, the resolution is made by the latter. For in the discrimination of the pure and impure, scripture alone is the recourse. When it obstructs, the inference of purity does not obtain itself. For they remember: 'One should not enter water wearing clothes and with oily, unwashed bones.' But '<s>Rudra</s> practiced the great vow, and he took up the skull'—this is merely an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage), not an injunction to carry a skull. And here, perception and the other [means of knowledge] themselves, each establishing its own respective object, are referred to by the word 'proof.' But how do perception and the other [means] alone have the capacity to sublate the thesis? Since in them too, sublation through general reasoning is apprehended? Hence he says—'by the avoidance of sublation.' For no sublation is seen in them to begin with; and the mere possibility of sublation at some point does not dislodge their validity. // 93½ //

children.text:
atra bhikṣuṇā 'pakṣadharmastadaṃśena vyāpto heturityekavacanena vivakṣitaikasaṅkhya eka eva heturiti darśitam /
ata eva viruddhāvyabhicāriṇorna hetatvamanekatvāt tayoriti /
na caitat ghaṭate /
na hi pratihetu viruddhayo
children.translated_text: Here, the Buddhist has stated with the singular 'a reason pervaded, through a part of the property of the thesis, which is a property of the thesis' that the reason is singularly intended—there is just one reason. And for precisely this reason, the <s>viruddhāvyabhicārins</s> are not reasons, because they are multiple. But this does not hold. For the counter-reasons with contradictory [meanings]—
In combination, resolution is [made] from those two, like [the combination of] tallness and crow-possession;
individually or in combination, the two indicators are non-contradictory.
Therefore, two separate reasons with contradictory meanings have been shown here;
they describe contradiction as sixfold, or fourfold, or even as single.

children.text:
ranekatvaṃ saṃśayahetutve hetu', api tarhiparasparaviruddhārthopaplāvakatvameva /
viruddhau hi dvābhyāṃ dvāvarthāvekatropaplāvitāviti tatra saṃśerate /
na tu hetvanekatvāt /
saṃśayahetvorapi pratyekamavagatayorubhayasamāveśādeva kvacinnirṇayo dṛṣṭa' /
yathā- ūrdhvatākākavattvayo' /
kevalā hyūrdhvatā sthāṇupuruṣasādhāraṇī nānyataranirṇayāya prabhavati /
kākanilayanasahakṛtā tu saivana sthāṇurayamiti niścāyayati /
tadatraikasyaiva saṃśayahetutvaṃ dvābhyāmeva tu nirṇaya ityaprayojakaṃ saṃśayahetutve dvitvaṃ, viruddhānekasādhyatvameva saṃśayahetu' /
yathā khalveka eva sādhārama' sapakṣavipakṣayorvartamāna' saṃśayaheturbhavati /
evaṃ viruddhārthasyāpi hetudvayasyāṃśābhyāmubhayavṛttireva saṃśaye kāraṇamiti na taddvitvena hetutvanirākaraṇaṃ yuktamityāha---kvaciditi /
nanu yuktaṃ
tāvadūrdhvatayā sthāṇupuruṣasandeho bhavatīti, kākavattāmātreṇa na saṃśayo dṛṣṭapūrva' /
satyam /
yastu kākavattāmātreṇa sthāṇuṃ siṣādhayiṣati tasyāsau kevalā saṃśayahetu', ūrdhvatāsanāthā tu nirṇāyiketyetāvadeva vivakṣitamityadoṣa iti /
api ca avirodhino' pratyekaṃ saṃhatayorapi kvacidarthe sādhye hetubhāvo dṛśyate /
yathaikasminneva śābdasya jñānasyānumātve 'nvayavyatirekajatvapratyakṣānyapramāṇatvayo', śakyate hi tābhyāmaikaikaśyena samastābhyāṃ cānumānatvaṃ sādhayitum /
dvitve ca hetvābhāsatvakāraṇe naikasmin sādhye 'nekahetava' prayujyeran /
prayoktārastvekameva sādhyaṃ kiñcānyaditaśceti nānāsādhanai' sādhayanto dṛśyante /
children.translated_text: But proponents are seen to prove one and the same probandum from various means [of proof] — 'such-and-such from this, and something else from that.'

children.text: tasmād virodhanibandhana evapa saṃśaya', na tu nānātvanibandhana ityabhiprāyeṇāha--- pratyekamiti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, doubt is grounded in contradiction alone, not in mere plurality — with this intention he says 'pratyekam.'
Previously, it was stated that when two individually doubt-producing [reasons] are combined, they become the cause of determination.

children.text: ga atra tu pratyekaṃ gamakāvapi saṃhatau ca gamakāviti pratipāditamiti ||95||
children.translated_text: But here it has been demonstrated that [two reasons] are individually indicative and also indicative when combined. (95)

The plurality [of the reason] is a cause of doubt — but then, is it rather the capacity to overflow with mutually contradictory meanings? For two meanings that are mutually contradictory are overflowed [i.e., suggested] by two [reasons] in one locus — and thus doubt arises therein. But not because of the plurality of the reasons. Even when two [properties] that are individually causes of doubt are combined, a determination is seen to arise in some cases. For example, uprightness and crow-perching: uprightness alone, being common to both a post and a person, is unable to determine either one. But that same [uprightness], when combined with a crow's roosting, leads to the determination 'this is not a post.' Thus here, the cause of doubt is one and the same, while the determination is from the two [combined]. Hence, duality in the causation of doubt is pointless — it is the having mutually contradictory things to be proved that is the cause of doubt. Just as indeed a single [property] that is common [to both] the <s>sapakṣa</s> (homologue) and the <s>vipakṣa</s> (heterologue), being present in both, becomes a cause of doubt — similarly, even for a pair of reasons for contradictory conclusions, it is the presence in both [sides] through their respective aspects that is the cause of doubt — hence the negation of reason-hood on the ground of their duality is not justified — he says 'kvacit.' Objection: It is proper that doubt arises about a post or a person from uprightness, but doubt has never been observed from crow-perching alone. True. But for one who wishes to prove a post from crow-perching alone, that [crow-perching] alone would be a cause of doubt; but when supported by uprightness, it becomes determinative — only this much is intended, so there is no fault. Moreover, even for non-contradictory [reasons], individually and in combination, reason-hood is seen for some probandum. For instance, both 'being-born-from-positive-and-negative-concomitance' and 'not-being-another-pramāṇa-than-perception' [can serve] for the same probandum of [proving] a certain cognition to be inferential. For it is possible to prove inference-hood by each one individually and by both together. And if duality were a cause of being a pseudo-reason, then multiple reasons could not be employed for a single probandum.

children.text:
tasmād viruddhārthāveva bhinnau saṃśayahetutvena darśanīyau /
yathāsmābhiruktaṃ na tu bhinnatāmātreṇetyāha---tasmāditi /
vyākhyātastriprakāro
children.translated_text: Therefore, only two [reasons] with contradictory conclusions should be shown as causes of doubt — as we have stated, not merely by virtue of their being separate. Hence he says 'tasmāt.' The threefold [contradictory reason] has been explained.
When the meaning of a thesis [established] by verbal testimony or by implication is to be defeated by a reason,
In the proof of eternality [of sound], the contradiction with 'being-produced' constitutes <s>dharma</s>-defeat and hence contradiction. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.97)
But when the defeat of a specific property occurs in the following manner,
The word-form would be meaningful prior to the ascertainment of the [word-meaning] relation. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.98)

children.text:
'pisaṃśayahetu' viparītaprakārān pratijānāti---ṣoḍhā viruddhatāmāhuriti /
dharmadharmisvarūpasvaviśeṣobhayasvarūpasvaviśeṣai' ṣaṭprakārāṃ viruddhatāmeke bruvata ityartha' /
anye tūbhayavirothayo' pratyekapakṣānatirekāt cāturvidhyaṃ pratipannā ityāha--- caturdhā
veti /
vayaṃ tu iṣṭavighātamātreṇaikameva prakāraṃ saṅgirāmaha ityāha--- ekadhāpi veti /
pūrvoktapakṣapakṣadvayanivṛttāvapi vā śabda' /
api vā śeṣabhājāṃ syāditi pakṣabādha eva viruddhatve kāraṇaṃ kimavāntarabhedopanyāseneti /
triṣvapi ca prakāreṣu śrutyarthopāttasya pratijñātārthasya bādhāyāṃ viruddhatāmāhurityāha--- śrutyārthoktasyeti /
dharmadharmyubhayasvarūpaṃ śrutyuktaṃ, tadviśeṣāstu prāyeṇārthoktā' /
te ca svarūpasvaviśeṣā' pratijñārthaśabdenopādīyante /
sarve hi te vakturabhipretā' /
na tu dharmādiviśeṣā' sākṣāt pratijñāyāmantargatā' /
tadasmin pratijñārthe hetunā bādhyamāne hetorviruddhatā bhavatīti /
tatpunaridaṃ vipratiṣiddhamiva manayāmahe /
kathaṃ hi pratijñārthe hetunā bādhyamāne heturviruddho bhavati /
sa hi pratijñārthaṃ pratijñārthena bādhyate yadviruddho bhavet prasiddhatvādasya /
prasiddhaṃ hi ghaṭasya kṛtakatvaṃ, na tadaprasiddhayā nityatayā bādhituṃ śakyam /
children.translated_text: For the producedness of a pot is well-established; it cannot be defeated by an unestablished eternality.
Therefore, this [reason] should simply be called a 'defeater.'

children.text: vārtikakṛtā tu paraprasiddhimātreṇa viruddha ityuktāmiti veditavyamiti /
children.translated_text: But it should be understood that the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> used the term 'contradictory' merely in the sense of being the opposite of what the opponent accepts.
He first illustrates the contradiction through the defeat of the essential nature of the <s>dharma</s> (property) — 'nityatve.' (97)

He announces the types of the contradictory [reason], the opposite of the doubt-causing [reason] — 'six-fold contradiction is declared.' Some say the contradiction is six-fold through the [defeat of the] essential nature and specific form of each of the property, property-bearer, and both — this is the meaning. Others, recognizing that the defeat of both does not exceed the individual cases, accept a four-fold [classification] — he says 'caturdhā va.' We, however, accept only one type, namely the mere obstruction of what is desired — he says 'ekadhā api va.' The word 'vā' (or) serves to negate even the preceding two positions. Or 'vā' may serve to include the remainder — hence [the point is that] defeat of the thesis alone is the cause of contradiction; what use is the enumeration of sub-divisions? And in all three views, when the meaning of the thesis — obtained through verbal testimony or by implication — is defeated, there is contradiction — he says 'śrutyārthoktasya.' The essential nature of the property, property-bearer, and both is stated in verbal testimony; but their specific forms are mostly implicitly understood. And those essential natures and specific forms are included by the term 'thesis-meaning.' For all of those are intended by the speaker. But the specific forms of the property and so forth are not directly contained in the thesis. So when this thesis-meaning is defeated by a reason, the reason [exhibits] contradiction. But we consider this seemingly self-contradictory: How can a reason be contradictory when it defeats the thesis-meaning? For [the reason] defeats the thesis-meaning by [demonstrating] the thesis-meaning [to be false] — it would be contradictory only because it [the thesis-meaning] is well-established.

children.text:
dharmaviśeṣabādhastvevaṃ prayukte bhavatītyāha---bādhaiti /
tameva prayogaṃ darśayati--- arthavaditi pādatrayeṇa /
svarūpābhidhānavādino hyāhu'--- gaurayamiti śabdākāraviśiṣṭor'tho 'vagamyate /
na ca viśeṣaṇamanabhidhāya viśiṣṭo 'bhidhātuṃ śakyata iti svarūpameva tāvadādau śabdo
children.translated_text: The defeat of the specific property occurs when formulated thus — he says 'bādha.' He shows that very formulation — 'arthavat' with the three quarters [of the verse]. For the proponents of denotation-by-form say: From [the expression] 'this is a cow,' the meaning that is qualified by word-form is understood. And since the qualified cannot be denoted without denoting the qualifier, the word first denotes its own form.
Because of having inflectional endings, and because of [the word's relation] being later, and when one relies [on the view that] by its own form —
The connection of the word with a meaning other than its own form is seen subsequently. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.99)
Therefore, even prior to the relation [being established], there would be meaningful-ness of a non-own-form meaning;
Due to being the cause of the 'here'-cognition, it is distinguished from substance and such. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.100)
Inherence, like [the cognition] 'this pot is here' — such a connection —

children.text:
'bhidhatte tato viśiṣṭam /
api cārthaśabdo vyabhicarati, ajñātasambandhasya tadanavagate' /
svarūpaṃ tu na kadācid vyabhicarati sambandhāvadhāraṇātprāgapi tadavagamāt, avyabhicārī ca śabdārtha iti yuktam /
ata' svarūpaṃ tāvadavaśyābhidheyaṃ śabdānāṃ, tadabhidhottarakālaṃ tu viśiṣṭābhidhānamapi bhavatu nāmeti /
evaṃ prasādhyānte prayogamāhu'--- śabdasvarūpaṃ sambandhāvadhāraṇāt prāgarthavad vibhaktisambandhāt, agṛhītasambandho 'pi hi svādivibhaktiyuktān śabdānavagacchati /
yadā ca vibhaktiyoga' tadārthavattvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ yathā sambandhagrahaṇāt paścāditi /
kathaṃ punarevaṃ prayujyamāne dharmaviśeṣabādho bhavatyata āha--- svarūpeṇeti cāśrita iti /
yadā hi svarūpeṇārthanārthavattvaṃ prathamamāśrityārthavattāmātraviśiṣṭaṃ sādhyate, tadārthādidamavagamyate--- svarūpārthavattvamasya siṣādhayiṣitamiti /
evaṃ ca bhavatyarthākṣiptasya dharmaviśeṣasya bādha iti /
kathaṃ puna' svarūpeṇeti cāśrite dharmaviśeṣo bādhyate /
ata āha--- asvarūpeti /
vibhaktimattvaṃ hi svarūpātirekeṇārthāntareṇārthavattvamavinābhāvabalena śabdasyāvagamayati,
sambandhagrahaṇātpaścādarthāntarasya darśāt /
ato vyāptibalena tadeva vibhaktimattayā sādhyate /
ator'thavattāyā viśeṣaṃ svasvarūpārthavattvaṃ heturayaṃ viruṇaddhīti bhavati dharmaviśeṣabādha iti ||99 1/2||
children.translated_text: It denotes, and then the qualified. Moreover, the word 'artha' (meaning) deviates [from its proper reference] for one whose relation [with meaning] is unknown — since there is no understanding of that [meaning] [when the relation is unknown]. But the own-form never deviates, because it is understood even prior to the ascertainment of the relation — and what does not deviate is the proper word-meaning. Therefore, the own-form is necessarily the denotation of words; but after denoting that, let there also be denotation of the qualified. Having argued thus, they state the formulation: 'The own-form of the word is meaningful prior to the ascertainment of the relation, because of the association with inflectional endings. For even one whose relation [with external meaning] has not been grasped understands words equipped with inflections such as the nominative.' And when the association with inflection is present, meaningfulness is seen — as [it is seen] after the grasping of the relation. How, then, when it is formulated thus, does defeat of the specific property occur? Hence he says 'svarūpeṇeti cāśrite.' For when meaningfulness qualified merely by own-form-meaningfulness is first posited on the basis of [the word's relation with meaning through] its own form, then it is implicitly understood: 'he wishes to prove that it is meaningful by [virtue of] its own form.' And thus there occurs the defeat of the implicitly understood specific property. But how is the specific property defeated when 'by its own form' is relied upon? Hence he says 'asvarūpa.' For the possession of inflectional endings causes one to understand, through the force of invariable concomitance, that the word has a meaningfulness through something other than [its own] form — an additional entity [i.e., external meaning] — since a different [kind of] meaning is seen after the grasping of the relation. Hence, by the force of pervasion, it is that very [meaningfulness through an external object] that is proved by the possession of inflectional endings. Therefore, this reason obstructs the specific form of meaningfulness — namely, meaningfulness-by-own-form — and thus there is defeat of the specific property. (99½)
He gives an example of the defeat of the essential nature of the property-bearer — 'ihapratyaya.'

children.text: yadā hisamavāyadharmiṇaṃ kṛtvā tasya dravyādivyatireka' sādhyate, ihapratyahetutvaṃ ca heturucyate ihāyaṃ ghaṭa iti, saṃyogo dṛṣṭānta', tadā dharmisvarūpabādha ityabhiprāya' ||100||
children.translated_text: The intention is: When inherence is made the property-bearer and its difference from substance and the like is to be proved, with 'being the cause of the here-cognition' stated as the reason — as in 'this pot is here' — and conjunction [given] as the example, then there is defeat of the essential nature of the property-bearer. (100)
Here too, the non-inherence [nature] of conjunction is likewise established. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.101)
Therefore, from the reversal of the essential nature of the property-bearer, there is contradiction.
And the oneness of inherence, posited as having the nature of existence, — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.102)
In that case, from the plurality [being established] like conjunction, there is contradiction of the specific property [of inherence].

children.text: nityamātmāstitā kaiścid yadā sautrāntikaṃ prati // Msv_5,4.103 //
children.translated_text: When the eternality and existence of the self is [to be proved] by someone against a <s>Sautrāntika</s> [Buddhist], — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.103)
From the absence of parts, like space — there is defeat of both [property and property-bearer].
When this is to be proved — that there is defeat of the specific [form] of both — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.104)
The other-directedness of the eye and such, being an aggregate, like a bed and the like —
When other-directedness of the aggregate is [the thesis regarding] a bed, and the reason is pervaded by [the property of] being material — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.105)

children.text:
kathaṃ punaratrodāharaṇe dharmisvarūpabādha', ata āha--- atrāpīti /
atrāpyudāharaṇe dharmisvarūpasya samavāyātmano vaiparītyāpādanāddhetorviruddhatā bhavati /
ihapratyayahetutvaṃ hyasamavāyātmana eva dṛṣṭamiti tādrūpyaṃ virundhyāditi dharmisvarūpabādha iti ||101 1/2||
children.translated_text: But how is there defeat of the essential nature of the property-bearer in this example? Hence he says 'atrāpi.' In this example too, from making the essential nature of the property-bearer — namely, [its being of] the nature of inherence — undergo reversal, there is contradiction of the reason. For 'being the cause of the here-cognition' is seen only for what is of the nature of non-inherence — hence it would obstruct that [inherence] form, and so there is defeat of the essential nature of the property-bearer. (101½)

children.text:
asminneva ca dharmiviśeṣabādho 'pi darśayitavya ityāha---yañceti /
samavāyo hi sattāsāmānyavadekarūpa iti kāṇādā manyante /
so 'pyasya viśeṣa' saṃyogavadbhedāpatterbādhyata iti bhavati dharmiviśeṣaviruddho heturiti ||102 1/2||
children.translated_text: In this very [case], the defeat of the specific property-bearer should also be shown — he says 'yañca.' For the <s>Kāṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣikas) hold that inherence is one [i.e., unitary], having the nature of the universal 'existence' (<s>sattā</s>). That specific form of it [i.e., its oneness] is also defeated, because plurality would follow as with conjunction — hence the reason is contradictory with respect to the specific property-bearer. (102½)

children.text:
ubhayasvarūpabādhāyāmudāharaṇamāha---nityamātmāstiteti /
yadā kaścit sautrāntikaṃ pratyevaṃ sādhayati--- ātmā nitya' niravayatvāt vyomavaditi, tadā dharmadharmidvayasya bādhanaṃ bhavati /
sautrāntikasya hyavayavābhāvo vyomnyabhāvenaiva sambaddho 'bhimata ityātmano 'pi tadvadabhāvaṃ gamayeta, āvaraṇābhāvamātraṃ hi nabha', na punastattvāntaramiti bauddhā manyante /
ato 'navayavatvādātmana' svarūpasya taddharmasya ca nityatvasya bādhādubhayabādha iti ||103 1/2||
children.translated_text: He gives an example of the defeat of the essential nature of both [property and property-bearer] — 'nityam ātmāstitā.' When someone proves against a <s>Sautrāntika</s> thus: 'The self is eternal, because of the absence of parts, like space' — then there is defeat of both the property and the property-bearer. For in the <s>Sautrāntika</s>'s view, the absence of parts is accepted as connected with the non-existence of space itself — hence it would lead to the non-existence of the self too in the same way. For the Buddhists hold that space is merely the absence of obstruction, not a separate reality. Hence, from the defeat of the essential nature of the self [as a property-bearer] and the eternality [as a property] of its property — there is defeat of both. (103½)

children.text:
ubhayaviśeṣabādhastvevaṃ sādhyamāne bhavatītyāha---tadeti /
yadā hi parārthāścakṣurādaya' saṅghātatvāt śayanādivaditi sādhyate, tadobhayaviśeṣabādha ityartha' /
kathaṃ punaratrobhayaviśeṣabādha', ata āha--- śayana iti /
śayanīye
children.translated_text: But the defeat of the specific [form] of both occurs when the proof is formulated thus — he says 'tat.' When it is proved that the eye and such are other-directed, being an aggregate, like a bed and the like — then there is defeat of the specific [form] of both — this is the meaning. But how is there defeat of the specific [form] of both here? Hence he says 'śayane.' In the bed —
The other-directedness toward the self is unestablished — hence [there is] defeat.
When other-directedness of the non-aggregate is [also to follow] —
Seen — then aggregate-hood too [follows]. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.4.106)
And the non-ego-derived-ness of the eye and such would follow.

children.text:
hikhaṭvādau mahābhūtasaṃhataśarīrapārārthyena saṅghātatvāditi heturvyāpto dṛṣṭa iti saṃhatapārārthyameva sādhayet /
ātmānaṃ ca prati pārārthyaṃ sādhayitumabhimatam, tanna sidhyet /
so 'yaṃ tāvat pārārthyasya dharmasya yo viśeṣo 'bhimata ātmapārārthyaṃ sa tāvad bādhyate /
cakṣurāderapi dharmiṇo yo viśeṣa āhaṅkārikatvaṃ nāma so 'pyanenaiva hetunā bādhyate /
saṃhatātmakatvaṃ hi śayanādāvanāhaṅkārikatvena vyāptaṃ dṛṣṭam, bhautikā hi te, atastannidarśanena cakṣurādayo 'pi bhautikā bhaveyu' /
āhaṅkārikāṇīndriyāṇīti kāpilā' saṅgirante, teṣāṃ cāyaṃ prayoga' /
tadayamartha'--- saṃhatapārārthyabhautikatvābhyāṃ vyāpto heturyasmin śayane tatrātmapārārthyamasiddhamiti dharmaviśeṣabādhanaṃ tāvad bhavati /
children.translated_text: The meaning is thus: First, the defeat of the specific property occurs — since the reason pervaded by the other-directedness-of-the-aggregate and by materiality, in the bed [as an example], establishes that the other-directedness-toward-the-self is unproved.

children.text: dharmiviśeṣabādho 'pi bhautikavayāptyā sūtrito 'nantarameva vivariṣyata iti na kevalamātmapārārthyaṃ na sidhyati, asaṃhatarūpātmapārārthye ceṣṭe vyāptibalenātmano 'pi saṃhatatā prāpnotītyāha--- asaṃhateti /
children.translated_text: The contradiction of the specific feature of the <s>dharmin</s> too, having been stated through the <s>vyāpti</s> with elemental [constitution], will be explained immediately after. Thus, not only does the purpose for the self fail to be established — when the purpose for an uncombined self is intended, through the force of <s>vyāpti</s>, combination of the self too would follow — thus he says 'asaṃhata' etc.
By this reason, the purpose for a self of uncombined nature is not established;
on the contrary, the self would come to have combination. // 106 //

In a bed and such, the reason 'being an aggregate' is seen pervaded by the other-directedness of an aggregate [made] of the great elements and of a material body — hence it would prove only the other-directedness of the aggregate. But the other-directedness toward the self is what is intended to be proved — and that would not be established. So first, the specific form of the property — namely, the other-directedness toward the self — is defeated. And the specific form of the property-bearer, the eye and such — namely, [their nature as] ego-derived (<s>āhaṅkārika</s>) — is also defeated by this very reason. For aggregate-hood is seen pervaded by non-ego-derived-ness in beds and such, since those are material. Hence, by using that [bed] as an example, the eye and such too would become material. The <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> (<s>Kāpilas</s>) maintain that the sense organs are ego-derived (<s>āhaṅkārika</s>), and this formulation is theirs.
He elaborates the contradiction of the specific feature of the <s>dharmin</s> — 'anāhaṅkārikatvam' (non-egoistic nature) etc. And this is already explained. // 106 1/2 //

children.text:
evaṃ tāvad jñātasambandhapadavyāvartanīyo viruddha' prapañcita' /
idānīṃ tadvyāvartyā eva dṛṣṭāntābhāsā darśayitavyā' /
tairhi nānumānāṅgasambandho jñāpayituṃ śakyate /
ataste 'pi jñātasambandhapadenaiva vyāvartyante /
idaṃ cāsmābhi' prāgevoktam /

children.translated_text: Elsewhere too it is said:
"'By the expression 'one whose relation is known,' three defects beginning with 'indeterminate'
of the reason and the example have been excluded by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>."

Thus far, the contradicted [reasons], which are to be excluded by the phrase 'one whose relation is known,' have been elaborated. Now the fallacious examples (<s>dṛṣṭāntābhāsas</s>) to be excluded by that very [phrase] must be shown. For through them, the relation that is a component of inference cannot be made known. Therefore they too are excluded by the very phrase 'one whose relation is known.' And this has been said by us already.
The <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of one part of the indicator is stated as what is to be indicated. // Msv_5,4.107 //
The example is presented as what demonstrates the similarity and dissimilarity with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved);
there, the mention of the <s>sādhya</s> is intended for the purpose of [illustrating] the <s>hetu</s> (reason). // Msv_5,4.108 //
The property that is being indicated is the <s>vyāpya</s> (pervaded), and the other is considered the <s>vyāpaka</s> (pervader);
that with whose occurrence there is priority — this is the definition of the indicated (<s>uddeśya</s>). // Msv_5,4.109 //
Its occurrence and the word 'eva' (alone/indeed) would be the definition of the <s>upādeya</s> (what is to be taken up).

children.text:
iti /
atastannirākaraṇārthaṃ dṛṣṭāntavacanameva tāvadavatārayati---gamakasyeti /
vyāptipradarśanāya dvividho dṛṣṭāntastāvad sādhanavākye darśayitavya' /
sādhya' pakṣa' tatsādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ yo dṛṣṭānta' sa pratipādyata ityartha' ||107 1/2||
children.translated_text: Therefore, to refute those [fallacious examples], he first introduces the statement about the example — 'gamakasya' etc. To demonstrate <s>vyāpti</s>, two kinds of examples are to be shown in the proof-statement. The example that is [presented] through similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>) with the <s>sādhya</s> (thesis) is being expounded — this is the meaning. // 107 1/2 //

children.text:
tatra sādharyadṛṣṭāntaprakāramāha---tatreti /
asyārtha'--- udāharaṇasādharmyālliṅgasya prasādhakatvavacanaṃ hetu' yadāhu'---
"udāharaṇasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanaṃ hetu'" iti /
sādhyasya prajñāpanavacanamiti yāvat /
tasya cārtho liṅgameva /
tañcoddiśya sādhyopādānaṃ sādharmyadṛṣṭānta iṣyate /
yo yo dhūmavān sa so 'gnimāniti yāvaditi /
kimevamupādīyamāne sidhyatyata āha--- uddeśya iti /
ukataṃ vyāptipradarśanāya dṛṣṭāntavacanamiti /
evaṃ copādīyamāna uddeśyo dhūmādirvyāptatayā kathito bhavati, itaraścopādeyo 'gnyādirvyāpakatvaṃ bhavatītyuktam ||108 1/2||
children.translated_text: There, he states the form of the <s>sādharmya</s> (positive) example — 'tatra' etc. Its meaning: The statement of the proving capacity of the inferential mark through similarity with the illustration is the reason — as they say: 'The reason is what proves the <s>sādhya</s> through similarity with the illustration.' That is, the pronouncement-statement of the <s>sādhya</s>. And its meaning is the inferential mark itself. And the mention of the <s>sādhya</s> with reference to that is accepted as the <s>sādharmya</s> (positive) example — meaning: 'whatever has smoke, that has fire.' What is accomplished by this manner of presentation? — therefore he says 'uddeśya' etc. It has been said that the statement of the example is for demonstrating <s>vyāpti</s>. And when presented thus, the indicated — smoke etc. — is stated as pervaded, and the other, the taken-up — fire etc. — acquires the status of being the pervader — thus it is said. // 108 1/2 //

children.text:
kīdṛśaṃ tu tayo' svarūpamata āha---yadvṛtteti /
yadvṛttatadvṛttābhyāṃ yattatpariniṣpannānāṃ yo ya ityādiśabdānāmupādānam, tadayamartho bhavati /
yadyad yadvṛttena saṃyuktaṃ prathamaṃ prayujyate pradhānaṃ ca taduddeśyaṃ, tattadvṛttuyaktaṃ ca paścāt prayujyamānaṃ sa so 'gnimāneveti caivakāreṇa yuktaṃ tadupādeyam /
sarveṣveva ca grahavrīhyādisaṃmārgāvaghātādiṣūddeśyopādeyeṣvayameva viveka iti veditavyamiti ||109 1/2||
children.translated_text: What then is the nature of these two? — therefore he says 'yadvṛtta' etc. The use of words like 'whatever' and 'that' formed from 'yadvṛtta-tadvṛtta' has this meaning: whatever is employed first, connected with the correlative 'whichever,' being primary — that is the <s>uddeśya</s> (indicated); and whatever is connected with the corresponding correlative, employed afterwards — 'that has fire' — connected with the particle 'eva' — that is the <s>upādeya</s> (taken-up). And this very discrimination between <s>uddeśya</s> and <s>upādeya</s> should be understood in all cases of threshing rice etc. and similar operations. // 109 1/2 //

children.text: vadatyarthaṃ svaśaktyā ca śabdo vaktranapekṣayā // Msv_5,4.110 //
children.translated_text: A word expresses meaning by its own capacity, independently of the speaker. // Msv_5,4.110 //
The <s>sādhya-hetu</s> (provable-reason) relationship of things follows the capacity of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion),
and when, through ignorance, the speaker, with the intention of showing mere co-existence, // Msv_5,4.111 //

children.text: viparyayeṇa vā hetau na pyāptatvaṃ vivakṣati /
children.translated_text: or by the reverse apprehension, does not intend the pervaded-ness of the reason,

children.text: vivakṣannapi vā śabdaṃ tadyogaṃ na vaded yadi // Msv_5,4.112 //
children.translated_text: or even when intending it, if he does not utter the word expressing that connection — // Msv_5,4.112 //

children.text: ghaṭe kṛtakanāśitve nāśi vyāptaṃ kṛtena vā /
children.translated_text: in a pot, 'being produced' and 'destructibility' — is 'destructible' pervaded by 'produced' or not?

children.text: na tadeṣṭasya hetutvaṃ syādaniṣṭasya caiva tat // Msv_5,4.113 //
children.translated_text: then the desired reason-hood would not be established, and the undesired would be established instead. // Msv_5,4.113 //

children.text: kiṃ punarevaṃ prayoganiyame prayojanam, vivakṣāparatantrā hi śabdā', te yathā tathā vā prayuktā yathābhiprāyaṃ vartiṣyanta eva /
children.translated_text: But what is the purpose of this rule of formulation? For words depend on the speaker's intention, and however they are used, they will function according to the intention.
Therefore he says 'vadati' etc.

children.text: na vaktrabhiprāyaparatantrā' śabdā', svābhāvikyaiva tu śaktyā kecideva kvacidevārthe vartante, ato na vivakṣānusāreṇeṣṭasiddhirbhavatīti vācya eva dṛṣṭāntavacanavinyāsaprakāra iti ||110||
children.translated_text: Words do not depend on the speaker's intention; rather, by their inherent natural capacity, certain words function only regarding certain meanings — therefore, the desired result is not achieved merely by following one's intention, and hence the manner of formulation of the example-statement must indeed be specified. // 110 //

children.text:
yadi tarhi svatantrā' śabdā' atathāsthite 'pyarthe śabdānusāriṇīṣṭasiddhirbhavedata āha---sādhyahetutvamiti /
ayamabhiprāya'---- nārthaśakti' śabdaśaktimanurudhya pravartate, na ca śabdaśaktirarthaśaktim, ato na yatā vaktrabhipretārthānusāriṇī śabdaśakti', evaṃ na śabdānusāriṇyarthavyavastheti, arthādīnāṃ kṛtakatvānityatvādīnāṃ vyāptiśaktyanurodhādeva sādhyahetubhāvo bhavati na śabdānurodhāditi ||110 1/2||
children.translated_text: If words are indeed independent, then even when the state of affairs is otherwise, the desired result would follow the words — therefore he says 'sādhyahetutvam' etc. The intention is: the capacity of things does not follow the capacity of words, nor does the capacity of words follow the capacity of things. Therefore, just as the capacity of words does not follow the meaning intended by the speaker, so too the arrangement of things does not follow words. Hence the <s>sādhya-hetu</s> relationship of things like 'being produced' and 'impermanence' follows the capacity of <s>vyāpti</s> alone, not the following of words. // 110 1/2 //

children.text:
vaktranapekṣayā svaśaktyaiva śabder'thamācakṣāṇe yattāvadāpadyate tad darśayati---tatrājñānāditi sārdhadvayena /
yadā hi dṛṣṭānta vaktumanabhijño vaktā sādhyahetvo' sahabhāvamātraṃ vivakṣati /
yathā--- śabdo 'nitya' kṛtakatvāditi prayoge,yathā ghaṭe kṛtakatvanāśitve sta iti /
viparītāvagraheṇa vā na hetorvyāpyatāṃ vivakṣati /
satyāmapi vivakṣāyāṃ kutaścid bhramanimittāt na vyāptiyogyaṃ śabdaṃ vadati /
sahabāvamātrameva tu pūrvavad vadet, viparītaṃ vā bhrānta' yatā nāsitā kṛtakatvena vyāpteti, tadā tāvanna kevalamiṣṭaṃ na sidhyati aniṣṭameva tu vyāptiviparyayādāpadyate /
iṣṭasya
children.translated_text: He shows what happens when words express meaning by their own capacity independently of the speaker — 'tatrājñānād' etc. with two and a half [verses]. Its meaning: When indeed a speaker ignorant of how to state an example intends to show mere co-existence of the <s>sādhya</s> and <s>hetu</s> — for example, in the formulation 'sound is impermanent because of being produced,' [he says] 'just as in a pot there is being-produced and destructibility.' Or with reverse apprehension, he does not intend the pervadedness of the reason. Even when he does intend it, due to some cause of confusion, he does not utter the word appropriate for <s>vyāpti</s>. He states mere co-existence as before, or, being confused, states the reverse: 'destructibility is pervaded by being-produced.' Then not only is the desired not established, but the undesired itself results from the reversal of <s>vyāpti</s>. Of the desired—
Therefore, the reason accepted as such must be stated in the form of <s>vyāpyatva</s> (being pervaded).

children.text: yadā samyak prayukte 'pi vākyer'tho na tathā bhavet // Msv_5,4.114 //
children.translated_text: When even with a properly formulated statement, the meaning does not hold thus — // Msv_5,4.114 //
because in ultimate reality it is devoid of the <s>vyāpti</s> of <s>sādhya</s>, <s>hetu</s>, or both —
'Sound is eternal because of being formless, like <s>karman</s> (action), like atoms.' // Msv_5,4.115 //
'Like a pot, like space' — and for one who denies its existence,
even when the <s>dharmin</s> (subject) is established, there would be the nature of a fallacious example. // Msv_5,4.116 //
Even if space exists, and even though it is mentioned as possessing both [properties],
upon consideration of action (<s>karman</s>) and such, there is no <s>vyāpti</s> of the reason — hence it is to be rejected. // Msv_5,4.117 //

children.text:
kṛtakatvasya hetutvaṃ na syāt /
aniṣṭasyaiva tu nāśitvasya bhavedityevañjātīyakāniṣṭaprayoganivāraṇāya yukto dṛṣṭāntaprayoganiyama iti /
etadevopasaṃharati---tasmāditi /
hetutvasaṃmata' kṛtakatvādivyāpyatvarūpeṇa vācya ityartha' ||113 1/2||
children.translated_text: The reason-hood of 'being produced' would not be established. But of the undesired — 'destructibility' — it would be. For the prevention of such undesirable formulations, the rule regarding the employment of the example is fitting. He summarizes this very point — 'tasmāt' etc. The meaning is: what is accepted as having reason-hood, such as 'being produced,' must be stated in the form of being <s>vyāpya</s> (pervaded). // 113 1/2 //

children.text:
arthānāṃ śabdatantratve yad bhavati tad darśayati---yadetipādarahitadvayena /
asyārtha'--- yadā hi vyāptiśaktyanusāreṇaivārthānāṃ sādhyahetutvaṃ tadā yadyapi vaktrā na sahabāvamātraṃ darśitaṃ,kintu samyageva dṛṣṭāntavacanam, arthāstu na tadanurūpavyāpyavyāpakabhāvanāvasthitā iti dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā bhavediti vakṣyamāṇena sambandha iti /
yathā nityo dhvaniramūrtatvāditi prayoge karmavat paramāṇuvad ghaṭavad vyomavaditi dṛṣṭānteṣu yathāsaṅkhyaṃ paramārthata' sādhyahetūbhayavyāptiśūnyatayā /
karma khalvanityamiti tat sādhyabhūtayā nityatayā śūnyaṃ, hetustvamūrtavāditi tatra vidyata eva /
paramāṇavastu bhūrtā iti teṣu hetuśūnyatā, sādhyaṃ tu nityatvaṃ teṣu vidyata eva /
ghaṭe tu na sādhyaṃ nityatvaṃ nāpyamūrtatvaṃ heturityubhayaśūnyatā /
children.translated_text: In a pot, however, there is neither the <s>sādhya</s> — eternality — nor the <s>hetu</s> — formlessness — hence there is absence of both.

children.text: vyomni tu dṛṣṭānte vyāptiśūnyatāmuttaratra svayameva vivariṣyati /
children.translated_text: In space as an example, the absence of <s>vyāpti</s> will be explained later by himself.

children.text: atraiva ca vyomavaditi dṛṣṭānte tadasadvādinaṃ sautrāntikaṃ prati prayujyamāne dharmyasiddhyā
children.translated_text: And here, in the example 'like space,' when it is employed against the <s>Sautrāntika</s> who denies its existence, due to the non-establishment of the <s>dharmin</s>,
there would be the nature of a fallacious example — thus he says 'tadasadvādinam' etc. // 116 //

He shows what happens when things depend on words — 'yadā' etc. with two [half-verses]. Its meaning: When indeed the <s>sādhya-hetu</s> relationship of things follows the capacity of <s>vyāpti</s> alone, then even if the speaker has not shown mere co-existence but has made the example-statement quite correctly, if the things themselves are not situated in the state of pervaded and pervader corresponding to that — then there would be the nature of a fallacious example — the connection is with what will be stated. For example, in the formulation 'sound is eternal because of being formless,' the examples 'like <s>karman</s>, like atoms, like a pot, like space' are respectively, in ultimate reality, devoid of the <s>vyāpti</s> of the <s>sādhya</s>, the <s>hetu</s>, or both. For <s>karman</s> (action) is impermanent — hence it is devoid of the <s>sādhya</s>, namely eternality; but the <s>hetu</s>, 'formlessness,' does exist therein. Atoms, however, are embodied (have form) — hence there is absence of the <s>hetu</s> in them; but the <s>sādhya</s>, eternality, does exist in them.
He elaborates the absence of <s>vyāpti</s> — 'tatsadbhāve 'pi' etc. Even though

children.text: vyāptyā sādharmya ukte ca na vaidharmyamapekṣyate /
children.translated_text: when <s>vyāpti</s> has been stated in the positive example, the negative example is not required;

children.text: sahabhāvitvadṛṣṭyā tu yadā vyāptiṃ na lakṣayet // Msv_5,4.118 //
children.translated_text: but when, from the perspective of mere co-existence, one does not discern the <s>vyāpti</s> — // Msv_5,4.118 //

children.text: para' sādharmyadṛṣṭāntāt taṃ vā nāpekṣate yadā /
children.translated_text: the opponent does not require the <s>sādharmya</s> (positive) example, or

children.text: vaktā vā sahabāvitvaṃ śuddhaṃ tena vaded yadā // Msv_5,4.119 //
children.translated_text: when the speaker, well-trained in negative examples only, states pure co-existence with the positive — // Msv_5,4.119 //
or even states a reverse positive concomitance — then, with the desire to rectify that,

children.text: vyomna' sadbhāvo bhavet, tacca hetusādhyadvayayuktaṃ nityatvādamūrtatvācca /
children.translated_text: space may well exist, and it possesses both <s>hetu</s> and <s>sādhya</s> — eternality and formlessness.

children.text: tathāpi karmādiṣvamūrteṣu anityeṣvālocyamāneṣu hetorvyāptirnāstīti īdṛśasyāpi dṛṣṭāntasya varjanameva /
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, when <s>karman</s> (action) and other formless but impermanent things are considered, there is no <s>vyāpti</s> of the <s>hetu</s> — hence even such an example is to be rejected.

children.text: ayamapi na sādhyasiddhye samartho yata iti ||117||
children.translated_text: This too is not capable of establishing the <s>sādhya</s>. // 117 //

children.text:
vyākhyāta' sābhāsa' sādharmyadṛṣṭānta' /
vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntamata' paraṃ vyākhyāsyati /
tatraitadeva tāvat prathamaṃ vaktavyam /
kiṃ sarvadaiva sādharmyavad vaidharmyavacanaṃ kāryaṃ na veti /
tatra tāvad vyatirekapradhānavādina' sarvadā vācyamiti ye vadanti tān pratyāha---vyāptyā sādharmya ukta iti /
evaṃ hi manyate--- vyāptiprajñāpanāya hi dṛṣṭāntavacanam, sā cet sādharmyavacanena jñāpitā kiṃ vaidharmyavacanena /
sādharmyaṃ cāvaśyameva vacanīyamanvayaprajñāpanāya, tatpradhānatvādanumānasya /
vyatirekasyāpi tanmukhenaiva siddhe' /
itarathā duradhigamatvāt /
ato yadi vyāptyā sahitaṃ sādharmyamuktam, alaṃ vaidharmyavacaneneti /
kadā tarhi vaidharmyaṃ vācyamata āha--- sahabhāvitvadṛṣṭyeti pādatrayeṇa /
children.translated_text: When then should the negative example be stated? — therefore he says 'sahabhāvitvadṛṣṭyā' etc. with three quarters [of a verse].

children.text: yadā hi vaktrā samyageva dṛṣṭānta ukte para' śrotā jānāti--- yathā hetusādhyayo' sāhityamātranenoktaṃ na vyāptiriti, tadā sādhyābhāve hetvabhāvaṃ jñāpayituṃ 'vaidharmyeṇeṣṭasādhana'miti vakṣyamāṇena sambandha iti /
children.translated_text: When indeed the speaker has stated the example correctly, but the listener — the opponent — understands: 'Only mere co-existence of the <s>hetu</s> and <s>sādhya</s> has been stated, not <s>vyāpti</s>' — then, to make known the absence of the <s>hetu</s> in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s>, the connection is with what will be stated: 'the desired is proved through <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity).'

children.text: yadā khalvabhyastavaidharmyastamevāpekṣate na sādharmyadṛṣṭāntaṃ tadā ca vaidharmyeṇeṣṭasādhanamityāha--- taṃ vā nāpekṣate yadeti /
children.translated_text: When indeed one who is accustomed to the negative example requires only that, and not the positive example — then too, the desired is proved through <s>vaidharmya</s> — thus he says 'taṃ vā nāpekṣate yadā' etc.

children.text: yadā vā vaktā suśikṣitavaidharmya' sādharmyaṃ vaktumajānānastena sādharmyadṛṣṭāntena sahabhāvamātrameva śuddhaṃ vyāptihīnaṃ kathayati, tadāpi paryanuyuktena tenaiva vaidharmyeṇeṣṭasādhanaṃ kāryamityāha--- vaktā veti ||119||
children.translated_text: Or when the speaker, well-trained in the negative, not knowing how to state the positive, with that positive example states mere co-existence alone — pure, devoid of <s>vyāpti</s> — then too, when challenged, the desired must be proved through that very negative example — thus he says 'vaktā vā' etc. // 119 //

The positive (<s>sādharmya</s>) example, along with its fallacious forms, has been explained. The negative (<s>vaidharmya</s>) example will be explained hereafter. There, first of all, this very thing must be stated: Is the negative example always to be stated, as with the positive, or not? Regarding this, first, those who hold that negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) is primary and who say it must always be stated — to them he replies: 'vyāptyā sādharmya ukte' etc. For his view is thus: The statement of the example is for making <s>vyāpti</s> known; if that has been made known through the positive statement, what need is there for the negative? And the positive example must necessarily be stated for making known positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), since inference has that as its primary element. For the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) too is established through that very means. Otherwise it would be difficult to understand. Therefore, if the positive example has been stated along with <s>vyāpti</s>, the negative statement is sufficient [without being separately stated].

children.text: yadā vā bhrānto viparītamanvayaṃ darśayati, tadāpi tatsamādhānecchagayā pūrvaviparītajñānopamardanena vaidharmyeṇeṣṭasādhanamityāha---viparītānvayamiti /
children.translated_text: Or when a confused person shows a reverse positive concomitance — then too, with the desire to rectify that, through the destruction of the prior incorrect knowledge, the desired is proved through <s>vaidharmya</s> — thus he says 'viparītānvayam' etc.
Through the destruction of prior knowledge, the desired is proved through <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity). // Msv_5,4.120 //
The mere co-existence stated previously is employed as the reason therein;
for the relationship of pervaded and pervader between the two positive entities, of whatever kind is accepted — // Msv_5,4.121 //
of the absences of those two, therefore, the reverse is understood;
when the absence of smoke is pervaded by the absence of fire — then 'no fire' is displaced from that — // Msv_5,4.122 //
'there is indeed no smoke' — thus the state of being pervaded is attained;
likewise, in the absence of fire, [when] pervaded by the absence of smoke, 'no smoke' is displaced from that — // Msv_5,4.123 //
Because there is no scope elsewhere, it is certainly pervaded by fire.

children.text:
nanvanvayavaipītye sa eva yathāvat pratipādyatāṃ kiṃ vaidharmyavacanena /
satyamevamapīṣṭaṃ sidhyatyeva, kintu bhrāntairidamasmābhiruktaṃ sādhyābhāve hetvabhāvo vivakṣita iti vaidharmyeṇāpi tāvadiṣṭasādhanaṃ bhavetyeveti /
yattu tatpūrvaṃ sāhityamātramuktaṃ tadvaidharmya evopayujyate tasyaiveṣṭaṃ sādhayato 'nugrahe vartate ityāha--- sāhityamātramiti ||120 1/2||
children.translated_text: "But let the <s>anvaya</s> (co-presence) and <s>vyatireka</s> (co-absence) themselves be properly demonstrated — what is the need for the <s>vaidharmya</s> (dissimilarity) statement?" True — even thus, the desired is indeed established. But this has been said by us to address those who are confused: 'The absence of the <s>hetu</s> (reason) in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s> (provable) is what is intended.' Thus, through <s>vaidharmya</s> too, the desired proof follows. And what was previously stated as mere co-occurrence — that is useful precisely in <s>vaidharmya</s>, since it serves to support the establishment of the desired. Hence he says — 'mere co-occurrence.'

children.text: evaṃ tāvad vaidharmyavacanasyāvasaro darśita', tadvavacanaprakāramidānīṃ darśayati---vyāpyavyāpakabhāvo hīti ||121 1/2||
children.translated_text: Thus the occasion for the <s>vaidharmya</s> statement has been shown. Now he shows the manner of its statement — 'for the pervaded-pervader relation.'

children.text:
vaiparītye kāraṇamāha--- dhūmabhāva iti /
yadā hi dhūmabhāvo 'gnibhāvena vyāpto bhavati tadānagniragnyabhāvastato dhūmāt pracyuta' sannadhūme dhamābhāva eva bhavatītyevaṃ tāvad vyāpto bhavati /
yo hi yasmin sati bhavati asati ca na bhavati sa tanniyatastadvyāpta ityucyate /
yathā dhūmo 'gnāveva bhavannagninā vyāpta iti siddho 'bhāvayorvyāptiviparyaya iti ||122 1/2||
children.translated_text: He states the reason for the reversal — 'the existence of smoke.' For when the existence of smoke is pervaded by the existence of fire, then in the absence of fire, [smoke] having fallen away from that fire, becomes, in the absence of smoke, the mere absence of smoke — and thus it is pervaded. For that which exists when something exists and does not exist when it does not exist — that is determined by it, and is said to be pervaded by it.
