eko hi sarvadā sarveṣāṃ ca bāva' prakāśate na paramāṇubhedā' /
na ca bhedenāgṛhyamāṇo 'bhedo gṛhyata iti sāmpratam /
saṃvidvirodhāditi bhāva' /
nanvayameva bhedā
children.translated_text: "But the very atoms, when different yet collected, are grasped — not one product-substance. Therefore, how can one say that it is a universal among part-possessing things? And the collected [atoms] themselves, being of non-occurrence elsewhere, are designated by the words 'particular,' 'uncommon,' etc., and so they will be perceptible. Let not each atom individually be the object of the senses" — hence he says 'through difference' etc. For always, the single appearance of all [atoms] shines forth — not the differences of atoms. And it is not appropriate that non-difference is grasped when what is grasped through difference is not grasped — because of the contradiction with cognition. This is the purport. "But this very non-differentiated

children.text: samudāyo na vāpyasti bhavatāṃ na ca sarvadā /
children.translated_text: and neither does the aggregate exist for you, nor always;
and the possibility of the arising of a cognition from a non-existent object for all does not exist.
And without the connection with a single universal, there is no aggregate-status;
and even in the aggregate, the atomic nature of these does not depart.
Even though the universal — thus called — is not visible, still, it is indeed the universal
that this cognition clings to — even without the positing of a single [entity].

children.text: vagraho yo 'yamabhinnaprakāśa',kiṃ bhedagrahaṇenāta āha---na ca bhinneti /
children.translated_text: — apprehension, which is this undifferentiated appearance — what use is the apprehension of difference?" Hence he says 'nor of what is different' etc. The meaning is: Difference is not what is cognized by a cognition of undifferentiated appearance — because the discrimination of difference and non-difference would be unjustified.
"But even without a single [entity], there would be a cognition based on the aggregate —
this undifferentiated appearance will be [possible]" — hence he says 'the aggregate' etc.

The purport is: For those who deny the well-known universal cognized by the entire world, how could they have an aggregate as a separate real entity, based on which there could be an undifferentiated appearance?

children.text: ye hi sāmānyameva sarvajagatsaṃviditamapalapanti kutasteṣāṃ samudāyo nāmārthāntaraṃ, yadālambano 'bhinnapratibhāso bhaviṣyati /
api ca sarvadā sarve caikaṃ dravyamavabudhyatnate kathaṃ tadanyathā bhaviṣyatītyāha--- na ca sarvadeti ||179||
children.translated_text: Moreover, if all [people] at all times cognize one and the same substance, how will it turn out to be otherwise? Hence he says—'and not at all times.' // 179 //
Moreover, even this aggregate is not possible without a single universal.

children.text: na hi nānājātīyeṣu vṛkṣaghaṭaloṣṭeṣu kasyacit samudāyabuddhirasti /
children.translated_text: For no one has an aggregate-cognition with respect to things of diverse universals, such as trees, pots, and clods.
Therefore, even when the aggregate is accepted, it would follow that atomicity-as-a-universal must be accepted by you—thus he says—'nor.' // And in the reason // 180 //
And in the reason.

children.text:
nanu nānekāvayavavṛttyanusandhānena vinā tatsāmānyarūpaṃ dravyamabhyupagantuṃ śakyam /
na caindriyakaṃ jñānametā(vi?va) ti samarthamavikalpakatvāt tasya /
ata āha---sāmānyamitīti /
yadyapyekānugamakḷptestannānāvayavavyāsaṅgi dravyaṃ sāmānyamityevaṃ vikalpya na gṛhyate /
tathāpi tadekarūpaṃ tāvannirvikalpakenāpi gṛhyata eveti nāpahnotuṃ śakyata iti vyāsajyavṛttyavayavisāmānyanyāyena prativyaktivartino 'pi gotvādisāmānyasyaikandriyakatvaṃ darśayitavyam /
tadapi sāmānyamityena rūpeṇāgrāhyaṃ vastuta' sāmānyameva gṛhyate /
children.translated_text: That too, though not graspable in the form of 'this is a universal,' is in reality a universal that is grasped.
But after the subsequent remembrance of words and such, it is grasped by conceptually determining 'this is a universal' through the reflection on multi-instance occurrence.
And this has already been stated in the establishment of determinate [perception].

children.text: ato naivaṃ vācyam--- astvavayavisāmānysaya svalakṣaṇāparanāmna indriyairgrahaṇam, na tu prativyaktiniveśina iti ||181||
children.translated_text: Therefore, it should not be said thus: 'Let there be grasping by the senses of the universal of parts, which is also called a particular; but not of what resides in each individual.' // 181 //

But surely it is not possible to accept a substance that has the form of a universal of many-part entities without the investigation of multi-component occurrences. And a sensory cognition is not capable of this, being non-conceptual. Hence he says—'the universal, thus.' Although the substance that is common to the various parts is not grasped by conceptually determining 'this is a universal'—since a single-form apprehension does not involve such conceptualization—still, that one-form [substance] is indeed grasped even by non-conceptual [perception], and this cannot be denied. Thus, by the method of the universal of parts that has a pervading operation, it should be shown that even universals like cow-ness, though residing in each individual, are objects of a single sense-perception.
Just as the grasping by the senses of a universal that operates in a pervading manner [is accepted],
so too should it be for one that resides in each individual.
And atoms are not necessarily accepted by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>;
should you posit the falsity of what is perceived by the powerful [perception].
One who denies the perceptual [reality of] the aggregate form through invisible atoms—

children.text: yo 'pahanute śaśasyāpi so 'bhāvaṃ śṛṅgato vadet // Msv_5,4.184 //
children.translated_text: he might as well declare the non-existence of a hare from its horns.
Because there is no difference in the cognition in both cases, he says—'pervading.' // 182 //

children.text: tadanenaitadāpāditam-kimidaṃ mudhaiva sāmānyasya pratyakṣatā neṣyate, viśeṣamapi hi pratyakṣamicchadbhirbalātsāmānyameva pratyakṣamāśrayaṇīyam, sarvasya hi sunipuṇaṃ nirūpyamāṇasya rūpāde' sāmānyarūpatvād, dravyasya ca nānāvayavasādhāramasya tādrūpyāt, svattraṃ paramāṇusañcayamātrasya cānupalambhād dravyāpalāpe ca pratyakṣavirodhāt /
children.translated_text: By this the following has been brought about: Why is the perceptibility of the universal pointlessly not accepted? For even those who wish to accept the particular as perceptual must perforce rely on the universal as perceptual, since everything, when most carefully examined, has the form of a universal with respect to form and so on, and since the substance that is common to diverse parts has that very nature, and since the mere accumulation of atoms considered independently is not apprehended, and since the denial of substance would contradict perception.

children.text: ato 'vayavisāmānyaṃ tatsamavetāni ca gotvādisāmānyāni sarvāṇyeva pratyakṣāṇi na viśeṣā eveti tātparyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the part-universal and all the universals such as cow-ness that are inherent in it are all perceptual—not the particulars alone. This is the purport.

And precisely because of the superiority [of the foregoing argument], by the demonstration of the perceptibility of the universal and the part-universal established elsewhere, there is no repetition to be objected to. // 182 //

children.text:
nanu bhavadbhirmīmāṃsakaistāvadavasyamabhyupagantavyā' paramāṇava' /
atasteṣāmevobhayasiddhānāṃ paramekākārabuddhijananaśaktimātramevopakalpitam /
kiṃ dharmikalpanayā /
laghīyasī hi tatkalpanāto dharmakalpanā /

children.translated_text: Hence he says—'and by the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>.'
The purport is this:

children.text: yaddhi pramāṇenopanīyate, tadasmābhiriṣyate, na ca sthūlaṃ hitvā paramāṇava evākṣajāyāṃ buddhau bhāsante, yattānupetya sthūlamavajānīmahe /
children.translated_text: What is presented by a means of valid knowledge is accepted by us. And atoms alone, apart from the gross [substance], do not appear in the sensory cognition, such that, relying on them, we would deny the gross.

children.text: tadānuguṇyena tu yadyaṇavo vyā(pa?pā) dyante, bhavantu, na tadvalena mūlabhūtaṃ sthūlamapalapitumutsahāmaha iti ||183||
children.translated_text: But if atoms are explained in conformity with that [gross substance], let them be; we do not have the strength to deny the gross, which is fundamental, on the strength of that. // 183 //

But surely you <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s> must necessarily accept atoms. Therefore, since they are accepted by both sides, only the capacity of those very [atoms] to generate a single-form cognition is postulated. What is the need for postulating a substance? For the postulation of a substance is lighter than the postulation of that [atom-based capacity].

children.text: pratyakṣaṃ tu sthūlamadṛśyai' paramāṇubhi' nihanuvānasya śaśo 'pi tadviṣāṇadhiyā nihnotavya' prāpta ityāha---samūharūpamiti ||184||
children.translated_text: But for one who denies the perceptual gross [substance] through invisible atoms, even a hare is something whose non-existence should be denied on the basis of its horns—thus he says—'the aggregate form.' // 184 //
When the ultimate reality of the aggregate has been established, the means of establishing it—
if the existence of atoms is then to be understood,

children.text: tasmād yad gṛhyate vastu yena rūpeṇa sarvadā /
children.translated_text: therefore, whatever entity is grasped, in whatever form, at all times,
that should be accepted just as it is—whether it is a universal or the other [particular].
Relative to the universals of existence (<s>sattā</s>) and so on, everything attains uncommonness through cow-ness and such.

children.text: tasmādasādhāraṇam akṣagamyaṃ vadan na sāmānyamapahanuvīta // Msv_5,4.187 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, one who says that the uncommon is an object of sense-perception would not deny the universal.

children.text: sāmānyarūpeṇa na gṛhyate cet kiṃ vāstyasādhāraṇabuddhiratra /
children.translated_text: If [the universal] is not grasped in the form of a universal, then what uncommon cognition is there at all here?
No, he says—'aggregate.'

children.text: na hyatra kalpanālāghavena pratyakṣasiddho dharmī paratyāgamarhati /
children.translated_text: For here, the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) established by perception should not be abandoned for the sake of parsimony of postulation.

children.text: siddhe ca tasmistadanuguṇā' paramāṇava iti kena neṣyate /
children.translated_text: And when that [aggregate substance] is established, who would not accept atoms that are in conformity with it?

children.text: siddhyupāyastu teṣāmanyo nāstīti paramāṇavo nāvaśyamiṣyanta ityuktaṃ bhavati ||185||
children.translated_text: But since there is no other means of establishing them, it is stated that atoms are not necessarily accepted. // 185 //
Are atoms now like hare's horns?

children.text: ato yadeva vastu sāmānyaviśeṣayoraparokṣaṃ gṛhyate, tat tathaivāparokṣamapahnotuṃ śakyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, whatever entity is directly grasped as non-mediated, whether through universal or particular, cannot be denied as non-mediated in that very form.
Because even the universals such as cow-ness are uncommon relative to the higher universals such as existence (<s>sattā</s>).

children.text: ato yadyasādhāraṇaṃ pratyakṣamityāgraho bhavatāmevamapi na gotvādisāmānyamapratyakṣamiti
children.translated_text: Therefore, if your insistence is that the uncommon is perceptual, even so, the universal cow-ness and the like is not non-perceptual.
Since it is established by the capacity of perception, it cannot be denied—hence he says—'existence and such.' // 187 //

children.text:
yadi tūcyate pratyakṣeṇa gṛhyamāṇamapi sāmānyaṃ na sāmānyollekhena gṛhyata iti(na) pratyakṣamiti, tadetadāśaṅkate---sāmānyeti /
pariharati kiṃ veti /
evaṃ hyasādhāraṇamapi na pratyakṣaṃ bhavet /
tatrāpi nirvikalpakā
children.translated_text: But if it is said that even though grasped by perception, the universal is not grasped with the characterization 'this is a universal,' and so is not perceptual—he raises this doubt: 'universal.' He resolves it: 'what then.' For then the uncommon too would not be perceptual. For there too, in the non-conceptual [stage]—

children.text: yadvastu loka' pratipadyate 'smin dvidhāpi tacchakyata eva vaktum // Msv_5,4.188 //
children.translated_text: Whatever entity the world apprehends in this [perception], it can be expressed in both ways.
Thus ends the chapter on inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
Now begins the chapter on verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>).
Among perception and the like, the definition of mere word alone is to be stated.
Why then, in such haste, is the definition of <s>śāstra</s> (authoritative teaching) stated here?

children.text:
vasthāyāṃ paravyāvṛttyakalpanādasādhāraṇollekho nāstyeveti /
yadi tu tādrūpyeṇāvikalpitamapi svarūpeṇa vikalpako 'vabudhyata

children.translated_text: then that is perception.

children.text: evaṃ tarhi dvyākārameva saṃmugdhaṃ vastu loka' pratipadyata iti parīkṣakairubhayathāpi tat śakyata eva vaktumiti siddhaṃ dvyākāremeva vastu pratyakṣeṇa gṛhyata iti /
children.translated_text: If so, the world apprehends an entity that is of dual aspect, as indistinct; and the examiners can express it in both ways—thus it is established that the entity, being of dual aspect, is grasped by perception.

children.text: siddhaṃ ca sāmānyata' sambandhadarśanamityabhiprāyeṇāha--- yadvastu loka' pratipadyate 'smin dvidhāpi tat śakyata eva vaktumiti /
children.translated_text: And since the seeing of relations through generals is established—with this purport he says: 'Whatever entity the world apprehends in this [perception], it can be expressed in both ways.'
'In this' means: in perceptual knowledge—such is the meaning. // 188 //

[continuing from above] —in the non-conceptual stage, there is no characterization as 'uncommon,' because of the impossibility of discrimination from others without conceptualization. But if even what has not been conceptualized as having that nature is understood in its own form by the conceptual [cognition],
Thus ends the chapter on inference in the <s>Kāśikā</s> commentary composed by the teacher <s>Sucaritamiśra</s>.

children.text:
atha śabdapariccheda' /
atra pratyakṣānumānayoraparīkṣytava ukte śāstrasyāpyaparīkṣyatāpratipādanārthaṃ bhāṣyam---"śāstraṃ śabdavijñānādasannikṛṣṭer'the vijñānam"iti /
nanu vṛttikāramate na parīkṣivyaṃ nimittamiti pratijñāyapratyakṣādīni hi prasiddhāni pramāṇāni tadantargataṃ ca śāstramityukte' pratyakṣavyabhicāreṇa parīkṣāmāśaṅkya tadavyabhicāra ukte 'nantarameva śāstrasyāparīkṣā pratipādyata iti yuktam, taddhi prakṛtam, kimanumānena vyavadhīyate /
satyamevam /
ayaṃ tu tantrāntarānusāreṇa krama āśrita' /
tathā hi nāpratyakṣaṃ pramāṇamiti lokāyatikā manyante /
te hi vaiśiṣikādyāśritapratyakṣānantarānumānaprāmāṇyapratipādanena pratibodhyanta /
evaṃ hivaiśiṣikā'paṭhanti--- dvividhaṃ pramāṇamālocitādhyavasānamanālocitānugamanaṃ ceti /
tathānye 'pi pratyakṣamanumānaṃ varṇitam /
tato mahāviṣayatayā prakṛtvena puruṣārthopayikatvena ca śāstram /
tadanantaraṃ ca yatra kvacana vācye bahūnāṃ prasiddhamityupamānamuktam /
nyāyavistare hi prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanamupamānamityuktam /
tata' pārāśaryamatenārthāpattiruktā /
taduttarakālameva tanmatānusāriṇā kṛtakoṭinokttavāt /
abhāvapramāṇasya tu bhāvapramāṇābhāva evātmeti taduttara' prastāva' /
ki punastantrāntareṣvevamimāni pramāṇāni prasiddhānīti prasiddhiprābalyaṃ kathitaṃ bhavati /
vyutthitāśca tena tena sākṣiṇā pratipāditā bhavanti /
atra ca śabdavijñānādityucyate, tat kathaṃ vigṛhyate /
kiṃ śabdād vijñānaṃ śabdasya vā vijñānamiti /
pūrvatra samāsānupapatti' /
bhayena hi pañcamī samasyate /
uttaratra tu savikalpakapratyakṣe 'pi śāstratvaprasaṅga', śabdavijñānādeva hi gaurityevamādayo 'sannikṛṣṭārthavikalpā bhavanti /
atrocyate /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa evāyam /
na ca savikalpake prasaṅga', na hi tacchabdapramāṇādutpadyate, api tu śabdasahāyādindriyāt /
yathaiva hi gandhasahakṛtamidandriyaṃ tailād vilīnaṃ ghṛtaṃ vivinakti /
evaṃ śabdasahakṛtaṃ jātyādīn /
tathā cākṣasambandhaphalaparokṣāvabhāsitā /
ta(tra?cca) savikalpake 'stītyaktaṃ pratyakṣānte /
ato yadeva śabdaśaktivimarśotthaṃ vijñānamasannikṛṣṭārthgocaraṃ tacchābdam /
ata eva na padārthamātrajñānaṃ śābdam /
na hi tadasannikṛṣṭārthagoca
children.translated_text: Now begins the chapter on verbal testimony. Here, since it was stated that perception and inference need not be examined [further], the <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary), intending to establish the non-examinability of <s>śāstra</s> (scripture) as well, states: 'Scripture is the cognition of a non-proximate object arising from verbal knowledge.' But is not the position of the author of the <s>Vṛtti</s> that the occasion for examination does not exist? Since, when it was stated 'perception and the like are well-known means of valid knowledge, and scripture is included within them,' and when, after apprehending the examination through the deviation of perception and establishing its non-deviation, the non-examinability of scripture is established immediately after—that is fitting, for that is the topic at hand; why is it interrupted by inference? True indeed. But this sequence has been adopted following the order of other systems. For the <s>Lokāyatikas</s> (materialists) hold that nothing other than perception is a means of valid knowledge. They are to be persuaded by establishing the validity of inference, which follows immediately after perception as held by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> and others. For the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> thus recite: 'The means of valid knowledge is twofold—examined apprehension and unexamined following.' Others too have described perception and inference. Then, because of its great scope, primary importance, and utility for human goals, comes scripture. And after that, wherever something well-known to many is to be expressed, analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) is stated. For in the <s>Nyāya</s> elaboration it is stated: 'Analogy is the means of establishing the <s>sādhya</s> through known similarity.' Then, following the view of <s>Parāśara</s>, <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is stated. After that, since it was expounded by the author in sequence. And the means of knowing absence, since its essence is the very absence of the means of knowing existence, is discussed thereafter. Why then is the order of these means of knowledge, as known in other systems, stated here—is it to declare the force of their being well-known? And they are made to stand, having been established by each respective witness. Here, the expression 'from verbal knowledge' (<s>śabdavijñānāt</s>) is used. How is it to be analyzed? Is it 'knowledge from word' or 'knowledge of word'? In the former analysis, the compound is untenable, because the fifth case (ablative) is compounded with 'fear' [not with 'knowledge']. In the latter analysis, even determinate perception would have the status of scripture, since conceptual cognitions such as 'this is a cow' are cognitions-of-words about non-proximate objects. To this it is replied: This is indeed a genitive compound. And there is no undesired consequence for determinate [perception], because that does not arise from the word as a means of knowledge, but rather from the sense-organ aided by the word. Just as the taste-organ aided by smell discriminates clarified butter dissolved in oil, so [the sense] aided by words [discriminates] universals and the like. And thus there is conformity with the result of sense-contact as non-mediated appearance. And it has been stated at the end of [the discussion of] perception that this exists in determinate [perception]. Therefore, only the cognition that arises from the reflection on word-capacity and has a non-proximate object as its domain is verbal [testimony].
Leaving aside the general definition, the definition of the particular alone

children.text: na śakyaṃ kevalaṃ vaktumito 'pyasya na vācyatā // Msv_5,5.2 //
children.translated_text: cannot be stated independently; hence from this too, the expressibility [of the general definition is not to be denied].
And what was stated as 'knowledge of an object from verbal knowledge'—

children.text: aviśiṣṭaṃ viśiṣṭasya na tat śāstrasya lakṣaṇam // Msv_5,5.3 //
children.translated_text: being unspecific, that is not the definition of the specific <s>śāstra</s>.
Action or cessation, whether by what is eternal or what is produced—
that by which people are instructed is called <s>śāstra</s> (authoritative teaching).

children.text:
caram /
vakṣyati hi--- 'smārakānna vimṛśyata' iti /
kiṃ nāma tarhi śābdam, vākyārthajñānamiti vadāma' /
na(nu) tatpadārthajñānādutpadyate, na śabdajñānāt /
na /
avāntaravyāpāratvātpadārthapratipādanasya śabdānām, pāka iva kāṣṭhānāṃ jvalanasya /
vakṣyati hi---
pāke jvālena kāṣṭhānāṃ padārthapratipādanam /
iti /
ato na kiñcidanupapannamiti /
idaṃ tu vaktavyaṃ kimidaṃ sāmānyalakṣaṇavasare viśeṣalakṣamaṃ praṇīyate /
śabdaviśeṣo hi śāstram /
tad yadi vaktavyam, evamapi sāmānyalakṣaṇamuktvā( vakṣyate?lakṣyeta) /
yat punaratitvaritenaiva sāmānyalakṣaṇavasare viśeṣo lakṣyate tadasāmpratam /
children.translated_text: But to define the particular with such haste, at the very occasion for the general definition, is improper.

children.text: na hīha pratyakṣādīnāṃ cākṣuṣatvādayo viśeṣā lakṣyante /
children.translated_text: For here, the particular aspects of perception and the like—such as being visual and so on—are not being defined.

children.text: tata' pratyakṣādiṣu sāmānyato vaktumārabdheṣu madhye śabdamātrasyaiva lakṣaṇaṃ vaktuṃ yuktam, na śāstrasyeti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, when perception and the like have been undertaken for general discussion, it is proper to state the definition of mere word in the middle, not of <s>śāstra</s>.
He states this—'among perception and the like.' // 1 //

[continuing] For it will be stated: 'it is not reflected upon from [mere] reminders.' What then is verbal [testimony]? We say: it is the knowledge of sentence-meaning. But that arises from the knowledge of word-meanings, not from the knowledge of words. No—because the presentation of word-meanings is an intermediate operation of words, like the burning of firewood is an [intermediate operation] of cooking. For it will be stated: 'The presentation of word-meanings by words is like the burning of firewood in cooking.' Therefore nothing is unjustified. But this must be said: why is a particular definition being formulated on the occasion for a general definition? For <s>śāstra</s> is a particular [type] of word. If that is to be stated, even so, having stated the general definition, [the particular] would be defined.
He states another objection—'general.'

children.text: nirjñātasāmānyalakṣaṇo hi tadviśeṣaṃ bodhayituṃ śakyo netara' /
children.translated_text: For one who has understood the general definition can be made to understand the particular thereof, but not vice versa.
For without defining the substance,
the particulars thereof—earth and so on—cannot be defined. // 2 //
Thus, first, it has been said that the designation of the definiendum as '<s>śāstra</s>' (scripture/authoritative teaching) is untenable.

children.text: śabdavijñānādityādi lakṣaṇamapi lakṣyaviśeṣe na saṅgacchata ityāha---yaccoktamiti ||3||
children.translated_text: The definition beginning with 'from verbal cognition' also does not apply to the specific definiendum — hence he says 'and what was said.' // 3 //
What then is the proper definition of <s>śāstra</s>? Hence he says — 'activity.' Activity and cessation —
But whatever description of the essential nature of something is seen therein,
its <s>śāstra</s>-hood too is understood through its being a component of that [injunctive sentence]. // Msv_5,5.5 //
Activity or cessation arises only from a sentence

children.text: pravṛttirvā nivṛttirvā tacchāstraṃ na padādyata' // Msv_5,5.6 //
children.translated_text: in the complete <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive operation) — that is <s>śāstra</s>, not from a word alone. // Msv_5,5.6 //

children.text: ityupadeśakaṃ hi nityaṃ vedavākyamanityaṃ tharmaśāstrādikaṃ śāstramucyate na śabdamākṣamiti ||4||
children.translated_text: For the instructive eternal Vedic sentence is called <s>śāstra</s>, as are the non-eternal <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> and the like — but not the word alone. // 4 //

children.text:
nanu svarūpamātrābhidhāyināmapi kṣepiṣṭhādivākyānāṃ śāstratvamiṣyate, kimucyate pravṛttinivṛttyaṅgaṃ śāstramiti /
ata āha---svarūpeti /
tadaṅgatveneti /

children.translated_text: meaning: through being a part of an injunctive sentence.

children.text: asti hi tatrāpi"vāyavyaṃ śvetamālabheta bhūtikāma"iti vidhyuddeśa' /
children.translated_text: For even there, there is an injunctive context: 'One who desires prosperity should consecrate a white [animal] to <s>Vāyu</s>.'
As a part of this single sentence [is the statement] '<s>Vāyu</s> is indeed the swiftest (<s>kṣepiṣṭha</s>)' and so forth.
Therefore, its <s>śāstra</s>-hood too is justified. // 5 //

But [objection:] even for sentences like '<s>kṣepiṣṭha</s>' that merely describe the essential nature [of something], <s>śāstra</s>-hood is accepted. Why then is it said that <s>śāstra</s> is a component of activity and cessation? Hence he says — 'essential nature.' 'Through its being a component' —

children.text:
nanvarthavādā na tāvat sākṣāt kriyāṃ pratipādayanti /
nāpi tadaśam /
trayo 'pi hi tadaṃśā' sādhyaṃ sādhanamitikartavyatā ceti /
na caiṣāmanyatamamamībhirabhīdhīyate /
ato 'kriyārthānāmekavākyatāmeva na manyāmahe /
ata āha---bhāvanāyāmiti śāstramityantena /
ayamabhiprāya'--- yadyapi na kriyāṃ gamayati, na ca kriyāsambaddhaṃ kiñcit sādhanādi, tathāpi vidhinā śabdabhāvanāparanāmadheyena sahaiṣāmekavākyatā /
vidhirhi puruṣaṃ pravartayituṃ viṣayapraśastyajñānamapekṣate /
taccārthavādā' śaknuvanti kartumiti tat kurvatāmeṣāmasti pravṛttinivṛttyorupayoga' /
ata' samastāyāṃ tryaṃśapūrṇāyāmeva bhāvanāyāṃ mahāvākyādevasārthavādakāt puruṣa' pravartate nivartate vā na vidhyuddeśamātrāditi sārthavādakameva vākyaṃ śāstramiti /

children.translated_text: And this will be elaborated in the <s>arthavāda</s> section (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>).
And some of this has been shown in the analysis of injunction — so enough of excessive elaboration.

children.text: yata eva sārthavādakāt pravṛttinivṛttijñānam, ata eva vidhinācina' pratyayamātrasyapadamātrasya vā yajetetyevamādikasya vidhiśrutāvapi kana śāstratvam /
children.translated_text: Since the knowledge of activity and cessation comes from the [sentence] inclusive of <s>arthavādas</s>, for that very reason, a mere cognition or a mere word such as 'let him sacrifice' — even when heard as an injunction — does not alone have the status of <s>śāstra</s>.

children.text: yatra hi tryaṃśabhāvanāvacanamapyavāntaravākyamanapekṣitārthavādakaṃ na pravṛttau samarthaṃ, kathamiva tatra padapratyayayo' śaktirbhaviṣyatīti duradhigamamityāha--- na padādyata iti ||6||
children.translated_text: For where even a subordinate sentence expressing the <s>bhāvanā</s> with all three components, without requiring an <s>arthavāda</s>, is not sufficient for activity — how could a mere word or verbal ending have the power? Hence this is difficult to comprehend — he says 'not from a word alone.' // 6 //

But [objection:] the <s>arthavādas</s> (laudatory passages) do not directly communicate an action, nor any part of it. For the three parts of action are: the end to be achieved (<s>sādhya</s>), the means (<s>sādhana</s>), and the procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>). And none of these is expressed by the <s>arthavādas</s>. Therefore, we do not accept the syntactic unity of the <s>arthavādas</s> with action-oriented [sentences]. Hence he says — 'in the <s>bhāvanā</s>' up to 'that is <s>śāstra</s>.' The purport is: Although [the <s>arthavāda</s>] does not communicate an action, nor any means connected with an action, nevertheless it has syntactic unity with the injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), whose other name is <s>śabdabhāvanā</s> (verbal productive operation). For the injunction requires the knowledge of the excellence of the object in order to impel a person [to act]. And the <s>arthavādas</s> are capable of producing that — so in performing that function, they are useful for activity and cessation. Therefore, it is only from the complete sentence inclusive of <s>arthavādas</s>, in the <s>bhāvanā</s> filled with all three components, that a person engages or refrains — not from the injunctive element alone. Hence, the sentence inclusive of <s>arthavāda</s> is <s>śāstra</s>.
Even while stating definitions under the pretext of not examining [the means of knowledge individually],
he does not speak without regard to the usefulness for the independent [subject]. // Msv_5,5.7 //
There, whatever definition of verbal testimony pertains to worldly sentences,
for one who wishes to explain the <s>Veda</s>, that is not particularly useful. // Msv_5,5.8 //
But having recognized the usefulness of perception and the like, from mere syllables and such, prior [to Vedic study],
at the time of knowing the meaning of scripture — he has formulated that definition with that consideration. // Msv_5,5.9 //

children.text:
evaṃ lakṣyalakṣamānupapattyā dūṣitaṃ bhāṣyamupapādayati---aparīkṣeti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- vedavyākhyā hi prakṛtā, ato yadeva tadupayogi tadeva vācyamityatikramyāpi sāmānyaprakramaṃ viśeṣamevaṃ lakṣitavān /

children.translated_text: For here, the formulation of the definition is not intended in its own right.
For the definitions are formulated under the pretext of non-examination.
And even therein, only the definition of <s>śāstra</s> that is useful for the subject at hand has been formulated.
The <s>Veda</s> is independent, because it is not of human authorship (<s>apauruṣeya</s>). // 7 //

Having thus criticized the <s>Bhāṣya</s> through the untenability of definiendum and definition, he now justifies [the <s>Bhāṣya</s>] — 'under the pretext.' The purport is: The exposition of the <s>Veda</s> is the subject at hand. Therefore, only what is useful for that should be stated. But transcending even the general procedure, he has thus formulated the specific [definition].

children.text: yadi svatantropayogitvanirapekṣāṇi na jalpati, tata' kimata āha---tatreti /
children.translated_text: If he does not speak without regard to the usefulness for the independent [subject], then what? Hence he says — 'there.'

children.text: yadā hyayaṃ jalpāka iva nānupayuktaṃ bhāṣata iti sthitam, tatra yadi lokavākyasthitaṃ śabdalakṣaṇaṃ kathayet tadasya vedaṃ vyācikhyāsārenupayuktaṃ syāditi ||8||
children.translated_text: For when it is established that he does not speak anything useless like a babbler, then if he were to state a definition of verbal testimony pertaining to worldly sentences, that would be useless for his purpose of explaining the <s>Veda</s>. // 8 //

children.text:
nanu yadyanupayuktaṃ na lakṣaṇīyaṃ, kimiti tarhi pratyakṣādi lakṣyate na hi teṣāṃ vedopayogo dṛśyate ata āha---pratyakṣādīti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- vedasvarūpāvadhāraṇa eva tāvanmahānupakāra' pratyakṣasya, na hi tadantareṇa pura'--- parthamameva svādhyāyagrahaṇakāle varṇamātrādyavadhārayituṃ śakyate, tadā cānavadhṛtaṃ śāstrārthajñānavelāyāmasmṛtatvānnopayujyetaiva /
ata' purastāt parastācca varṇamātrādita' kṛte pratyakṣādyupayogaṃ matvā tallakṣaṇaṃ kṛtam /
anumānamapi pratīkaviniyuktamantraśeṣānumāna upayujyate /
yathā devasya tveti nirvapatīti /

children.translated_text: Analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) too is useful in analogical comparisons of specific <s>prakṛti</s>-modifications in rites like the <s>Saurya</s>.
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) too is useful in the supplying of an unheard portion of a sentence.
<s>Abhāva</s> (absence) too is useful in the ascertainment of what is and what is not in a word or sentence, and in [determining] the absence of substance, deity, and so forth,
and it is useful in the ascertainment that rites have unexpressed injunctive force — thus the two words beginning with 'ādi' (and the like) have this meaning. // 9 //

But [objection:] if what is useless should not be defined, why then are perception and the like defined? For their usefulness for the <s>Veda</s> is not apparent. Hence he says — 'perception and the like.' The purport is: Perception has a great service even just in the ascertainment of the form of the <s>Veda</s> itself. For without it, at the very first time of receiving the recitation, one cannot ascertain even mere syllables and such. And what has not been ascertained at that time would not be useful at the time of knowing the meaning of scripture, since it would not be remembered. Therefore, considering the usefulness of perception and the like with respect to mere syllables and such, both before and after, that definition was formulated.
But the definition of verbal testimony that pertains to sentences like 'bring the cow,'
is of no use here; hence the definition pertaining to <s>śāstra</s> was formulated. // Msv_5,5.10 //
And there is no specific [definition] without the general;

children.text: tasmāt tampayudāhratya sāmānyaṃ lakṣayet sukham // Msv_5,5.11 //
children.translated_text: therefore, having illustrated that [general], one may easily define the specific. // Msv_5,5.11 //
Even this general form is specified through the context (<s>adhikāra</s>);
<s>codanā</s> (injunction) and <s>upadeśa</s> (instruction) are cited as being <s>śāstra</s> alone. // Msv_5,5.12 //
And just as the word <s>codanā</s> is used only in the Vedic context,

children.text: na caivañjātīyaka' kaścidupayogo gāmānayetyādivākyasthasya śābdalakṣamasyāstīti tadupekṣyaiva śāstragatameva lakṣaṇaṃ praṇītamityāha---yatviti ||10||
children.translated_text: no such usefulness exists for a definition of verbal testimony pertaining to sentences like 'bring the cow' — hence, setting that aside, the definition pertaining to <s>śāstra</s> alone has been formulated — he says 'but what.' // 10 //

children.text: yatpunaralakṣite sāmānye na viśeṣo lakṣayituṃ śakyata ityuktaṃ tatpariharati---viśeṣaśceti /
children.translated_text: He resolves the [objection] that was stated — that without defining the general, the specific cannot be defined — 'and the specific.'

children.text: sāmānyalakṣaṇe hi viśeṣo na sidhyati, vyabhicārāt /
children.translated_text: For in a general definition, the specific is not established, because of deviation.

children.text: viśeṣastu sāmānyāvyabhicārīti tasmin lakṣite tadantargataṃ sāmānyaṃ sukhameva lakṣitaṃ bhavet /
children.translated_text: But the specific is invariable with respect to the general — hence, when that [specific] is defined, the general contained within it would easily be defined.

children.text: yadā hi vidhāyakavijñānādasannikṛṣṭer'the vijñānaṃ śāstramityuktaṃ tadārtād vidhāyakaviśeṣarahitācchabdamātrajñānācchābdamiti śakyamavagantumiti na pṛthagucyata iti ||11||
children.translated_text: When it is said that '<s>śāstra</s> is the cognition regarding an object not in contact [with the senses], arising from an instructive cognition' — from this, by implication, it can be understood that verbal cognition [in general] is merely 'from word alone' without the specification of being injunctive — hence it is not stated separately. // 11 //
Hence he says — 'general.'

children.text: nāvaśyamupāttameva viśeṣaṇaṃ bhavati, kintu adhikāralabhyamapi, yathāgneyādiṣu vakṣyate, ta(dva)dihāpi codanālakṣaṇādhikārācchabdavijñānādityukte 'pi vidhāyakaviśeṣaṇaṃ pratyeṣyata iti /
children.translated_text: A qualifier is not necessarily only what is explicitly taken up; it may also be obtained from the context — as will be stated in the <s>Āgneya</s> and other [sections]. Similarly here too, even though 'from verbal cognition' is stated, the specification of being injunctive will be understood from the context of the definition of <s>codanā</s> (injunction).
But if only what is useful for the subject is to be defined, [then the word] <s>codanā</s>
— these are synonyms — this is the purport. // 12 //
But [objection:] it was said that this is not a specific definition because no specification is taken up.

children.text:
ayaṃ cādhikārato viśeṣalābho jaimineraṣyanumataścodanāśabdamaviśeṣitaṃ dvitīye sūtre prayuñjānasyetyāha---yathā ceti /
evaṃ hi manyate--- yadyapi codanāśabda' pravartakavākyamātravacana', tathāpi prathamasūtre 'thaśabdena vedā
children.translated_text: And this obtaining of the specific from the context must be accepted by <s>Jaimini</s> too, since he uses the word <s>codanā</s> without specification in the second <s>sūtra</s> — hence he says 'just as.' For he thinks thus: Although the word <s>codanā</s> means merely an impelling sentence, nevertheless, in the first <s>sūtra</s>, through the word 'atha' (now), the Vedic
The two words 'verbal-cognition' and 'object-cognition' are thus established in [the definition of] <s>śāstra</s>. // Msv_5,5.13 //
When the non-examination of perception and the like [is also desired], the non-examination of <s>śāstra</s> too
is caused by its inclusion within them — this has been stated by this very cognition. // Msv_5,5.14 //

children.text: dhyayanānantaryasyopāttatvāt tadadhikārādeva codanāśabdo vaidikyāmeva codanāyāmavatiṣṭhate,evamihāpi śāstralakṣame codanāprāmāṇyādhikārāt śabdavijñānārthajñānaśabdau viśiṣṭaśabdārthaparau,vidhāyake śabdaśabdo vidheye cārthaśabda iti ||13||
children.translated_text: Since the context of Vedic study has been taken up in the preceding [<s>sūtra</s>], from that context alone the word <s>codanā</s> applies only to Vedic injunction. Similarly here too, in the definition of <s>śāstra</s>, because of the context of the authority of <s>codanā</s>, the two words 'verbal cognition' and 'object cognition' refer to a specific word and its meaning — the word 'śabda' refers to the injunctive [word], and the word 'artha' to the enjoined [object]. // 13 //

children.text:
yadyapi vṛttikāramatopanyāsāvasare'pratyakṣādīni hi prasiddhāni pramāṇāni tadantargataṃ śāstram' iti bhāṣyakāreṇoktaṃ tatrāpi viśeṣaśāstrāparīkṣāpratijñānaṃ prakṛtopayogitvābhiprāyeṇaiveti darśayati---pratyakṣādīti /
idaṃ tu cintanīyam /
yadi vidhāyakaśabdajanitaṃ vijñānaṃ śāstram, kimidānīmaṅgāni mīmāṃsā karmānuśāsanāni ca na sāstrāṇi, laukikāni ca gāmānayetyādivākyāni śāstrāṇi /
yadyevaṃ mahān lokavirodha' /
na hi laukikā gāmānayetyādiṣu śāstraśabdamupacaranti /
svavacanavirodhaśva /
yato gāmānayetyādivākyasthaṃ śābdalakṣamamiti hi vadanti /
mīmāṃsādiṣu vedavat tato 'pi vā sātiśayaṃ śāstraśabdopacāramupalabhāmahe /
api cāyaṃ śāstraśabdo rūḍho vā syād yaugiko vā, sarvathā, sarvathā ca vaidāṅgādiṣu vartitumarhati, asti hi teṣu yathāyathamarthānusāsanaṃ, rūḍhiśca sātiśeyati varṇitam /
atrābhidhīyate /
yogarūḍhiriyaṃ paṅkajādivat, ato na tāvadnāmānayetyādiṣvatiprasajyate /
satyapi yoge laukikānāṃ teṣvaprayogāt /
puruṣārthopadeśāneva laukikā' śātrsamiti manyante /
tathā cāṅgānīti teṣāṃ śāstratvam /
nanu vidhāyakaṃ śāstramiti śāstralakṣamam,na ca tāni kañcid vidadhati /
maivam /
sarveṣāmevānuṣṭhānopadeśaparatvāt /
vyākaraṇe hi yatsādhubhirbhāṣeta tadebhirityupadiśayate /
mīmāṃsāyāmapi pratyadhikaraṇaṃ nyāyavyutpādanenānuṣṭhānopadeśa eva sarvatra /
ato yacchāstraṃ tatpravṛttinuvṛttyupadeśakameveti niyama', na punastadupadeśakaṃ śāstrameveti laukikī prasiddhiriha bhāṣyakāreṇānūditā, napunastannirapekṣaṃ śāstralakṣaṇaṃ praṇītam /
ato yadasannikṛṣṭārtha
children.translated_text: Although, at the occasion of presenting the <s>Vṛttikāra</s>'s view, the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> said 'for perception and the like are well-established <s>pramāṇas</s>, and <s>śāstra</s> is included within them' — even there, the declaration of non-examination specifically regarding <s>śāstra</s> is made with the intention of usefulness for the subject — he shows this 'perception and the like.' But this must be considered: If cognition produced by an injunctive word is <s>śāstra</s>, then are not the auxiliary sciences (<s>aṅgas</s>), <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, and the codes of conduct (<s>karmānuśāsana</s>) also <s>śāstras</s>? And are worldly sentences like 'bring the cow' <s>śāstras</s>? If so, there would be great conflict with common usage. For people in the world do not apply the word '<s>śāstra</s>' to sentences like 'bring the cow.' And there would be self-contradiction, since [the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>] says 'the definition of verbal testimony pertaining to sentences like "bring the cow."' In the case of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> and the like, we observe the figurative use of the word '<s>śāstra</s>' even more than in the <s>Veda</s>. Moreover, the word '<s>śāstra</s>' is either conventional (<s>rūḍha</s>) or derivative (<s>yaugika</s>) — in every case, it deserves to apply to the auxiliary sciences and the like, for in them too there is instruction regarding objects in the appropriate manner, and the convention has been described as subordinate. To this we reply: This is a case of conventional-derivative meaning (<s>yogarūḍhi</s>), like the word <s>paṅkaja</s> ('mud-born' = lotus). Therefore, it does not over-extend to sentences like 'bring the cow.' Even though the etymological meaning applies, because of the non-usage by the world in those [cases]. People in the world consider only instructions regarding human goals to be <s>śāstra</s>. And thus, 'auxiliary sciences' — their <s>śāstra</s>-hood [follows from this]. But [objection:] the definition of <s>śāstra</s> is 'an injunctive <s>śāstra</s>' — and those [auxiliary sciences] do not enjoin anything. Not so — because all of them have as their purport the instruction of practice. For in grammar, it is instructed: 'One should speak with the correct forms — these [are them].' In <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> too, through the elucidation of principles in each <s>adhikaraṇa</s> (topic), the instruction of practice is everywhere. Therefore, the rule is: Whatever is <s>śāstra</s> instructs activity and cessation — but it is not the case that whatever instructs [activity and cessation] is necessarily <s>śāstra</s>. The well-known usage of the world has been followed here by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>; a definition of <s>śāstra</s> independent of that has not been formulated. Therefore, what has as its scope an object not in contact [with the senses],
There, inference is resorted to as non-Vedic by the <s>Buddhists</s> and <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>;
but the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> and others hold it to be different [from the Veda] — yet the reason for the difference has not been stated. // Msv_5,5.15 //
The construction of the final syllable, word, sentence, etc., endowed with prior dispositional impressions,

children.text: vivakṣādi ca dhūmādau nāstītyetena bhinnatā // Msv_5,5.16 //
children.translated_text: and the speaker's intention (<s>vivakṣā</s>) and such are absent in smoke and the like — by this there is the distinction. // Msv_5,5.16 //

children.text: gocaraṃ puruṣaśreyovidhāyakaṃ loke śāstramiti prasiddhaṃ tacchāstram /

children.translated_text: But what has as its scope an object not in contact [with the senses], whether enjoining or not enjoining — that is verbal testimony (<s>śābda</s>). This is the distinction.
And here too, as in the case of perception, the alternatives of the <s>pramāṇa</s> — among the word, its cognition, and so forth — are to be shown according to the speaker's intention.
One should not insist that cognition alone is the <s>pramāṇa</s>.

children.text: pūrvapramāṇe cottaraṃ vākyārthajñānaṃ phalaṃ tatprāmāṇye ca hānādibuddhiriti viveka iti ||14||
children.translated_text: And in the case of the prior <s>pramāṇa</s>, the subsequent cognition of the sentence-meaning is the result; and when that is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, the cognition of avoidance and the like is the result — this is the distinction. // 14 //
What is well-known in the world as <s>śāstra</s> — that which has as its scope the enjoining of what is beneficial for humans — that is <s>śāstra</s>.

children.text: idaṃ caśāstramanumānādabhinnamiti pramāṇadvayavādino manyante, tānnirākartṛkāmasteṣāṃ matamupanyasati---tatreti /
children.translated_text: Now, those who hold a twofold <s>pramāṇa</s> theory consider this <s>śāstra</s> to be non-different from inference. Wishing to refute them, he presents their view — 'there.'

children.text: idaṃ ca pratijñāmātrameva teṣāmuktama, tadīyābhedahetūpanyāsastu paroktabhedahetunirāsāvasare kariṣyata iti /
children.translated_text: And this is merely a thesis stated by them; the presentation of their reasons for non-difference will be made at the occasion of refuting the reasons for difference stated by others.

children.text: kiṃ punarabhedopanyāsanirāsayo' prayasyate, nanvayaṃ sāṅkhyādibhireva bhedavādibhirabhedo nirākṛta eva, ata āha--- bheda iti /
children.translated_text: But what is being attempted through the presentation and refutation of non-difference? Has not this non-difference already been refuted by the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> and other proponents of difference? Hence he says — 'bheda.'
The meaning is: They [the Sāṅkhyas etc.] did not state the proper cause of difference. (15)

children.text:
tāneva taduktān bhedahetūnnirākartṛmupanyasyati--- pūrvasaṃskāretyuktāntena /
evaṃ hi tairuktam--- śābde hi pūravasaṃskārayukto 'ntyo varṇo, vākyaṃ, ādyo 'pi vā varṇa', sarve vā pratyekaṃ, sahitā vā, teṣāmeva krama' padānāṃ vā vākyatvajātireva vāvayavī vā nirdhūtanikhilavarṇādivibhāga' sphoṭo vā padānyava vā saṃhatyārthamabhidadhati /
ete ca padeṣvapi vikalpā darśayitavyā' /
tathā vivakṣāprayatnādayaśca śabdaniṣpattihetava iti /
sarvamidaṃ dhūmādau na dṛṣṭamiti tadvaidharmyāda(na) numānatvamiti /
atra dūṣaṇamāha--- tatreti /
bauddhena śābdamanumānādabhinnamanvayavyatirekābhyāmutpatte', dhūmādagnyanumānavadityukte, yadetad dhūmādivairadharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam,iyaṃ vaidharmyasamā nāma jāti', vikalpāsamā vā /
kā punarjāti' /
sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ pratayvasthānaṃ jāti' /
vādinā hi pruyakte prayoge prasaṅgo jāyate, sa jāyata iti jātirityucyate, sa ca prasaṅga sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ pratyavasthānam /
children.translated_text: He presents those very causes of difference that they stated, in order to refute them — from 'pūrvasaṃskāra' to the end. For they have stated thus: In the case of verbal [cognition], the final phoneme endowed with the impressions of the preceding [phonemes], or the sentence, or the first phoneme, or all [phonemes] individually, or all combined, or the sequence of those very [phonemes], or the words themselves, or the universal 'sentence-hood,' or the whole, or the <s>sphoṭa</s> (the manifested word-meaning unit) purged of all divisions of phonemes and such — or the words themselves collectively denote the meaning. And these alternatives should be demonstrated for words [taken individually] too. Likewise, the desire to speak, effort, and such are causes in the production of words. All of this is not observed in smoke and the like — hence, from this dissimilarity with them, [verbal cognition] is not inference. He states the refutation of this — 'tatra.' When the Buddhist argues that verbal [cognition] is non-different from inference, because it arises from positive and negative concomitance, like the inference of fire from smoke and such — the objection raised through the dissimilarity with smoke and the like constitutes the pseudo-refutation called <s>vaidharmyasamā</s> (the 'similarity of dissimilarity' fallacy), or <s>vikalpāsamā</s> (the 'similarity of alternatives' fallacy). But what is a <s>jāti</s> (pseudo-refutation)? A counter-argument through similarity or dissimilarity is [called] a <s>jāti</s>. For when a proponent makes a formulation, a complication arises — that which arises (<s>jāyate</s>) is called <s>jāti</s> — and that complication is a counter-argument through similarity or dissimilarity.
By those who declared there the [pseudo-refutation of] <s>vaidharmyasamā</s> and <s>vikalpāsamā</s> — (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.17)
From mere particularities such as smoke, impermanence, horns, and so forth, there is no difference. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.17)

children.text:
yatrodāharaṇasādharmyeṇa vādinā heturukta', tatra yadā prativādino vaidharmyeṇa pratyavasthānaṃ bhavati /
yathā--- kriyāvānātmā kriyāhetuguṇayogāt loṣṭavaditi vādinokte, prativādino vaidharmyeṇa pratyavasthānaṃ bhavati--- yathā kriyāvad dravyamavibhu daṣṭam, yathā loṣṭam,na tathātmā, tasmānniṣkriya iti /
seyaṃ vaidharmyasamā jātirutyucyate /
tathā dharmāntaravikalpāt /
yadā pritavādinā sādhya(vār)masyāpi vikalpa āpādyate, asau vikalpasamā nāma jātirucyate /
yathāsminneva prayoge prativādī vadati, kriyāhetuguṇayuktaṃ kiñcidavibhu dṛṣṭaṃ yathā loṣṭam, kiñcid vibhu yathātmā, evaṃ kiñcit kriyāvad bhaviṣyati kiñcidakriyāvaditi /
evamihāpi pareṇābedasādhane ukte dhumādivaidharmyamātreṇa pratyavasthāne vaidharmyasamā nāma jātirāpādyate /
dhūmādagnyanumānaṃ hi vākyavikalpādirahitam /
na ca tathā śābdam /
ato nānumānamiti /
tathā vikalpasamāpyevaṃ darśayitavyā /
anvayavyatirekajameva kiñcid vākyavikalpādimad dṛṣṭaṃ yathā śābdam, kiñcicca na, dhūmādināgnijñānam /
evaṃ kiñcidanumānaṃ bhaviṣyati, kiñcidananumānamiti /
jātidvayapra(tipādanātpra)tyuttaraṃ ca sādhakamiti na vacanīyamiti ||16 1/2||
children.translated_text: When a proponent states a reason through similarity with the example, and then the opponent makes a counter-argument through dissimilarity — for example, when the proponent says 'the self has action, because it possesses qualities that are causes of action, like a clod of earth,' the opponent's counter-argument through dissimilarity is: 'What is observed as a substance with action is non-pervasive, like a clod of earth; the self is not so, therefore it is without action.' This is called the <s>vaidharmyasamā</s> pseudo-refutation. Similarly, from the alternative of another property: when the opponent introduces an alternative regarding even the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) itself, that is called the <s>vikalpāsamā</s> pseudo-refutation. For example, in this very formulation, the opponent says: 'Some things possessing qualities that are causes of action are seen to be non-pervasive, like a clod of earth; some are pervasive, like the self. Similarly, some will have action, some will not.' In the same way here too, when the opponent asserts the proof of non-difference, the counter-argument through mere dissimilarity with smoke and such constitutes the <s>vaidharmyasamā</s> pseudo-refutation. For the inference of fire from smoke and the like is devoid of sentence-alternatives and such. But verbal [cognition] is not like that. Hence it is not inference — [they argue]. Similarly, the <s>vikalpāsamā</s> should also be demonstrated: 'Some things born from positive and negative concomitance are seen to possess sentence-alternatives and the like, like verbal [cognition]; some are not, like the cognition of fire from smoke. Thus some will be inference, some will not.' Since the two pseudo-refutations are demonstrated, it need not be said that the counter-argument is a valid proof. (16½)

children.text:
kathaṃ punariyaṃ jāti', evaṃ hi sādhanamidam--- śābdamanumānād bhinnaṃ tadvaidharmyātaṃ pratyakṣavaditi,ata āha---dhūmeti /
na
tāvat trailakṣaṇyapa(rityāgena) vaidharmya tairuktam /
kiñcid viśeṣaṇamātreṇa tu vaidharmyamaviśiṣṭamarthātmakānānumānānāmiti teṣāmapyanumānād bhedo bhavet na cāsāvāsti, na hi dhūmādīnāṃ--------------------------------------------------------
children.translated_text: Rather, [it involves] mere particularities; but dissimilarity that is unspecified [in this way] belongs to [all] inferences that have meaning as their content — hence even those would become different [from inference], which they are not. For smoke and such do not —
— possess such dissimilarity as to make [verbal cognition] a non-inference.
The abandonment of the triple characteristic — [that is what would make] impermanence a reason for produced-ness [into a non-inference].
Only when the abandonment of the triple characteristic is demonstrated would difference from inference be established. (17)

But how is this a pseudo-refutation? For the proof [seems to be] valid: 'Verbal [cognition] is different from inference, because of its dissimilarity with perception and such.' Hence he says — 'dhūma.' It is not the case that the dissimilarity stated by them involves the abandonment of the triple characteristic [of the inferential mark].
As long as the abandonment of the triple characteristic is not demonstrated,
So long, for one stating mere particularities, the status of pseudo-refutation (<s>jāti</s>) applies. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.18)
Even the cognition from words, through arbitrary assignment [of meaning],
Is not [different] from [cognition from] smoke and such — here too, the deviation [applies] through the operations of bodily gestures. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.19)

children.text: vailakṣaṇyamātreṇa tu bhedaṃ vadato vailakṣaṇyavacanasya jātataivāpadyetetyāha---trailakṣaṇyeti ||18||
children.translated_text: But for one asserting difference through mere dissimilarity, the assertion of dissimilarity itself becomes a pseudo-refutation — he says 'trailakṣaṇya.' (18)

children.text:
yadapi cadamaparaṃ śābdānumānayorvailakṣaṇyamuktam--- dhūmādayo hi sāvābhāvikenaiva pratibandhena pratibandhakabuddhimanumāne
janayatanti, śabdāttu yatheṣṭaviniyuktādevārthapratyayo dṛśyate, ato bheda iti, tatrāpyāha---yatheti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- atrāpi yadi kiñcidvaidharmyamātreṇa bheda ucyate, ato jātireva /
athāyaṃ prayoga'--- śābdamanumānād bhinnaṃ yateṣṭaviniyogenārthapādayatīti /
tadayuktam /
tatrāpi svābhāvikyaivātmaśaktyā rūpādipratipādanāt /
atha svagocare yatheṣṭaviniyogena pratipādanaṃ heturucyate, ato liṅgamapi parārthaprayoge yameva prati prayujyate tameva pratipādayatīti sāmanam /
atha yatheṣṭaviniyoga' saṅketo 'bhidhīyate, tato 'yamartho bhavati, yatraiva saṅketyate tameva gamayatīti, tato dṛṣṭāntābhāva', na hi śabdādanyat saṅketānuvidhānenārthaṃ bodhayati /
athāvītamaheturam /
anumānaṃ hi yatheṣṭaviniyogānanuvidhāyipratipādanam, na cedaṃ tathā, ato bhinnamiti /
tanna /
vyatirakamātrasyāgamakatvādanvayavyatirekī hi heturiṣyate /
na cāyaṃ heturanumānādabedena vyāpta' kvacidavagata', śabdātirekiṇa' kasyacid yatheṣṭaviniyogenāpratipādanāt /
athāsti hastasaṅketādīnāṃ yathāsamayaṃ pratipādanamityucyate /
tat tarhi pramāṇāntaramanumānaṃ vā /
na tāvat pramāṇāntaram, tallkṣamābhāvāt /
ato vyāptibalena jñāyamānamanumānameva tat /

children.translated_text: And this being so,

children.text: tenaiva vyabhicāra iti nānumānād vyāvṛttirheto' sidhyati /
children.translated_text: There is deviation with that very [hand-gesture inference] — hence the exclusion of the reason from inference is not established.
This is what is meant by 'deviation through the operations of bodily gestures.'
The operations of the limbs — the contractions, extensions, and such of the hands and other limbs — are 'bodily gesture operations.' (19)

And as for this other dissimilarity stated between verbal [cognition] and inference — namely, that smoke and such generate the cognition that gives rise to the inferential binding through their own natural binding alone, but from words, the cognition of meaning is seen to arise through arbitrary assignment — hence there is a difference — to this too he responds — 'yathā.' The intention is: Here too, if difference is asserted through mere dissimilarity, it is simply a pseudo-refutation. If the formulation is: 'Verbal [cognition] is different from inference because it conveys meaning through arbitrary assignment' — that is improper. For there too [in inference], the conveying of [the meaning of] form and such is by the natural power [of the sense organs] alone. If, then, the reason is stated as 'conveying within its own domain through arbitrary assignment' — then the inferential mark too, in a formulation for the sake of others, conveys [the probandum] only to the person for whom it is formulated — hence there is commonality [with verbal testimony]. If 'arbitrary assignment' means convention — then the meaning becomes: it conveys only what has been conventionally designated. In that case, there is no example [to support it], for nothing other than words conveys meaning in accordance with convention. If the reason is stated without [establishing its] pervasion — [then consider:] inference conveys [meaning] without following arbitrary assignment, and this [verbal cognition] is not like that, hence it is different — [one might say]. That is wrong. For mere absence [of concomitance] does not serve as an indicator. For what is desired [as a reason] has positive and negative concomitance. And this reason has not been ascertained anywhere to be pervaded by non-difference-from-inference. For nothing beyond words is seen to convey meaning without following arbitrary assignment. If it is said that hand-gestures and such convey according to convention — then that would be either another <s>pramāṇa</s> or inference itself. It is not another <s>pramāṇa</s>, because it lacks the definition [of any other <s>pramāṇa</s>]. Hence, by the force of pervasion, it is known as inference.
Hand-signals and such, whatever [arbitrary] assignment there may be in conveying a certain meaning,
Those, having had convention established, are considered the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) of that — this is the settled position. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.20)
And when dependence on a person [is the basis], the same deviation [applies];
For words, Vedic sentences, the [claim of] true non-pervasion would not hold. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.21)

children.text:
etadeva vivṛṇoti--- hasteti /
hastādyaṅgāśritavṛttaya evārthaviśejñānāṅgatayā hastasaṃjñetyucyante /
kathaṃ punaridamanumām, na hi hastādisanniveśā' saṅkhyāviśeṣādibhirarthairvyāptā' /
tairvināpi kadācid bhāvāt /
kintu aṅgulyādisanniveśātsaṅketakālabhāviśabdasmaraṇenārthaṃ pratipadyamānā' śabdādeva pratipadyante /
tanna /
antareṇāpi śabdasaṅke(ta?taṃ) vyavahāra evāvyutpannasyāṅgulyādisanniveśadarśinasatdarthāvagate' /
na cātra vyabhicāra' /
na hi yādṛśe sanniveśe vyāptiravagatā tādṛśasya vyabhicāro dṛśyate /
tadidaṃ 'tena dharmyantareṣveṣe'tyatra varṇitam /
ato 'numānamevedam /
tadidamuktaṃ--- te talliṅgamiti sthitiriti /

children.translated_text: And the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> has given this refutation by following through [the opponent's arguments].
For it is not the case that the cognition of meaning from words arises through arbitrary assignment.
For words like 'cow' and such convey their own meaning in accordance with their own inherent power alone.

children.text: yadṛcchāśabdāstu hastasaṃjñāditulyāste saṅketānusāreṇārthaṃ bodhayanto 'numānameveti kiṃ tadbhedapratipādaneneti ||20||
children.translated_text: But arbitrary words, being equivalent to hand-signals, convey meaning in accordance with convention and are inference itself — so what is the point of demonstrating difference based on them? (20)

He elaborates on this very point — 'hasta.' The operations based on the hands and other limbs — as constituents of knowledge of a specific meaning — are called 'hand-signals.' But how is this inference? For the configurations of hands and such are not pervaded by specific numbers and other meanings, since those [configurations] sometimes exist even without them. Rather, from the configuration of fingers and such, through the memory of the word [associated with that sign] at the time of convention, they understand the meaning from the word itself. That is wrong. For even without verbal convention, understanding of meaning occurs for one who, though untrained, observes the configuration of fingers and such — that is practical usage itself. Nor is there deviation here. For deviation is not seen of that very [type of configuration] for which pervasion was ascertained. This was explained under 'tena dharmyantareṣu eṣa.' Hence this is indeed inference. This is what is meant by 'those are considered the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark) of that — this is the settled position.'

children.text:
idamaparaṃ bhedakāraṇaṃ, śabdāddhi puruṣāpekṣor'thaniścaya', na ca tathā śabda ityato bhidyata iti /
etadapi dūṣayati---puruṣeti /
vyatirekaheturvyatirekapuraskāreṇaivārthaṃ sādhayati, prāṇādaya ivānātmakād dehād vyāvṛttamātmānam /
puruṣāpekṣitā tvanumāne 'pyarthaniścayāṅgamaṅgavṛttiṣu dṛṣṭā /
yādṛśo hi saṅketo yadarthapratipādane puruṣai' kṛta', tameva parapuraṣāpekṣayā budhyante /
ato 'trāpi vyabhicāriteti /
api cāvyāpakatvādasiddho heturityāha--- padeti /
padāni hi svamahimnaivārthaṃ pratipādayanti na puruṣāpekṣayā /
children.translated_text: This is another cause of difference: 'From words, the ascertainment of meaning depends on a person; inference does not, hence they differ.' He refutes this too — 'puruṣa.' The negative-concomitance reason establishes [its object] only through the prioritization of negative concomitance, as [one infers] the self as distinct from the body, [which is] non-self, from <s>prāṇa</s> and the like. But dependence on a person is seen as a component of meaning-ascertainment even in inference — in bodily gesture operations. For whatever convention persons have made for conveying a particular meaning, [others] understand it precisely through dependence on other persons. Hence there is deviation here too. Moreover, the reason is unestablished because it is non-pervasive — he says 'pada.' For words [of speech] convey meaning by their own authority, not through dependence on a person.
And this experience of relation [between word and meaning] is different elsewhere too;
In this [case] it depends on a person; in the case of fire and smoke, it depends on location. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.22)
And another [case] with dependence on time and such; and by others, non-difference has been stated,
From the general [principle of] non-deception of trustworthy speech, [it is established as being] from inference. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.23)

children.text: vedavākyānyapi na svārthapratipādayanāya puruṣamapekṣante, svarūpāvadhāraṇamātra eva teṣāmāptāpekṣeti ||21||
children.translated_text: Even Vedic sentences do not depend on a person for the conveyance of their own meaning; their dependence on a trustworthy [authority] is only for the ascertainment of their own form [i.e., that they are genuine Vedic sentences]. (21)

children.text:
nanu nāgṛhītasambandhaṃ padaṃ pratyāyakaṃ bhavati /
na ca puruṣānapekṣā sambandhāvagatirasti /
vedavākyānyapi nāgṛhīte padapadārthasambandhe svārthaṃ pratipādayanti /
ato 'yaṃ padapadārthasambandha' puruṣāpekṣa eveti nāvyāpakatvam /
ata āha---sambandheti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- arthapratipādane tāvadanapekṣameva padaṃ vaidikāni ca vākyāni /
sambandhānubhavaśca yatheha puruṣāpekṣastathānyatrāpyanumāne 'sau vilakṣaṇo dṛsyata eveti /
vailakṣaṇyameva darśayati--- etasminniti anyo 'ntena /
etasminniti /
hastasaṃjñādau puruṣāpekṣa', pauruṣeyo hi samaya' /
agnidhūmayostu deśāpekṣa' /
candrodayasamudravṛddhyostu kālāpekṣa' /
ādiśabdenāvasthāpekṣitāṃ darśayati /
tadanenaitaduktaṃ bhavati---anumāne 'pyanekaprakāra' sambandhāvagamo deśādyapekṣayā bhedāt /
evamihāpi puruṣāpekṣo bhaviṣyati /
anumāne 'pi tadapekṣa' sambandhabodho dṛṣṭa iti /
api ca paroktābhedahetunirāso 'pi tairna kṛta ityāha--- uktā ceti ||22 1/2||
children.translated_text: Objection: A word whose relation [with meaning] has not been grasped cannot serve as a conveyor. And there is no apprehension of the relation without dependence on a person. Even Vedic sentences do not convey their own meaning when the relation between word and meaning has not been grasped. Therefore, this relation between word and meaning does depend on a person — hence the [reason] is not non-pervasive. Hence he says — 'sambandha.' The intention is: The word, and Vedic sentences, are indeed independent in conveying meaning. But the experience of the relation — just as here [in verbal testimony] it depends on a person, so too elsewhere in inference, that [experience of relation] is seen to be different [i.e., dependent on other things]. He demonstrates the difference — from 'etasmin' to the end 'anya.' 'In this [case]' — in hand-signals and such, [the experience of relation] depends on a person, for the convention is human. But for fire and smoke, it depends on location. For the [conjunction of] moonrise and ocean-tide, it depends on time. By the word 'ādi' (and such) he shows [cases of] dependence on condition. By this, what is being said is: In inference too, the apprehension of the relation varies in multiple ways, due to differences of location and such. Similarly here too, it will be dependent on a person. Even in inference, such dependence of relational cognition is observed. Moreover, the refutation of their stated cause of non-difference has not been accomplished by them [the opponents] — he says 'uktā ca.' (22½)

children.text:
tamevābhedahetumupanyasyati---āptavādeti /
ayamartha'--- yathā dhumādiṣu bhedahānena sāmānyadharmayorvyāptiravadhāryate, evaṃ śābde 'pyāptavādāvisaṃvādasāmānyayorvyāptiravagatā /
(āptavādāvisaṃvādeti?) evaṃ ca viditvā vede 'pīśvarāptavādatvādavisaṃvādo 'numīyate,ato 'numānamevedam /
yāvatvavisaṃvādo nānumīyate tāvadarthagocaraṃ jñānamutpannamapyaniścāyakatvādapramāṇameva /
sāmānyaśabda' pratyekamabhisambadhyate /
lyablope pañcamī /
children.translated_text: He now presents that very cause of non-difference — 'āptavāda.' The meaning is: Just as in the case of smoke and such, the pervasion of two general properties is ascertained by disregarding difference, so too in the case of verbal [cognition], the pervasion of the two general [properties] of 'trustworthy speech' and 'non-deception' is ascertained. And having thus ascertained, even in the <s>Veda</s>, non-deception is inferred because of its being trustworthy speech of the Lord — hence this is indeed inference. As long as non-deception is not inferred, the cognition that has arisen regarding the subject matter, even though it has arisen, is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all, because of its non-determinative nature. The word 'sāmānya' (general) connects separately with each [term]. The ablative [case ending] is by elision of the <s>lyap</s> [gerundive suffix].
And from the difference of words for <s>apūrva</s> (unprecedented entities) and the like, there is not difference everywhere;
And here, no difference of those [words] from 'horse' and other words is perceived. (Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika 5.5.24)
Nor is any word whose relation [to its meaning] is unknown capable of illuminating [anything];
therefore, due to the non-experience of the relation, there would be non-inference. // Msv_5,5.25 //
And even through the similarity of form here, of verbal cognition, meaning, and its cognition—
because this is not observed in fire-smoke [cases], there is no difference, since that [similarity] precludes it. // Msv_5,5.26 //

children.text: tadayamanvayo bhavati--- yadyapyāptavādavisaṃvādaviśeṣāṇāṃ bhedānna sambandho 'vagantuṃ śakyate, tathāpi tayo' sāmānyapratītyānumānatā śakyate vaktum, sāmānyayorvyāptasambhavāditi ||23||
children.translated_text: The positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) is as follows: even though, due to the differences between the specific features of trustworthy speech and non-deception, the relation cannot be comprehended, nevertheless, through the cognition of both as universals, inference-status can be maintained, since <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of the universals is possible. // 23 //

children.text: nanvidamasti bhedakāraṇam, anumānaṃ sambandhāvadhāraṇādhīnam, śabdāstvapūrvādaya' sambandhajñānānapekṣā eva svārthaṃ pratipādayantīti, ato bhidyate ityata āha--- na ceti /
gavādayastāvat viditasambandhā evārthaṃ pratipādayantīti teṣāṃ durvāramanumānatvam, yadi tvapūrvādidṛṣṭāntena teṣāmapi bhedo 'bhidhīyate /
children.translated_text: Words like 'cow' etc. convey meaning only when their relation is known — hence their inference-status is irresistible. But if a difference is claimed through the example of '<s>apūrva</s>' and such,
that is not so.

children.text: śaknoti hi vaktumitaro 'pi teṣāmanumānatvaṃ sambandhāvadhīnabodhakatvād dhūmādivaditi /
children.translated_text: For the other party too can state their inference-status, since they are indicative dependent on the ascertainment of the relation, like smoke etc.

children.text: api cāpūrvaśabdā api nāśvādiśabdebyo viśiṣyante, padatvenābhedādityāha--- na ceti ||24||
children.translated_text: Moreover, even the words for '<s>apūrva</s>' etc. are not different from words like 'horse' etc., because there is no difference insofar as they are words — thus he says 'na ca' etc. // 24 //

Objection: But there is this cause of difference — inference depends on the ascertainment of the relation, while words like '<s>apūrva</s>' and such convey their meaning without depending on the knowledge of the relation — hence there is a difference. Therefore he says 'na ca' etc.

children.text:
kimato yadyevamata āha--- na ceti /
yata' khalvetāni padāni, na ca padamajñātasambandhaṃ prakāśakamasti /
ato 'mībhirapi viditasambandhairevārtho vedanīya', padatvāt /
kathaṃ puna' pramāṇāntarādṛṣṭapūrveṇāpūrvasvargādinā sambandho 'nubhavituṃ śakyate /

children.translated_text: It could not be, if they were beyond the reach of other <s>pramāṇas</s>.
But <s>apūrva</s> is warranted by the <s>pramāṇa</s> of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) — from the otherwise-inexplicability of the relation between the heard ritual action and its fruit.

children.text: svargaśca niratiśayānandasvabhāvo vaidikavākyaśeṣebhyo 'vagamyata iti tathāvagatayo' sambandhagrahaṇopapattiriti /
children.translated_text: And heaven, being of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, is understood from the remaining Vedic sentences — so the comprehension of the relation of those thus understood is justified.

children.text: ato yat parairuktaṃ śabdo nānumānaṃ sambandhānapekṣatvādakṣavaditi taddhetorasiddhyā dūṣitamityāha--- sambandheti ||25||
children.translated_text: Therefore, what was said by the opponents — 'verbal testimony is not inference because it does not depend on the relation, like the sense organs' — that has been refuted through the non-establishment of the reason — thus he says 'sambandha' etc. // 25 //

What follows from this? — therefore he says 'na ca' etc. Since indeed these are words, and no word whose relation is unknown is capable of illuminating — therefore, through these too, meaning is to be known only when the relation is known, because they are words. But how can the relation with <s>apūrva</s>, heaven, etc., which have not been previously observed through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, be experienced?
'Śabda' (word), by proximity, 'tajjñāna' (its cognition), '<s>artha</s>' (meaning), and 'taddhī' (its cognition)' — this is the analysis.
This too should be shown to have an unestablished reason.
And its refutation is to be investigated in connection with the refutation of <s>adhyāsa</s> (superimposition).
Therefore, the similarity of form is unestablished. // 26 //
He adduces another cause of difference and refutes it — 'tulya' etc.
In reflections, there is non-determination — for whatever the image is like in the mirror,
the face etc. are cognized as being just like that — and yet there is no inference-status here. // Msv_5,5.27 //
If you grant perceptibility here, then by others, this deviates [from the analogy];
where the feet etc. of those who have gone are inferred through the image. // Msv_5,5.28 //
From a single statement uttered once, of multiple [meanings], at that moment,
there cannot be cognition of both contradictory and non-contradictory — hence its distinctness. // Msv_5,5.29 //

children.text:
api ca vivakṣānivṛtteranaikāntiko heturityāha---pratibimbeṣviti /
ekānto nirṇaya', so 'sya kāryaṃ, tannāstītyanekānta iti /
kathamanekānta', ata āha--- bimbamiti /
yādṛśaṃ hi darpaṇe bimbamupalabhyate tādṛśameva mukhādi budhyate, ato 'styatrāpi gamyagamakayo' sādṛśyamiti pratibimbeṣu vartamāno heturanaikāntiko bhavatīti /
nanu naidamanumānam, ādarśatejasā hi pratihatena nāyanena tejasā prakāśitaṃ pratyakṣameva mukhamavagamyata iti śabdādhikaraṇe vakṣyate /
ata āha--- na ceti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- yadā hyayaṃ paratyakṣeṣvaṅgulyādiṣvādarśavartinā pratibimbena tādṛktve viditavyāptirbhavati, tadā mukhamapyādarśagataṃ bimbānurūpamanuminoti /
children.translated_text: The intention is: When this person, having ascertained the <s>vyāpti</s> regarding similarity through the reflection in the mirror of perceptible things like fingers etc., then infers the face too, present in the mirror, as conforming to the image.
Otherwise, even contact with a finger would cause him to think it has a different form and different nature.
He would suspect this.
Therefore he would not ascertain the similarity. // 27 //

Moreover, the reason is inconclusive due to the non-cessation of the speaker's intention — thus he says 'pratibimbeṣu' etc. 'Ekānta' means determination; that is the result of this, and 'anekānta' means its absence. How is there inconclusiveness? — therefore he says 'bimba' etc. For whatever image is perceived in the mirror, the face etc. are cognized as being just like that — hence there is similarity between the indicated and the indicator even here, and therefore the reason, pertaining to reflections, is inconclusive. Objection: But this is not inference — for the face is cognized as directly perceived through the visual ray reflected by the brilliance of the mirror — this will be stated in the <s>Śabdādhikaraṇa</s> (section on verbal testimony). Therefore he says 'na ca' etc.

children.text: astu vedaṃ pratyakṣaṃ, kimiti sūkṣmekṣikayā, viśadataramevānumānamupadarśayāma', yatra gamyagamakayo' sādṛśyamavagamyata
children.translated_text: Let this be perception — why, with subtle examination, do we not show inference more clearly, where the similarity between the indicated and indicator is understood? —
thus he says 'pratyakṣata' etc.
'Gatānām' (of those who have gone) — he shows non-perceptibility for the purpose of establishing the object of inference. // 28 //

children.text:
yadapīdamuktam--- śābde hi sakṛduktameva vākyaṃ sahasā nānārthān pratibhāsayati viruddhānaviruddhāṃśca, codanālakṣaṇor'tho dharma', śveto dhāvatīti ca yathā, naivamanumāne /
dhūmo hi yenaiva viditavyāptistatraikatraiva dhiyamādadhāti /
ata' śabdānumānayorbheda' /
prayogaśca bhavati--- śabdo 'numānād bhinna' ekadā nānārthapratibhāsādakṣavaditi /
anītaheturvā, liṅgamekameva
children.translated_text: As for what was said: 'In verbal testimony, a single utterance suddenly presents multiple meanings, both contradictory and non-contradictory — [for example] "the object designated by injunction is <s>dharma</s>," and "the white one runs" — but not so in inference. For smoke, having <s>vyāpti</s> known with one thing alone, produces cognition of that one thing alone. Hence there is a difference between verbal testimony and inference. And the formal argument would be: "Verbal testimony is different from inference because of the simultaneous appearance of multiple meanings, like the sense organs." Or the reason is unestablished [because] the inferential mark too, being one—'
For even of the inferential mark, such a nature has been seen, of both reason and contradicted;
if [you say] because of contradiction it is not inference, then for you too there would be non-<s>āgama</s> (non-scriptural) status. // Msv_5,5.30 //
And where there is unity of meaning in the sentence, there would be inference-status;
and when this is uttered once, only one intention is observed. // Msv_5,5.31 //
But the arising of multiple appearances from things whose meaning is undetermined—
that is seen even in the case of an unclear inferential mark; hence no difference is established by this. // Msv_5,5.32 //

children.text: prakāśayati, yathā dhūmādi,na ca tathā śabda',ato bhidyata iti /
children.translated_text: illuminates, just as smoke etc. — but words do not [illuminate] thus; hence they are different.
Having presented this, he refutes it — 'ekavākyāt' etc.
The meaning is: even by this mode, there is no difference. // 29 //

children.text:
kimiti na bhinnatā, ata āha---liṅgasyāpīti /
anaikāntiko hetiriti bhāva' /
heturhi dhūmo 'gnitvamuṣṇatvaṃ dāhakatvamindhanavikāratvaṃ ca ekadaiva pratipādayati /
tathā viruddha'- nitya' śabda' kṛtakatvāditi, vivakṣānusāreṇa tāvannityatāṃ pratipādayati, vyāptibalena cānityatvamato 'naikāntiko heturiti /
nanu na viruddho 'naikamartha pratipādayati, vyāptibalena hi liṅgaṃ pratipādakaṃ bhavati /
ata' kṛtakatvamanityatvena vyāptamiti tadeva gamayati, viruddhārthavyāptistvekasya virodhādeva na sambhavatīti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, 'being produced,' being pervaded by impermanence, indicates only that — but the <s>vyāpti</s> with a contradictory meaning is impossible because of the very contradiction of one [property with another].
He first raises this doubt — 'virodhāt' etc.
He gives the reply — 'syāt' etc.

children.text: vivakṣitārthapratipādane hi śabdasya śaktiravagatā, ata' so 'pyekadaikamarthaṃ pratipādayati, arthāntare tvasāvapi virodhādanāgamaka eveti ||30||
children.translated_text: For the capacity of words to convey the intended meaning is well known — hence they too indicate one meaning at a time; regarding another meaning, they too, because of contradiction, are non-indicative. // 30 //

Why is there no difference? — therefore he says 'liṅgasyāpi' etc. The purport is that the reason is inconclusive. For the reason — smoke — simultaneously indicates fire-ness, hotness, burning capacity, and being a transformation of fuel. Similarly, the contradicted [reason]: 'sound is permanent because of being produced' — following the speaker's intention, it indicates permanence, but through the force of <s>vyāpti</s>, it [indicates] impermanence — hence the reason is inconclusive. Objection: But the contradicted does not indicate multiple things — for the inferential mark indicates only through the force of <s>vyāpti</s>.

children.text: bhūyasāṃ caikārthānāṃ vākyānāṃ nānena hetunā bheda' sidhyatītyāha---yatraceti /
na kevalaṃ viruddhamanekaṃ śabdo na pratipādayati, kintu aviruddhamapi /
children.translated_text: Not only does a word not convey multiple contradictory [meanings], but it also does not [convey] non-contradictory [ones simultaneously].
This has been said: 'A word is a <s>pramāṇa</s> with respect to what is intended.'
And when uttered once, [only one meaning] is cognized.
Therefore, there is no conveyance of multiple meanings anywhere — hence the reason is unestablished — thus he says 'sakṛt' etc. // 31 //
And of the majority of sentences that have a single meaning, no difference is established by this reason — thus he says 'yatra ca' etc.

children.text:
nanvasti tāvadanekārthapratibhānaṃ śabdāta, pramāṇaṃ tvekatra bhavatu nāma, etāvatā ca siddhamanumānād vaidharmyamata āha---yastviti /
yathā hi
children.translated_text: Objection: But there is indeed the appearance of multiple meanings from words; let it be a <s>pramāṇa</s> for only one — even this much establishes the dissimilarity from inference — therefore he says 'yas tu' etc. Just as—
The non-statement of the example is deviant in the case of smoke etc.;
for even there, because of its being well-known, the example is not stated. // Msv_5,5.33 //
But when the word is unfamiliar, one requires the memory of the related [meaning];

children.text: atra prayukta ityevaṃ budhyante hi cirāt kvacit // Msv_5,5.34 //
children.translated_text: for in some cases, they understand only after a long time 'it was used in this sense.' // Msv_5,5.34 //
And the reasons stated by others have not precluded the non-difference;
the identity of verbal testimony and inference, like the inference of fire from smoke. // Msv_5,5.35 //
Because of arising from positive and negative concomitance, and because of arising from the observation of a single perceptible [instance],
and because of being preceded by the [knowledge of] relation, and because of the cognition arising therefrom— // Msv_5,5.36 //
