children.translated_text: existence is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for absence. And that will be explained later in two ways: 'either the non-transformation of the self [is absence], or absence is the cognition of what does not exist.' Or [the alternative is]: 'the ground alone is apprehended and nothing else exists'—this is the cognition. Granted. What is its object? The absence of the knowable is deployed fourfold. For in the absence of that [absence as a valid category], activities such as walking and the like, which are preceded by the ascertainment of the absence of thorns and the like, would not be possible—and that too, if the absence has no knowability, would not be possible. If the ground alone is apprehended here and there is no discrimination of thorns and the like, then even when they exist, it would be apprehended—and so it would be grasped by the cognition 'it does not exist.' But those of corrupted intellect are contradicted by experience itself. For the manifestation of existence and non-existence is not differentiated. As for what was said—'the cognition of that alone is designated as "the pot does not exist"'—there we do not know what is excluded by the word 'alone.' If it excludes nothing, then it is meaningless. If it does exclude something, then there is an object of exclusion—otherwise the expression 'it excludes' would apply at all times. This is the distinguishing feature of the cognition 'that alone' from the cognition of admixture: that it has a discriminated object. And the discrimination from another object is absence. If [you say] 'the cognition alone is the object, not anything beyond it'—then that [cognition] would manifest as both 'exists' and 'does not exist' even when the connection is apprehended. Moreover, what is negated here—that is said to be non-existent there. And here, the cognition 'the pot does not exist' is not negated—for when [the pot] is within the range of cognition, the word 'does not exist' would [entail] the absence of cognition itself. But if it is said that the meaning of 'the pot does not exist' is 'the ground alone is apprehended'—ordinary people do not understand it thus, to begin with. Moreover, in this case, there would be no inquiry into the existence or non-existence of a subtle entity. For if absence is not something at all, then when an entity is apprehended, what is this additional doubt regarding subtle things like hair-tips and the like? The apprehension of that alone is [said to be] the absence of other entities—and that is already known and not to be doubted, since cognition is self-luminous. What more is to be investigated? If [you say] 'the cognition of that alone is absence when the counter-positive is visible, not when invisible'—but what then [constitutes] invisibility, when absence does not differ from cognition? If absence were a separate category, then for its ascertainment the visibility of the thing would be useful. For the contact of self, sense organ, mind, and object is the cause of the generation of knowledge. When, even though the sense organs and the like are present and unimpaired, the sought object is not seen even when searched for with effort, then, from the non-seeing, it is imagined that [the object] is absent. Thus, the inquiry into subtlety for the purpose of establishing visibility is proper. But if absence is [merely] the apprehension of that alone, the qualification of visibility for an invisible object would be pointless. As for what was said—'the cause of absence is the cognition of that alone, because of the parsimony of postulation'—that is not correct. For parsimony of postulation cannot override what is established by a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Nor is it correct [to say] that the cause of absence is the cognition of that alone. For a hammer-blow and the like are the cause of absence, and yet the cognition of 'that alone' is not generated by them. For the manifestation of the nature of the ground and such objects is caused by the sense organs and the like, and that [manifestation] does not require the removal of a pot or a blow. As for what was said—'non-seeing that is not ascertained does not determine absence, because of the unwanted consequence in deep sleep'—that is not correct. For absence does not manifest without a support when the entity has not been grasped; somewhere, indeed, the absence of something appears—not independently. Hence he says: 'it is not generated in the form of a thing.' And nothing at all appears to one in deep sleep. Where would one discern absence? Moreover, it is the non-arising of the appropriate <s>pramāṇa</s> that determines absence. But for one in deep sleep, there is no object that is appropriate for the <s>pramāṇa</s> and that does not manifest—so how can the determination of absence arise? Therefore, non-seeing is not [merely] not-grasped—hence for one in deep sleep, absence does not manifest; rather, this [absence requires] appropriate non-seeing, which does not obtain [in sleep]. And as for what was also said—'even when non-seeing has ceased, the non-existence of something previously [present] is predicated even of what is presently being seen'—that is not so. For there, among many things equally fit to be remembered that are being remembered, when one alone is not remembered, through the cessation of memory—and consequently through the cessation of perception—the absence of that is cognized, by memory itself [cognizing] the existence of other things. The absence at that time and the cessation of memory are indeed present at that time. And [something] is not cognized [that does not manifest]. But [the cognition] makes known the past absence alone—hence there is no infinite regress. Therefore, the cognition 'does not exist' is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, and absence, differentiated into <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence) and the like, is the knowable—this is the established position. The meaning then is as follows: Where the five <s>pramāṇas</s>, capable of generating the cognition of the existence of a real entity such as cloth and the like as appropriate, do not arise—in that domain, absence has the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. By this he has shown that the word '<s>pramāṇa</s>' is used for the group of five <s>pramāṇas</s> from the context. And 'it is not generated in the form of a thing' shows that the mere independent cognition of absence is not a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And from the statement of the definition of worldly <s>pramāṇa</s>, only where the capacity of the <s>pramāṇas</s> is possible—the non-arising of those very [<s>pramāṇas</s>] is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the determination of absence. For it is by this very [means] that ordinary people understand 'it does not exist.' And this is also the meaning of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>: 'Absence too—ordinary people do not understand "it does not exist" [otherwise].' Because of non-deviation. For the absence of <s>pramāṇa</s>, in the case of an object not in contact [with the senses] called absence, manifesting in the form 'does not exist,' generates a cognition—and that is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for absence.
And the establishment of the non-confusion of substances depends on the validity of that [absence-pramāṇa].

children.text: kṣīre dadhyādi yannāsti prāgabhāva' sa ucyate // Msv_5,8.2 //
children.translated_text: The yogurt and such that does not exist in milk—that is called <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence). // Msv_5,8.2 //
The non-existence of milk in yogurt is accepted as <s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s> (destructional absence).
The absence of horse and such in a cow—that is called <s>anyonyābhāva</s> (mutual absence). // Msv_5,8.3 //
The parts on the head [of a hare] that are hollow, devoid of growth and hardness—
in the form of hare's horns and the like—that is called <s>atyantābhāva</s> (absolute absence). // Msv_5,8.4 //

children.text: kṣīre dadhi bhavedevaṃ dadhni kṣīraṃ ghaṭe paṭa' /
children.translated_text: In this way, yogurt would exist in milk, milk in yogurt, cloth in a pot,

children.text: śaśe śṛṅgaṃ pṛthivyādau caitanyaṃ mūrtarātmani // Msv_5,8.5 //
children.translated_text: horns on a hare, consciousness in earth and the like, and [consciousness] in embodied selves. // Msv_5,8.5 //
And there is no possibility of deviation for [an absence] of this kind.
And even what is separated [from this context], through the force of expectancy, the cognition that it generates—that should be connected [with the above].
'That by which something is related, even when distant, by that very thing that [relation obtains]'—
by this principle. // 1 //

children.text: yatra vastusadbhāvabodhārthaṃ yogyapramāṇānudayastatrābhāva' pramāṇamityuktam,kiṃ punastatrānena pramīyate, abhāvastāvat svapramāṇaireva yathāsvamavagamyate, ata āha---vastvaśaṅkaraiti ||1 1/2||
children.translated_text: Where it was said that the non-arising of the appropriate <s>pramāṇa</s> for the cognition of the existence of a real entity is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for absence there—what then is measured by this? To begin with, absence is cognized by its own <s>pramāṇas</s> respectively. Therefore he says—'vastvasaṅkara' (non-confusion of substances) etc. // 1½ //

children.text:
vastvasaṅkarameva vivṛṇoti--- kṣīre dadhīti sārdhadvayena /
yo 'yaṃ kāryakāraṇādinā parasparavivekaścaturdhā darśita' sa vastvaṅkara ityākhyāyate /

children.translated_text: That is measured by absence.
'In the form of hare's horns and the like'—
when examined in that form, the parts on the head of a hare are absences,
but in their own nature, they are indeed existents. // 2-4 //

He elaborates the non-confusion of substances—'kṣīre dadhi' etc. with two and a half [verses]. The fourfold distinction shown through cause-effect and the like is called non-confusion of substances (<s>vastvasaṅkara</s>).

children.text:
asati tvabhāvaprāmāṇye sarva' sarveṇa saṅkīryata ityāha--- kṣīra iti dvayena /

mahābhūtānāṃ ca vāyvādīnā
children.translated_text: But if the validity of absence [as a pramāṇa] is not [accepted], everything would be confused with everything—hence he says—'kṣīre' etc. with two [verses]. 'Evam' (in this way) means: just as yogurt in milk, so milk in yogurt—such is the meaning. From 'hare's horns' onward, the faults consequent upon the non-establishment of absolute absence [are shown]. For without relying on the <s>pramāṇa</s> of absence, the absolute absence of horns and the like in hares and such is not established. And the opponents who maintain that the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) possess consciousness cannot be refuted. And of the great elements—<s>Vāyu</s> and the like—

children.text: apsu gandho rasaścagnau vāyau rūpeṇa tau saha /
children.translated_text: odor and taste in water, in fire—along with those two, form in wind,

children.text: vyomni saṃsparśitā te ca na decasya pramāṇatā // Msv_5,8.6 //
children.translated_text: tangibility and those [others] in space—[if so,] the <s>pramāṇa</s>-status of the sense organs would not obtain. // Msv_5,8.6 //
And this worldly practice of distinguishing causes and effects would not exist,
if absence differentiated into <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence) and the like does not exist. // Msv_5,8.7 //
These divisions would not belong to a non-entity—hence its thinghood [is established].

children.text: kāryādīnāmabhāva' ko yo bhāva' kāraṇādinā // Msv_5,8.8 //
children.translated_text: What is the absence of effects and the like, which is the existence of causes and such? // Msv_5,8.8 //
the absolute absence of odor and the like [in certain elements] would not be established.
For the established position is that the four great elements, successively, are each devoid of one quality. // 5, 6 //
He states the fault in the case of universal confusion—'na ca' etc.

children.text: yo 'yaṃ kāraṇādivibhāgena laukikānāṃ vyavahāro dṛśyate, sarvasaṅkare na syāt, kṣīramānayeti niyukto yat kṣīramevānayati na dadhi, dadhyānayane kṣīram, idamasati kāryakāraṇādīnāmatiretaraviveke na sidhyatīti ||7||
children.translated_text: The worldly practice that is observed through the distinction of causes and the like would not obtain if there were universal confusion. When commanded 'bring milk,' the fact that one brings only milk and not yogurt, [and] milk when [commanded to bring] yogurt—this would not be established without the mutual discrimination of cause-effect and the like. // 7 //

itaścabhāvo
children.translated_text: Now, absence is not apprehended as a separate category. For we cognize the ground through its own <s>pramāṇa</s>, and when no <s>pramāṇa</s> is present, we do not see the pot — but there is no other thing called 'absence of the pot' in the cognition. Even in 'the pot does not exist,' the meaning is 'the pot is not cognized' — not that 'the absence of the pot is cognized.' Therefore, absence is merely characterized by the freedom from all designations, not any separate category — hence he says 'nor also.' As for [the objection] that it is not apprehended by the <s>pramāṇas</s> of positive entities — true, and for this very reason absence is a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>. Even in 'the pot does not exist,' the meaning is not 'the pot is not cognized,' for even an existing pot is said to be 'not cognized.' For this very reason, one who is asked 'does the pot exist or not?' and has not ascertained the absence, designates mere non-apprehension — not absence — as 'it does not exist.' Therefore, this 'the pot does not exist' is indeed a cognition of absence. And the fourfold division that was described — that too is not established in an absence characterized by freedom from all designations. And the argument can be formulated: A real entity is fourfold, because of its fourfold division, like substance and the like. As for what they say — 'Absence is not any category; for blue and the like are mutually differentiated by their own nature, specific to each object; but there is nothing that differentiates absence from a positive entity; therefore, we do not apprehend it as distinct — so how can we establish it as a separate category? But the practical usage regarding it — in the form of the application of conceptual construction and words such as "does not exist" — is to be somehow accounted for as based on positive entities alone; it is not the case that one absence, confined to a single form and unassociated with others, is different from another absence.' That too has been refuted merely by refuting the partial view. Moreover, if the conceptual construction 'does not exist' has no object, how is it cognized? — this must be stated. For the object of conceptual construction is a form associated with verbal expression, and that does not exist here. Nor is the self fit to be associated with verbal expression in conceptual construction, because of its uncommon nature. For this very reason, since the self is non-conceptual, conceptual construction is said to be self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvitti</s>) — i.e., perception. As [<s>Dignāga</s>] states: 'This [self-awareness] does not associate it [the self] with verbal expression. Likewise, because of the contradiction of such a function with respect to the self.' If it is thought: 'Just as in the case of universal and the like, conceptual constructions of absence too have superimposed objects — so the conceptual construction of absence is not thereby refuted' — that is not so. For whatever is universal-like and superimposed, that is different in each conceptual construction — how could it be the basis of a single word? Among [entities] with differences of constructed forms, there is some single unifier who, from the ascertainment of unity superimposed on the prior and the posterior, would employ a single word. But conceptual constructions, being momentary and confined to their own object, do not enter into each other's domain — so how could they unify? And in the absence of this reversal [of the position], the statement of having superimposed objects is simply false. Therefore, one must necessarily accept some real form, called 'absence' like 'existence,' which is in contact with the single word 'does not exist,' though it is not permanent. For this very reason, when asked 'what then is reality?,' reality has been taken in only two ways by those who know reality: 'The existence of what exists, and the existence of what does not exist is its being non-existent.' Moreover, if absence does not exist, for what reason is there non-apprehension of the destroyed pot? If [you say] because of its being destroyed — what is destruction? If it is nothing, then there would follow apprehension as before. For we now see no cause for the non-apprehension of a pot whose prior capacity for causal efficacy has not departed, if destruction is not accepted as some other category — thus, it is established as a separate category. And this [argument about] the indesignability of absence was stated in order to refute [the objection]: 'But absence is not a real entity, because it contradicts common usage.' For just as 'the moonless one is the moon' contradicts common usage, so does 'absence is a real entity.' For existence is reality, and that is not present in absence — so the claim of reality [for absence] is not in the primary sense. But absence is indeed capable of causal efficacy, as it is seen to produce cognition. And in the case of non-performance of a prescribed act, prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) itself, as a qualifier of another action, is the cause of sin (<s>pratyavāya</s>). Similarly, the establishment of reality in what follows too is to be understood. For this further reason too, absence
is a real entity — whether apprehended by cognitions of co-occurrence (<s>anuvṛtti</s>) or of exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>),

children.text: tasmād gavādivad vastu prameyatvācca gamyate // Msv_5,8.9 //
children.translated_text: therefore, like a cow and the like, it is a real entity, and it is known because it is an object of valid knowledge (<s>prameya</s>). // 9 //
And neither figurativeness nor erroneous cognition by chance
obtains; therefore, the nature of possessing universal and particular is not false. // 10 //

children.text:
vastvityāho---- kāyādīnamiti /
vastveva sadasadātmakamiti siddhānta' /
tatra kathaṃ vasturūpasyaivābhāvasya ni' svabhāvatvam /
kimidānīṃ bhāvābhāvayorabheda eva, neti vadāma', bhedo 'pi hyanayordharmadharmitayā kiyānapyastyeva rūpādīnāmiva /
ka' punaranayo' sambandha', saṃyoga' samavāyo vā, na tāvatsaṃyoga', dravyadharmatvāt tasya /
na ca samavāya', bhāvābhāvaprasaṅgāt /
abhāvasamavāye hi bhāvo na syādeva /
nābhāvasamavāyādasattvam, na hi ghaṭo 'bhāvasamavāyādasan bhavati /
asati samavāyānupapatte' /

children.translated_text: Rather, the absence of the pot [arises] from the impact [that destroys it] alone.

children.text: yattvanāhatamanapasāraṃ ca bhāvāntaramabhāvarūpeṇāvagamyate tat kathamasad bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: But that which is apprehended as something of the nature of absence — something other than the positive entity that has not been struck and has not departed — how could that be non-existent?

children.text: ata' svahetoreva jāyamāno nityo vā sarvo 'saṅkīrṇasvabhāva eva jāyata iti siddhamasya jātyādivad bhāvadharmatvam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, every [absence], arising from its own cause alone, or being eternal, arises with an unmixed inherent nature — thus its property-status with respect to the positive entity, like that of universals and the like, is established.
And therefrom, its reality. // 8 //

A real entity — hence he says 'of bodies and the like.' The established conclusion is: a real entity alone is of the nature of both existence and non-existence. Given this, how can non-existence, which is of the nature of a real entity, lack inherent nature? What then — is there simply no difference between positive entity and absence? No — we say that there is indeed some difference between them too, in the manner of property and property-bearer, just as in the case of form and the like. But what is the relation between these two — conjunction or inherence? Not conjunction, because that is a property of substance. Nor inherence, because of the undesirable consequence of [requiring] positive entity and absence [of the inherence relation itself]. For if absence inhered [in a positive entity], the positive entity would simply not exist. Nor does the positive entity become non-existent through the inherence of absence — for a pot does not become non-existent through the inherence of absence, because of the impossibility of inherence in what does not exist.
For this further reason too, absence is a real entity — hence he says 'whether' ending in 'real entity.'

children.text: abhāva iti sāmānyātmanā prāgabhāvādibedena ca vyāvṛttyātmanā gṛhyamāṇo 'bhāva' sāmānyaviśeṣātmaka', tataśca vastuviṣayaprayogārtha'--- abhāvo vsatu, sāmānyaviśeṣātmakatvāt gavādivaditi /
children.translated_text: Absence, apprehended in its general nature as 'absence' and in its exclusion-nature through the division into prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and the like, possesses both universal and particular nature; and therefore, for the argument targeting the real-entity-status: 'Absence is a real entity, because it possesses the nature of universal and particular, like a cow and the like.'
He states another reason for the same thesis — 'because of being an object of valid knowledge.' // 9 //

children.text:
nanvayamasiddho hetu',aupacāriko hi sāmānyaviśeṣabhāvo 'bhāve /
ekaśabdavācyaṃ sāmānyarūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ gavādi, nānāśabdavācyaṃ ca viśeṣarūpaṃ śābaleyādi /

children.translated_text: Therefore, here too the universal-particular nature is merely figurative for one who has discriminating knowledge.

children.text: asati tu viveke ekaśabdanibandhanabhrama evāyam--- abhāva' sāmānyaviśevātmeti /
children.translated_text: But in the absence of discrimination, this [attribution] — 'absence possesses the nature of universal and particular' — is simply an error based on a single word.
Hence he says — 'nor also.'

children.text: sati hi bādhake bhrāntirupacāro vā kalpyate, na ceha tatheti bhāva iti ||10||
children.translated_text: For figurativeness or error is postulated when there is a sublating cognition, and there is none such here — this is the purport. // 10 //

Now, this reason is unestablished, for the universal-particular nature in absence is merely figurative. What is seen as having a universal form, being denoted by a single word, is a cow and the like; and what is seen as having a particular form, being denoted by different words, is <s>Śābalī</s> (a particular cow) and the like.
The non-arising of perception and the like is called the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>;
or the non-transformation of the self; or the cognition of another object. // 11 //
In a real entity that is eternally of the nature of both existence and non-existence,

children.text: vastuni jñāyate kaiścidrūpaṃ kiñcit kadācana // Msv_5,8.12 //
children.translated_text: by its own form and by the form of others, some aspect is known by some [cognizers] at some time. // 12 //
In whichever [entity], wherever, whatever has become manifest, or the desire to grasp arises,
the experience of that is cognized and is designated by that [aspect]. // 13 //

children.text:
evaṃ tāvat 'vāstītyasyārthasyāsannikṛṣṭasya' iti yadutaktaṃ bhāṣye tad vivṛtam /
idānīṃ pramāṇābāvaśabdaṃ vyācaṣṭe---pratyakṣāderanutpattiriti /
anutpattireva keti cedata āha--- sātmana iti /
children.translated_text: The non-arising of what, exactly? To this he says — 'of the self.'
For the transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of the self is of the nature of cognition.

children.text: tad yadā ātmā bhūtalādau na ghaṭādijñānātmanā piraṇamati sā tasya pratyakṣādyanutpatti' svarūpāvasthānaṃ pramāṇābhāva ityākhyāyate, tatprāmāṇye ca nāstīti jñānaṃ phalam /
children.translated_text: When the self does not transform in the form of cognition of a pot and the like with respect to the ground and such, that non-arising of perception and the like — the remaining in its own form — is called 'absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>'; and when that is authoritative, the cognition 'does not exist' is its result.

children.text: nāstītyeva vā bhāvajñānaṃ pratyakṣādyanutpattirityucyate, atastadeva pramāṇam, (nā?hā) nādibuddhi' phalamiti viveka' ||11||
children.translated_text: Or alternatively, the very cognition that '[it] does not exist' in relation to a positive entity — the non-arising of perception and the like — is itself called [the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>]; therefore, that itself is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, and the cognition 'does not exist' is the result — this is the distinction. // 11 //

Thus, what was stated in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> — 'of this meaning that is "does not exist," which is not in proximity [to the senses]' — has been elaborated. Now he explains the term 'absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>' — 'the non-arising of perception and the like.'

children.text: nanu yadi dvyātmakaṃ vastu, tarhi sakṛdeva tathā pratibhātagiti kiṃ pramāṇāntareṇāta āha--- svarūpeti /
children.translated_text: Now, if a real entity has a dual nature, then it should appear as such all at once — so what is the need for another <s>pramāṇa</s>? Hence he says — 'by its own form.'
That real entity — a cow, for example — is of the form of existence by its own nature, and of the form of non-existence by the nature of a horse and the like.

children.text: tadasminneva dvirūpe kiñcideva kadācit pratīyate na tu sarvātmakameva gṛhītavyamiti niyama iti ||12||
children.translated_text: In this very dual-natured [entity], only some [aspect] is cognized at some time — there is no rule that it must be grasped in its entirety. // 12 //

children.text:
kiṃ puna' kāraṇaṃ dvyātmakasyaikameva rūpaṃ gṛhyate nāparaṃ kiñcidata āha---yasya yatreti /
udbhūtaṃ hi gṛhyate nānudabhūtam, agneriva rātrau rūpaṃ na sparśa', jidhṛkṣitaṃ vā prāyeṇa /
ato yadeva sadasatorudbhūtaṃ bhavati tenaiva buddhivyapadeśau bhavata' /
cetyate 'nubhava iti kimidam, na hyanubhavaścetyate, sa eva cetanā, viṣayastu cetyate /
children.translated_text: 'Is cognized' and 'experience' — what does this mean? For experience is not what is cognized; it itself is cognition. Rather, it is the object that is cognized.
True.
Because of the impossibility of accounting for it otherwise than through the attainment of the object, experience too is indeed cognized.
By this mode, [the verse] shows precisely the illumination of the object — so there is no fault. // 13 //

But what is the reason that of the dual-natured [entity], only one form is grasped and not the other? Hence he says — 'in whichever, wherever.' For what is manifest is grasped, not what is unmanifest — just as at night, the form of fire, not its touch, [is prominent]; or generally what is desired to be grasped [is grasped]. Therefore, whatever of the existent and non-existent [aspects] becomes manifest, by that alone do cognition and designation occur.
Of the other [aspect] that functions as subsidiary to that [cognized aspect], there is a portion;
in the cognition of both, there is indeed the concomitance of both. // 14 //

children.text: ayameveti yo hyeṣa bhāve bhavati nirṇaya' /
children.translated_text: The determination 'this alone' that occurs with respect to a positive entity —
this is not [possible] without the concomitance of the cognition of the absence of another real entity. // 15 //
And the cognition 'does not exist' too is not [possible] without the concomitance of a real entity;
no cognition whatsoever arises without a supporting basis. // 16 //
But the entry of perception and the like [occurs] when the positive-entity aspect is grasped;
[their] operation is the non-arising [of cognition] when the absence-aspect is desired to be grasped. // 17 //
To begin with, this cognition 'does not exist' is not produced by the sense-organs;
for the contact of the sense-organ is only with the positive-entity aspect, because of its fitness [for that alone]. // 18 //
When the manifest or the desired-to-be-grasped alone is apprehended, the other [aspect] remains present only as a subsidiary, in a latent state —
just as when one of the two — universal and particular — is grasped, the other [remains latent] — hence he says 'of that.'
And this has been stated by us through a following-upon statement.
But there is indeed the concomitance of the other in the cognition of both positive entity and absence — hence he says 'of both.' // 14 //
means: unmixed with another positive entity — that is the meaning.

children.text: na hyapratisaṃhite bhāvāntarābāve saṅkīrṇasvabhāvo na niścetuṃ śakyate /
children.translated_text: For without the exclusion of another positive entity, something of mixed nature cannot be ascertained.
Even in the negation 'does not exist,' no cognition arises without the support of both that which is negated and that which negates.

children.text: kiñcicchabdena bhāvasyābhāvānugamaśūnyamapi jñānamastyeva, na tvevabhāvasyeti darśayati ||15,16||
children.translated_text: By the word 'some' he shows that there is indeed cognition of a positive entity devoid of the concomitance of absence — but not [cognition] of absence [devoid of the concomitance of a positive entity]. // 15, 16 //
He demonstrates the concomitance of both — 'this alone' with two [verses]. 'This alone' —
Thus it has been shown that a real entity is of the nature of both existence and non-existence,
and that at some time only some [aspect] is experienced.
He now shows the division of <s>pramāṇas</s> for the two aspects — 'perception and the like.' // 17 //

children.text:
kathaṃ punaridamavagamyate, visphāritākṣasya hi sahasā neha ghaṭo 'sti, aghaṭaṃ vā bhūtalamityabhāvaviśiṣṭaṃ bhūtalajñānaṃ jāyamānamupalabhyate?daṇḍipratyakṣavat, tadabhāvasyāpratyakṣatve nāvakalpate /
na hyapratyakṣa eva viśeṣaṇe viśiṣṭa' pratyakṣo bhavati, daṇḍa iva daṇḍī /
na ca nāstyeva viśiṣṭā dhīriti vaktavyam, anāśrayābhāvasaṃvittyabhāvāt /
api cātmā bhāvasyābhāva', sa kathaṃ svatantro 'nubhūyate /
na hi rūpādayo bhāvadharmā' svatantrā evāvasīyante /
svatantrābhāvavādastu svātantryameva, sadasadātmake vastunīti hi darśayati /
bhāvāṃśo 'bhāvāṃśa iti ca vispaṣṭaṃ tadabhāvaviśiṣṭaṃ grahaṇamityāha /
kiñcāsya svātantrye pramāṇam, na hyaṃ kadācidapi tathāvasīyate /
kimidānīmabhāvo nāvasīyata eva, svatantro vāvasīyate /
na tāvat pūrva' kalpa',tadavagame pramāṇāntarābhāvāt nityāsaṃvittisaṅgāt /
na ca saṃyogapratiṣedhe svatantrābhāvāvasāyo 'sti, pratiyogisaṃyogparatiṣedhātmai va hyabhāva', sa cādhāratantra eveti saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatvalakṣaṇayā pratyāsattyā satīndriyasannikarṣe aindriyajñānagocara eva /
ekaṃ hīdaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ jñānam /
tadasyābhāva' pramāṇamindriyaṃ vā, yadyabhāva' sa tarhi bhāvamapi gocarayet /
na caitadiṣṭam /
ata' satyupalabhyamāne tadaiva yannopalabhyate tannāstīti sata eva prakāśakamasato 'pīti na pramāṇavibhāgaṃ paśyāma' /
ata āha--- na tāvaditi /
tāvacchadoliṅgāpekṣayā /
taccopariṣṭhānnirākariṣyata iti /
atra kāraṇamāha--- bhāvāṃśeti /
yogyatā hi kāryadarśanasamadhigamyā, sā cendriyāṇāṃ bhāvātmakagrahaṇa evopalabhyate nābhāve 'pi /
vināpi tu tena tadgrahaṇāditi vakṣyāma' /
atra tu yogyatāsahitā prāptirindriyārthayo' sambandha ityabhiprāya' /
yattvekajñānasaṃsargiṇorekapramāṇatvamiti /
tanna /
ekasyā api buddhernānākāraṇatvadarśanāt /
ekaṃ hīdaṃ bhāvanendriyasamāhārajaṃ pratyabhijñānamiti vakṣyāma' /
ekajñānapratibhāsinorapi ca gṛhyamāṇasmaryamāṇayorviveka ukta' /
viviktā eva te hyarthā iti /
na hi smṛtyupasthāpitanāmaviśiṣṭo ḍittho na pratyakṣo bhavati /
nāma cāpratyakṣaṃ smaryamāṇatvāt, tasyāgṛhīte hi viśeṣaṇe viśiṣṭo nāvagamyate nāpratyakṣe /
evamihāpi pramāṇābhāvopanītābhāvaviśiṣṭe satyupalabhyamāne na kiñcidanupapannam /
daṇḍinyapi śābde tāvad daṇḍapadopanītaviśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭa eva pratyayārtho na daṇḍo 'pi /
pratyakṣaṃ tu yogyatayobhayatra pravartatāṃ nāma, na caivamubhayatrākṣāṇāṃ yogyatā /
abhāvajñāne tadanapekṣāyā
children.translated_text: [continuing] How then is this understood? For when one with eyes wide open suddenly [perceives] "There is no pot here" or "The ground is pot-less," a cognition of the ground qualified by absence is seen to arise. Like the perception of the staff-bearer — if the absence of that [staff] were imperceptible, this would not be possible. For a <s>viśiṣṭa</s> (qualified entity) whose qualifier is imperceptible does not become perceptual, just as a staff-bearer [is perceived through] the staff. Nor should it be said that there is simply no qualified cognition, because of the impossibility of cognition of absence without a substrate. Moreover, absence is the <s>ātman</s> (nature) of an existent entity — how then is it experienced independently? For <s>rūpa</s> (form) and other properties of the existent are not ascertained independently. But the doctrine of independent absence-[cognition] shows that there is independence with respect to the entity that has both the existent and non-existent aspects. The fact that there is a being-aspect and an absence-aspect clearly means that the apprehension is of that [substrate] qualified by absence — hence he says "being-aspect." Moreover, what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for its independence? For it is never ascertained in that way. Now then, is absence not ascertained at all, or is it ascertained independently? Not the first alternative, because in the absence of another <s>pramāṇa</s> for its cognition, there would be the consequence of perpetual non-cognition. Nor is there an independent ascertainment of absence in the negation of conjunction, for absence is just the negation of the conjunction of the counter-correlate, and that depends on the substrate — therefore, when there is the sense-organ contact characterized by the relation of qualified-qualifier, it falls within the domain of sensory cognition. For this is one qualified cognition. Is its <s>pramāṇa</s> the absence or the sense-organ? If absence [is the <s>pramāṇa</s>], then it would also make the existent entity its object — but that is not desired. Therefore, when the apprehended [substrate] is present, that which is not apprehended at the same time does not exist — thus [the sense-organ], being a revealer of what exists, also [reveals] what does not exist — so we do not see a distinction of <s>pramāṇas</s>. Hence he says "not indeed" — the word "indeed" is with reference to the marks of <s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony). And that will be refuted later. He states the reason — "being-aspect." For capacity is ascertained through the observation of effects, and the capacity of the sense-organs is found only in the grasping of existents, not also in [grasping] absence. But we shall say that even without that, there is grasping of it. Here, however, the intention is that the contact of sense-organ and object is <s>prāpti</s> (reaching) accompanied by capacity. As for what was said — that two things appearing in one cognition have one <s>pramāṇa</s> — that is not so, because even of a single cognition, multiple causes are observed. For we shall say that this is a recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) born from the combination of the existent [entity perceived] through the sense-organs. And even of two things appearing in one cognition — the grasped and the remembered — the distinction has been stated: "those objects are indeed distinct." For an individual (<s>Ḍitthaḥ</s>) qualified by a name presented through memory is not imperceptible. And the name is imperceptible because it is remembered — for without grasping that qualifier, the qualified is not cognized, nor [is it cognized] when [the qualifier is] imperceptible. Similarly here too, when what is qualified by absence — presented through the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> — is an apprehended [substrate], nothing is untenable. Even in the verbal cognition of a staff-bearer, the object of cognition is only [the person] qualified by the qualifier presented through the word "staff" — not the staff independently. But let perception operate in both [domains] through capacity — yet the sense-organs do not have capacity in both. Because in the cognition of absence, there is no dependence on that [sense-organ].
Objection: Since [absence] is non-different from the existent, there is contact with it too —
but there is no absolute non-difference, nor here as with <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like. // 19 //

children.text: dharmayorbheda iṣṭo hi dharmyabhede 'pi na' sthite /
children.translated_text: For the difference of the two properties (<s>dharmas</s>) is accepted even though the non-difference of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) is maintained;
and because of the nature of emergence and suppression, the [distinction in] apprehension is established. // 20 //

children.text:
vakṣyamāṇatvāt /
kimidānīmanumāne 'pi pratyakṣānumānasamāhārajo viśiṣṭabodha' /
na /
anumānasyānvayādhīnajaṃmatvāt /
viśiṣṭenaiva cānvayānugamāt /
dhūmavānagnimāniti hi vyāptiravagatā /
uktaṃ ca---
"naivaṃ na hyatra liṅgasya śaktyanantatvakalpanā" iti /
atrāpi cāyamagnimāniti viśeṣabodhe 'styeva pratyakṣāpekṣā /
ayamevābhāvasya pratītiprakāra', yatpramāṇāntaraprāpitāśrayaṃ viśinaṣṭīti na kiñcidanupapamannam /

children.translated_text: As for what was said — that through the relation of qualified-qualifier, the sense-contact belongs to absence — that is not proper,
because the qualifier-status of what is unconnected is untenable, and because of over-extension;
otherwise, when the contact is established merely through what is desired for the qualifier,
the resort to the status of being the object of qualified-qualifier conjunction is pointless — enough with this. // 18 //

Because of what will be stated later. Now then, in inference too, is the qualified cognition a composite born from perception and inference? No — because the birth of inference depends on <s>anvaya</s> (co-presence), and because <s>anvaya</s> is ascertained only through the qualified [entity]. For the <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) is cognized as "that which has smoke has fire." And it has been said: "Not so — for here there is no need to postulate infinite capacities of the mark." And here too, in the cognition of the particular "this has fire," there is indeed dependence on perception. This is precisely the mode of cognition of absence — that the <s>pramāṇa</s> determines what is presented through the substrate obtained from another <s>pramāṇa</s> — so nothing is untenable.
And there is the reaching of the sense-organ by absence, which is non-different from the existent, just like the existent itself.

children.text: atra ca yogyatāyā uddhāṭanenaivottaraṃ deyam, tadupekṣyaiva tāvadatyantābhedamevāyamāha, tadetameva tāvannirākaro(ṣī?mī)tyabhiprāyeṇāha--- nahīti /
children.translated_text: And here, the reply should be given precisely by pointing out capacity (<s>yogyatā</s>); disregarding that for now, he first states the absolute non-difference — with the intention "let me refute just this for now" — hence he says "not indeed."

children.text: yadi bhāvābhāvayorekāntaramabheda eva syāt tato bhāvendriyasannikarṣe tadabhinnasyābhāvasyāpi syāt, na tvevamasti /
children.translated_text: If there were absolute non-difference between existence and absence, then when there is sense-contact with the existent, there would also be [contact] with absence that is non-different from it — but this is not so.
Because even for absence, as for <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like, there is no absolute non-difference. // 19 //
Not understanding the intention, he raises an objection — "objection." For mere reaching (<s>prāpti</s>) of the object and sense-organ is [their] contact.

children.text:
rūpāditulyatāmevābhāvasya darśayati---dharmayoriti /
bhāvābhāvātmanordharmayordharmyabhede 'pi sthite bhedo 'pīṣṭa ityartha' /

children.translated_text: He states the reason for the difference — "emergence."
Even of existence and absence, the distinction in apprehension and non-apprehension of the emerged and the suppressed is observed.
And this cannot be conceived if oneness is postulated.

children.text: na hyekameva tattvamudbhūtamabhibhūtaṃ ceti pratīyata iti ||20||
children.translated_text: For one and the same entity is not experienced as both emerged and suppressed. // 20 //

He shows the similarity of absence with <s>rūpa</s> and the like — "of the two properties." Even though the non-difference of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) consisting of existence and absence is maintained, the difference [of the two properties] is also accepted — this is the meaning.
And this itself is experienced as the ground of the distinction —
the cognitions of existence and absence have connection with the sense-organs, [while absence-cognition has] non-dependence on sense-organs. // 21 //
And some describe the difference of <s>rūpa</s> (form) and the like too as based on the difference of the cognizer;
just as one and the same person has the forms of son and the like. // 22 //
The difference in <s>rūpa</s> and the like is always merely cognition-made;
and for those that are undifferentiated in space and the like, there is no postulation of an aggregate. // 23 //
And this is the ground of the distinction between them — hence he says "this itself."
And the non-dependence of absence-cognition on sense-organs will be stated later. // 21 //

children.text: ayaṃ ca grāhakabhedanibandhano bhedo rūpādīnāmiti kaiścidiṣyate /

children.translated_text: That can be understood for these two [existence and absence] as well — hence he says "of <s>rūpa</s> and the like."

children.text: evaṃ hi kecid vadanti--- yathā hyekameva mukhaṃ maratakapadmarāgādyupādhibhedād bhinnamiva pratibhāti, yathā caika eva puruṣo 'pekṣābhedāt bhinnamiva pratibhāti, evamihāpi bhāvābhāvayoraupādhiko bhedo bhaviṣyatīti /
children.translated_text: For some say thus: just as one and the same face appears as if different due to differences in the conditioning adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) such as emerald, ruby, and the like, and just as one and the same person appears as if different due to differences in perspective, so here too there will be a conventional (<s>aupādhika</s>) difference between existence and absence.
Objection: In this way, with the difference being merely conventional, real unity would follow.
Let it be so on this view — even then, the distinction of <s>rūpa</s> and the like is established. // 22 //
And this difference grounded in the difference of the cognizer is accepted for <s>rūpa</s> and the like by some.

children.text:
idaṃ cānvārudyavacanenāsmābhiruktam, na hi rūpādīnāṃ grāhakabhedanibandhano bheda', kintu buddhibhedanibandhana eva, mukhaṃ hi pramāṇāntarādekarūpamavagataṃ tadupādhibhedād bhidyata iti yuktam /
na tvekatve rūpādīnāṃ bhedaheturbhāvābhāvayorapi samāna evetyabhiprāyeṇāha---buddhimātreti /
ka' punarayaṃ bhāvābhāvātmako dharmī, yaddharmau bhāvābhāvau, naikaṃ rūpādisamudāyād bhinnamupalabhyate, vṛttyādivikalpākṣamatvāt /
children.translated_text: What then is this property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) that has the nature of existence and absence, whose properties are existence and absence? No single [entity] is apprehended as distinct from the aggregate of <s>rūpa</s> and the like, because of the incapacity for alternatives such as inherence and the like.

children.text: ato deśādyabhinnānāṃ rūpādīnāṃ samudāyo dharmī, na tattvāntaramata āha--- na ceti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the aggregate of <s>rūpa</s> and the like, which are undifferentiated in space and the like, is the property-bearer — not another reality. Hence he says "and not."

children.text: nātra vana iva bādhikā buddhirastīti bhāva' /
children.translated_text: The purport is that here there is no sublating cognition as [there is] for a forest.

And this, though stated in [the section on] <s>savikalpaka</s> (determinate cognition), has been restated here solely for the purpose of establishing the substrate of absence — so there is no repetition. // 23 //

And this has been stated by us as a concessive reply: for the difference of <s>rūpa</s> and the like is not grounded in the difference of the cognizer, but rather is grounded in the difference of cognition alone. For it is proper that a face, cognized as having one form through another <s>pramāṇa</s>, is differentiated by differences in conditioning adjuncts. But it cannot be said that when <s>rūpa</s> and the like are one, the cause of difference is the same for existence and absence too — with this intention he says "cognition-made."
In the form of substance, quality, and being (<s>sat</s>), the oneness of <s>rūpa</s> and the like is accepted;
and with respect to their own nature, these are mutually distinct. // 24 //

children.text: yadi tadvadapekṣātra na syād bhedo 'tra naiva hi /
children.translated_text: If such a relative [distinction] were not [accepted] here, then there would be no difference here at all;
the cognition would not have the character of both existent and non-existent with respect to either. // 25 //
In connection with the existent, the cognition "it is existent" — thus the existent-form — is experienced;
"This does not exist here" — this, however, is caused by the non-conjunction with that. // 26 //
Having grasped the real existence of the entity and having remembered the counter-correlate,
the mental cognition of non-existence arises without dependence on the sense-organs. // 27 //

children.text:
evaṃ tāvadabhāvasya bhāvād bhedābhedau darśitau /
tāveva rūpādidṛṣṭāntena draḍhayati--sadguṇadravyeti /
na hi rūpādaya' sadādirūpeṇa na bhidyanta iti svarūpāpekṣayāpi teṣāṃ bheda' śakyate vārayitum, tayā vā bheda iti na sadādyātmanābheda' pratikṣipyate /
children.translated_text: For <s>rūpa</s> and the like are not [absolutely] undifferentiated in the form of <s>sat</s> (being) and the like — so their difference with respect to their own nature too cannot be prevented; nor, because of that difference, is the non-difference in the form of <s>sat</s> and the like rejected.

children.text: evamabhāvo 'pi bhāvadharmatayā tato bhinno 'pi svarūpāpekṣayābhinna iṣyate /
children.translated_text: Similarly, absence too, though different from the existent as a property of the existent, is accepted as non-different with respect to its own nature.
"In the form of substance" means:
<s>rūpa</s> and the like are non-different from substance, and that [substance] is non-different [from being] — so in that form, there is non-difference of these. This is the meaning. // 24 //
Thus, the difference and non-difference of absence from the existent have been shown. He now confirms the same with the illustration of <s>rūpa</s> and the like — "substance, quality, and being."

children.text: svarūpāpekṣayā rūpādivad bhedānāśrayaṇe bhāvābhāvayoranyataratra na buddhe' sadasadrūpatā bhavedityāha---yaditi ||25||
children.translated_text: If one does not accept the difference as relative, like <s>rūpa</s> and the like, then the cognition would not have the character of both existent and non-existent with respect to either of existence and absence — hence he says "if." // 25 //

children.text: etena, yadāhu'--- na bhāvād bhedakamabhāvasya rūpamupalabhāmaha iti, tannirākṛtam /
children.translated_text: By this, what they say — "we do not apprehend any form of absence that differentiates it from the existent" — is refuted.
Because of the distinction of the existent and non-existent forms.
When the ground that is conjoined with the sense-organ [is perceived], "it exists" is experienced;

children.text: yanna sambadhyate ghaṭādi tannāstīti pratīyata iti ||26||
children.translated_text: what is not conjoined, such as the pot, "it does not exist" is experienced. // 26 //
But there is this difference of cognitions caused by the connection and non-connection with the sense-organ — hence he says "in connection with that."

children.text:
nanvindriyavyāpāranantarameveha ghaṭo nāstīti jñānamutpadyate , tat kuto 'yaṃ viveko nendriyeṇābhāvabudghirjanyata iti /
na hyasati tadvyāpāre bhāvabuddhivadabhāvabuddhirapi jāyamānā dṛśyate /
yadyapi bhāvādabhāvo bhidyate, tathāpi tasya rūpādivatsaṃyuktasamavāyena vā tadviśeṣaṇatayā vendriya
children.translated_text: Objection: Immediately after the operation of the sense-organ, the cognition "there is no pot here" arises — so whence this distinction that the cognition of absence is not produced by the sense-organ? For in the absence of its operation, the cognition of absence, like the cognition of existence, is not seen to arise. Even if absence is different from the existent, still, like <s>rūpa</s> and the like, through the contact of qualified-qualifier conjunction or through its being a qualifier of that [substrate], the sense-organ
Having seen merely the own-form [of the substrate], and then remembering something,
when asked about the non-existence of another thing there, one understands it at that very moment. // 28 //

children.text:
sannikarṣo 'styeva /
atastajjñānamaindriyakaṃ bhavedata āha---gṛhītatveti /
ayamabhiprāya'--- nānāśrayo 'bhāva' śakyate grahītumityāśrayagrahaṇārthamevātrendriyāpekṣā nābhāvagrahaṇāya, yathā nāsmṛte pratiyoginyabhāvo gṛhyata iti tatsmaraṇārthaṃ prācīnajñānajanmana' saṃskārasyodabodhāpyapekṣita', evamāśrayagrahaṇārthamindriyam /
na ca prāptimātramaindriyakajñānajanmani kāraṇam /
api tu yogyatāsahitā prāptiriti pratyakṣe varṇitam /
na cendriyāṇāmabhāvajñānajananayogyatā, teṣvasatsvapi tadbhāvāditi vakṣyate /
mānasamiti kor'tha' /
kiṃ sukhādijñānavanmanasā janyata iti /
yadyevaṃ tathāpi pratyakṣataiva /
na cānantariva bahirmanasa' svātantryamasti /

children.translated_text: True.
But what is described here is the operation of the mind that is common to all <s>pramāṇas</s>.

children.text: kevalātmamana' sannikarṣādeva bāhyendriyānapekṣaṃ pramāṇābhāvenābhāvajñānaṃ janyata ityuktaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: It is stated that through the contact of the self and mind alone, without dependence on the external sense-organs, the cognition of absence is produced by the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>.
And the statements "having grasped" and "having remembered" refer to the same agent because of the non-difference of the property and the property-bearer. // 27 //

[the sense-organ] contact does indeed exist. Therefore, that cognition [of absence] would be sensory — hence he says "having grasped." The intention is this: absence cannot be grasped without a substrate — so the dependence on the sense-organ here is for the purpose of grasping the substrate, not for grasping the absence. Just as absence is not grasped without remembering the counter-correlate — and therefore the awakening of the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) born from prior cognition is also required for the purpose of remembering the counter-correlate — so too the sense-organ is [required] for grasping the substrate. And mere reaching is not the cause of the birth of sensory cognition; rather, reaching accompanied by capacity — as was described in [the section on] perception. And the sense-organs do not have the capacity to produce the cognition of absence — because even in their absence, that [cognition of absence] exists — as will be stated. What then is the meaning of "mental"? Is it produced by the mind, like the cognition of pleasure and the like? If so, even then it is perceptual. But the mind has no independence with respect to external [objects], as in the case of the inner [sense].

children.text:
kathaṃ punaridamavagamyate bhāvagrahaṇamidandriyāpekṣaṃ nābhāvagrahaṇamiti /
samāno hi tadbhāvabhāva' /
ata āha---svarūpeti /
yo hi gṛhasvarūpemevāvadhārya kvacidgata' pṛcchyate--- tatra caitro 'sti na veti, tadāsau pṛṣṭastatra nāstītāṃ tadaiva pratipadyate /
yadi tvindriyādhīnamabāvajñānaṃ bhavet nā sati tadvyāpāre jāyate /
na ca pūrvāvagatābhāvasmaraṇameveti vācyam /
na hyasati pratiyogismaraṇe bhāvo dṛśyate /
na cāśrayagrahaṇakāle pratiyogismaraṇamasti /
bahūnāmeva hi pṛṣṭenābhāva' kathyate /
na ca tāvātāṃ smaraṇaṃ samprati viśeṣeṇa smaryata iti, tadayuktam /
na hyabhāvatvaṃ nāma sāmānyanyato 'vagato viśeṣeṇa smaryata iti, yuktam /

children.translated_text: For that memory has as its seed the dispositional impression (<s>bhāvanā</s>) deposited by prior experience, and it is not capable of having as its object something slight and non-deviant.

children.text: tastadānīmeva pratiyogismaraṇapura' saramindriyānapekṣamabhāvajñānaṃ jāyata iti manoharamidam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, at that very time, the cognition of non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) arises, preceded by the remembrance of the counter-positive, independent of a sense organ — this is an elegant [account].
This is what was said: 'he cognizes at that very time.'
And this has been said as: 'through the cessation of the memory that is the result of perception, [absence is known] as having perception as its non-arisen [result].' // 28 //

But how is it ascertained that the cognition of existence requires a sense organ while the cognition of non-existence does not? For their being-conditioned-by-that is the same. Hence he says — 'of the essential nature.' For one who ascertains the essential nature of the house itself...
And here the status of being inference is not apprehended, because of the absence of an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>);

children.text: bhāvāṃśo nanu liṅgaṃ syāt tadānīṃ nājighṛṇāt // Msv_5,8.29 //
children.translated_text: but [objection:] would not the positive entity be the inferential mark? [Reply:] At that time, it was not desired to be apprehended. // Msv_5,8.29 //
For when the positive element is not desired to be apprehended, the cognition of non-existence arises;

children.text: tasmin pratīyamāne tu nābhāve jāyate mati' // Msv_5,8.30 //
children.translated_text: but when that [positive element] is being cognized, no cognition of non-existence arises. // Msv_5,8.30 //
And this [positive entity] does not establish itself as a property of the thesis (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>), like a word [would];
and along with all [types of] non-existence, the positive entity is considered inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>). // Msv_5,8.31 //

children.text: kvacid bhāve 'pi sadbhāvo jñāto yasya kadācana /
children.translated_text: When the existence of something is known in the presence of a certain entity at some time,
the non-existence of that very thing is also ascertained in that very [place] at another time. // Msv_5,8.32 //

children.text:
evaṃ tāvadakṣajatvamabhāvadhiyo nirākṛttam /
idānīṃ laiṅgikatvaṃ nirākaroti---na cāpyatreti /
atra codayati--- bhāvāṃśeti /
pariharati--- tadānīmiti matirantena /
dvāvatra bhāvau pratiṣedhya' pratiṣedhādhāraśca, tatra na tāvat pratiṣedhyo liṅgam, avagataṃ hi liṅgaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: Two entities are relevant here: what is negated and the substratum of negation. Of these, first, what is negated is not the inferential mark — for an inferential mark must be [something already] ascertained.

children.text: na ca tadā ghaṭo gṛhyate, na hi tasmin gṛhyamāṇe tadabhāvo grahītuṃ śakyate /
children.translated_text: And at that time, the pot is not being apprehended — for when it is being apprehended, its absence cannot be apprehended.
And given the thesis, a non-existent, unseen [entity] cannot have the status of an inferential mark.
Therefore, the positive entity whose negation is not desired to be apprehended is not the inferential mark for non-existence. // 29, 30 //

Thus, first, the sense-organ-born nature of the cognition of absence has been refuted. Now he refutes [the view that] it is inferential — 'and here also.' Here he raises an objection — 'the positive element.' He replies — 'at that time.'

children.text: astu tarhi pratiṣedhādhārabhāvo liṅgamata āha---na caiṣaiti /

children.translated_text: By 'this' he points to the positive entity that is present before one and is manifest (<s>aparokṣa</s>).

children.text: yathārthe pakṣīkṛte padamataddharmatayā na heturityuktam, evameṣo 'pi bhūtalabhāvo na ghaṭādyabhāvadharma iti /
children.translated_text: Just as it was said that when an object is made the thesis, a word is not a valid reason because it lacks the property of being a property of that [thesis] — similarly, this positive entity, the ground-existence, is not a property of the absence of the pot and the like.

children.text: api cānvayādhīnātmalābhamanumānajñānam, na ca bhūtalabhāvasya sarvairabhāvai' sambnadho jñāyate /
children.translated_text: Moreover, inferential knowledge depends for its very existence on positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), but the connection of the existence of the ground with all [types of] absences is not known.

children.text: tat kathaṃ tataste pratyeṣyanta ityāha--- saheti ||31||
children.translated_text: Therefore, how can those [absences] be cognized from it? He says — 'along with.' // 31 //
Let then the positive entity that is the substratum of negation be the inferential mark — hence he says 'and this.'

children.text: astu tāvadabhāvānvaya' kvacid bhūtalādau bhāve, sadbhāvo 'pi yasya ghaṭāde' kadācit jñāta' tasyāpi

children.translated_text: its non-existence too is ascertained there — he says 'in some cases.' // 32 //
Granted that there is a connection of absence with existence in some [cases] like the ground; but even of that pot and the like, whose existence is known at some time,
Where the prior observation [of something] is present, and [where] of the non-existence of that [thing], there too
the cognition of that non-existence has been observed without dependence on a sense organ in [apprehending] the relation. // Msv_5,8.33 //
If the observation of the relation of some positive entity with some non-existence
were [required], then everything could be [inferred as] a <s>pramāṇa</s> there — this would over-extend. // Msv_5,8.34 //
And even when the positive element is apprehended, it is not the case that there is cognition regarding the absence of every other thing —
thus, because of deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>), it has no status as an inferential mark. // Msv_5,8.35 //
And when the relation is being apprehended, the apprehension of the relatum is certain;
by what <s>pramāṇa</s> does the cognition of absence arise then? // Msv_5,8.36 //
For at that time, the apprehension of the relatum would not be by the inferential mark;
there, the cognition of non-existence must necessarily come from another <s>pramāṇa</s>. // Msv_5,8.37 //

children.text: na kevalaṃ yadyatra kadācid dṛṣṭaṃ tanmātrasya tatrābhāvo 'vagamyate, yasyāpi tu yatrābhāvo na dṛṣṭapūrvastasyāpi tatrābhāvo 'vagamyata ityāha---yatreti ||33||
children.translated_text: Not only is the non-existence of that very thing which was once seen somewhere ascertained there — but even the non-existence of something whose absence was never previously observed there is also ascertained — he says 'where.'

children.text: yadi tu yena kenacidekenābhāvenagṛhītasambandhād bhāvādabhāvāntarānumānamiṣyate, tato 'tiprasaktirityāha---kasyaciditi ||34||
children.translated_text: But if the inference of another absence from a positive entity whose relation has been apprehended with some one absence is accepted, then there would be over-extension — he says 'of some.' // 34 //

children.text: na caivamastīti vyatirekeṇa darśayati---gṛhīte 'pi ca bhāvāṃśe naicābhāve 'nyavastuna' /
children.translated_text: And he shows by negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) that this is not so — 'even when the positive element is apprehended, it is not regarding the absence of another thing';
up to 'the cognition of everything.'
And this positive entity is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) because of its connection with other absences as well.

Therefore, because of its inconclusiveness, it has no status as an inferential mark for communicating the absence of the pot and the like — he says 'thus, because of deviation, it has no status as an inferential mark.' // 35 //
Moreover, the apprehension of the relation depends on the apprehension of the relatum.

children.text: tadihābhāvākhye sambandhini grahītavye kiṃ pramāṇamiti vaktavyamityāha--- sambandha iti ||36||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the relatum called 'absence' is to be apprehended here, what is the <s>pramāṇa</s>? — this must be stated, he says — 'the relation.' // 36 //

children.text: na tāvalliṅgagaviditasambandhaṃ tadavadhāraṇe pramāṇam, itaretarāśrayaṃ hi tathā syādityabhiprāyeṇāha---tadānīmiti /
children.translated_text: Now, the inferential mark whose relation has been ascertained is not the <s>pramāṇa</s> for establishing that [absence], for that would involve mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>) — with this intention he says 'at that time.'
Therefore, another <s>pramāṇa</s> must necessarily be sought for its apprehension — he says 'there.' // 37 //
The non-arising of perception and the like will not be an inferential mark;
its relation with a qualifier would not arise from mere generality. // Msv_5,8.38 //

children.text:
atredānīmanupalabdhiliṅgavādino bauddhasya pratyavasthānamāha--- pratyakṣāderiti /
dvedhā hi hetavo bauddhairvibhajyante--- kāryaṃ svabhāva iti, anupalabdhiścekajñānasaṃsargiṇorekopalabdhireva, tasyāśca svarūpaṃ jñeyarūpaṃ ca prakāśate iti jñānajñeyasvabhāvā /
na hyasau svarūpamiva jñeyasattāmapi vyabhicarati /
tasyāśca svasādhyena nāstīti vikalpaśabdātmakavyavahāreṇa tadyogyatayā vā tādātmyameva pratibandha' /
na hyasau nāstīti vyavahāraṃ vyabhicarati śiṃśapeva vṛkṣatām /
tadevaṃ jñātapratibandhānupalabdhi' yo nāma bhrāmyan viviktadeśopalabdhāvapi ghaṭāya ghaṭate taṃ prati nāstīti vyavahāraṃ tadyogyatāṃ vānumāpayati /
evaṃ ca ghaṭādyabhāvānupalabdhiprayoga'--- yad dṛśyaṃ hi sadyatra nopalabhyate tattatra nāsti /
nopalabhyate copalabhyamāne deśe dṛśyo ghaṭa iti /
etadapi dūṣayati--- na viśeṣaṇasambandhastasyā iti /
ya evānupalabdhyānumātumiṣyate ghaṭābhāvo nāstīti vyavahārastadyogyatā vā naikenāpi viśeṣeṇānupalabdhe' sambandho 'vagata', kathaṃ tato viśeṣānumānam /
bhūtalopalabdhirhi sā, tasyāśca nānāvidhānekaghaṭapaṭādiviṣayā nāstīti vyavahārā dṛśyanta iti kathaṃ viśeṣeṇa ghaṭo nāstīti vyavahārayet /
ghaṭānupalabdhirasau, ato ghaṭābhāvaṃ tadvyavahāraṃ vā prasādhayatīti cet /
kastasyā ghaṭena sambandha' /
deśopalabdhirhi sā, tāvadeva tasyā ghaṭānupalabdhitvam /
tacca sarvān pratyaviśiṣṭamiti kathamekenaiva vyapadiśyate ced ghaṭābhāvo nāma kaścit_ /
kasmācca satyapi ghaṭe ghaṭo nāstīti vyavahāro na pravartate /
sadvyavahāravirodhāditi cet /
kathaṃ ghaṭānupalabdhau sadvyavahāra' /
asti hi tadānīmapi deśopalabdhi' /
viviktopalabdhirhi ghaṭānupalabdhi', nāsau ghaṭe satīti cet, ko vivekārtha iti /
nanvayamabhāva eva /
tadabhāve 'narthakaṃ viviktavacanam, ato 'nupalabdherayamapi viśeṣo du' sādha eva, yadasati ghaṭe nāstīti vyavahāro na satīti /
yaccedaṃ ghaṭābhāvamatilaṅghya nāstīti vyavahārānumānamavasthitaṃ tadapi kena viśeṣeṇeti na vidma' /
so 'pi bhāvātirekī na kaścidupalabhyate /
yogyatā tadanatirekiṇī tasmin buddhe buddhaiveti na kiñcidanumeyaṃ paśyāma' /

children.translated_text: By the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>,
however, having set this aside for now,
another refutation has been stated. // 38 //

Here now he states the response of the Buddhist who advocates non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) as an inferential mark — 'of perception and the like.' For the Buddhists divide reasons into two kinds: effect (<s>kārya</s>) and essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), and non-apprehension...
And no <s>pramāṇa</s> arises for the general [concept of] non-existence;

children.text: vyabhicārādā viśeṣāstu pratīyeran kathaṃ tayā // Msv_5,8.39 //
children.translated_text: and because of deviation, how could particulars be cognized through it? // Msv_5,8.39 //
And an inferential mark that has not been ascertained — if it is apprehended, that [mark] too,
being a non-existence, would have to be apprehended by [another] non-existence, or by another reason. // Msv_5,8.40 //

children.text: sa cānyena grahītavyo nāgṛhīte hi liṅgatā /
children.translated_text: And that [other reason] must be apprehended by yet another — for [there is] no status of being an inferential mark for what has not been apprehended;
the apprehension of that would be by an inferential mark, [and that] by another — thus there is an infinite regress. // Msv_5,8.41 //
In the absence of an inferential mark, it would be just the same — therefore, to avoid this regress,

children.text: kvāpyasya syāt pramāṇatvaṃ liṅgatvena vinā dhruvam // Msv_5,8.42 //
children.translated_text: it must have the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s> somewhere without having the status of an inferential mark. // Msv_5,8.42 //
And the cognition 'it does not exist' is the result — and it belongs to [a <s>pramāṇa</s>] that is the non-arising of perception and the like;
and the <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of that very [non-arising] is understood from its immediate [production of the result]. // Msv_5,8.43 //

children.text: abhāvasāmānyena tvanupabdhe' sambandha' sidhyatyeva, na tvabhāvasāmānye pramāṇamupajāyata ityāha--- sāmānyeti /
children.translated_text: The relation of non-apprehension with non-existence in general is indeed established; but no <s>pramāṇa</s> arises for non-existence in general — he says 'in general.'

children.text: viśeṣāstvanaikāntikatayā nānupalabdhyā bodhayituṃ śakyanta ityāha--- vyabhicārāditi ||39||
children.translated_text: But particular [absences] cannot be made known through non-apprehension because of inconclusiveness — he says 'because of deviation.' // 39 //

children.text: api ca--- nānavagatarūpaṃ liṅgamanumāne liṅgaṃ bhavati, tadiyaṃ pratyakṣādyanutpattirabhāvatvādapareṇa liṅgenāvagantavyā /
children.translated_text: Moreover — an inferential mark whose form has not been ascertained is not a valid mark in inference; therefore, this non-arising of perception and the like, being itself a non-existence, must be ascertained by another inferential mark.

children.text: evaṃ hi vadanti,yāvān kaścit pratiṣedha' sa sarvo 'palabdhereveti /
children.translated_text: For they say thus: 'Every negation whatsoever is [known] through non-apprehension alone.'

children.text: evaṃ ca tatra tatra sadṛśāparāparaliṅgānusāreṇānavasthāpāta ityāha--- na ceti dvayena /
children.translated_text: And thus, by pursuing one similar inferential mark after another for each [case], there is a fall into infinite regress — he says 'and not' through two [verses].

And this was stated as: 'non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension' — a formulation arrived at [by them]; but [the reply] that 'non-apprehension is [something whose] other referent is distinguished' was the counter-response. // 40, 41 //

children.text: evaṃ yo 'pyasau liṅgirūpābhāva' so 'pi sambandhagrahaṇārthamavaśyaṃ prathamavagantavya' /
children.translated_text: Thus, even that form of absence which is the inferential mark must first be ascertained for the purpose of apprehending the relation.
Even upon its ascertainment, because of the acceptance of yet another inferential mark of that very form, there is just an infinite regress.
Therefore, somewhere the absence of inference must be accepted and another <s>pramāṇa</s> must be admitted — he says 'inferential mark.' // 42 //

children.text:
yadi tu nāstīti buddhireva liṅgamityucyate tanna /
phalaṃ hi sā, pratyakṣādyanutpādasya kathaṃ talliṅgam, tatsiddhyarthameva hi liṅgamiṣyate /
children.translated_text: But if it is said that the cognition 'it does not exist' is itself the inferential mark — that is not so. For it is the result (<s>phala</s>). How can the non-arising of perception and the like be its inferential mark, when the very purpose of the mark is to establish that [non-arising]?
The cognition that is produced by [a reason possessing] the three characteristics is accepted as inference;
but nothing in the form of non-arising requires a cause [in the manner of an inferential mark]. // Msv_5,8.44 //
If non-existence is a <s>pramāṇa</s>, what is its <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge)?
Just as non-existence is the object of knowledge, so too should the <s>pramāṇa</s> be accepted [as non-existence]. // Msv_5,8.45 //
When the object of knowledge is of the nature of a positive entity, non-existence does not have the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s>;
likewise, when the object of knowledge is non-existence, a positive entity does not have the status of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. // Msv_5,8.46 //
But when the cognition is already established, what is the need for an inferential mark?
This is what he says — 'not.'

children.text: yadi sā phalaṃ kiṃ tarhi pramāṇata āha--- tasyaiveti /
children.translated_text: If that [cognition] is the result, then what is the <s>pramāṇa</s>? He says — 'of that very.'

children.text: yasyaiva sā phalaṃ tadeva pratyakṣādyanutpatte' phalānantaryātpramāṇamiti ||43||
children.translated_text: That of which it is the result — that very [non-arising], because of its immediately producing the result of the non-arising of perception and the like, is the <s>pramāṇa</s>. // 43 //

children.text:
kiñca saugatasamayasiddhānumānalakṣaṇagranthānusāreṇāpi na pratyakṣādyajanmano 'numānatvamityāha---trilakṣaṇeti /
evaṃ hi te paṭhanti /
'trirūpālliṅgator'thadṛganumāna'miti /
na cānutpattirutpatte' prāgabhāvo buddhe' kenacijjanyate, prāgeva trilakṣaṇena hetuneti /

children.translated_text: Objection: But non-apprehension is accepted as inference by way of being a reason, not that the inferential cognition is inference — rather, [it is inference] by way of establishing an existing entity.
What then [is the point] of refuting that?
True — to begin with, the inference-status [of non-apprehension] has been refuted [on the ground] of its not being a reason.
But by this, the non-conformity with the definition is being described. // 44 //

Moreover, even following the treatises on the definition of inference established in the Buddhist system, the non-arising of perception and the like is not inference — thus he says — 'trilakṣaṇa' etc. For they recite thus: 'From a mark possessing three characteristics, the cognition of the object is inference.' And the non-arising [of perception], being the prior absence of the arising of cognition, is not generated by anything — much less by a reason possessing the three characteristics.

children.text:
atra codayati--- (mānamiti) pramāṇatā hi bhāvātmanā vyāptā pratyakṣādiṣvavagatā, tannivṛttyā nivartyata iti bhāva' /
itarastu--- varṇito 'smābhi' prāgbhāvanāmasaṅkaraścaturdhā /
na ca tabdodhasya bhāvabodhavailakṣaṇyamupalabhyate, bādhavirahasāmānyāt /
sa ca prāmāṇye kāraṇaṃ na bhāvasvarūpatā /
children.translated_text: And that [absence of sublation] is the cause of validity, not the nature of existence.

children.text: sā tu prāmāṇyaṃ pratyaprayojikaiva kathañcitteṣu saṅgatā, ato nābhāvatvenāprāmāṇyaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: That [existence-nature], however, is irrelevant to validity; it is somehow associated with those [pramāṇas] — hence there is no invalidity on account of being an absence.
But with respect to an existent object of knowledge, that [absence] is indeed not a <s>pramāṇa</s> — with this purport he says — 'prameya' (knowable) etc.
It is indeed fitting that absence is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for absence — thus he says — 'meya' etc. // 45 //

Here he raises an objection — ('māna' etc.) — The thought is: <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood (validity) is pervaded by the nature of existence, as cognized in perception and the like; by the cessation of that [existence-nature], it is removed. But the other [view] is: We have described the fourfold non-confusion [of substances] called <s>prāgabhāva</s> (prior absence) and the rest. And no dissimilarity of its cognition from the cognition of existence is apprehended, because of the commonality of the absence of sublation.

children.text: yathā bhāvātmake meye 'bhāva' pramāṇaṃ nānurūpaṃ tathā tadabhāve bhāva ityāha--- bhāvātmaka iti ||46||
children.translated_text: Just as absence is not a fitting <s>pramāṇa</s> for a knowable that has the nature of existence, so too existence [is not fitting] for the absence of that — thus he says — 'bhāvātmaka' etc. // 46 //

children.text: bhāvātmakasya mānatvaṃ na ca rājājñayā sthitam /
children.translated_text: The <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of what has the nature of existence is not established by royal decree;
rather, the <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of both [existence and absence] would be due to having discrimination as their result. // Msv_5,8.47 //
But if the <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood of this [absence] is not accepted on account of its being an absence,
[then consider:] the causality of a [real] entity is [merely] observed — [and this is merely] a presupposition. // Msv_5,8.48 //
The mark-hood and knowability [of absence] would not obtain — just like that indeed;

children.text: tathā sati ca pūrvokto vyavahāro na sidhyati // Msv_5,8.49 //
children.translated_text: and if that were so, the worldly practice stated earlier would not be established. // Msv_5,8.49 //
From the non-arising of the <s>pramāṇas</s>, [the non-arising] is not a property of absence;

children.text: yatrābhāvo 'sti tenāsyā' sambandho naiva vidyate // Msv_5,8.50 //
children.translated_text: where absence exists, there is no connection whatsoever of this [non-arising] with it. // Msv_5,8.50 //

children.text: yo na sannihitastatra tasya dharmo bhavediyam /
children.translated_text: This could be a property of what is not present there;

children.text: na ca tasya prameyatvaṃ dharmadharmitvavarjanāt // Msv_5,8.51 //
children.translated_text: but the knowability of that [absent entity] would not obtain, due to the abandonment of property and property-bearer [relationship]. // Msv_5,8.51 //

children.text: na bhāvatmakameva pramāṇamiti rājājñā, yadeva tu paricchedaphalaṃ tadeva tu pramāṇam, tacca pratyakṣādyajanmano 'pi samānamityāha---bhāvātmakasyeti||
children.translated_text: It is not a royal decree that only what has the nature of existence is a <s>pramāṇa</s>; rather, whatever has discrimination as its result is a <s>pramāṇa</s> — and that is common to the non-arising of perception and the like as well — thus he says — 'bhāvātmakasya' etc.
One might say: Since <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood has been observed only in real entities, the non-apprehension, being a non-entity, does not have <s>pramāṇa</s>-hood.

children.text: tathā ca sati bauddhānāmapi liṅga prameyatve na syātām, te 'pi hi nāvastuno dṛṣṭe ityāha-- yadīti sārdhena /
children.translated_text: And if that were so, for the Buddhists too, mark-hood and knowability would not obtain — for they too have not observed [these] in a non-entity — thus he says — 'yadi' etc. with one and a half [verses].
He states the fault in granting [this objection] — 'tathā sati' etc.

children.text: na ca syād vyavahāro 'yamiti kāraṇādivibhāgenokto vyavahāra ityartha' ||48,49||
children.translated_text: 'And this worldly practice would not exist' — the meaning is: the worldly practice stated through the distinction of causes and the like [would not exist]. // 48, 49 //
When absence is made the thesis, the non-arising of perception and the like is not cognized as being its property.
The purport is: because of the absence of connection with absence.

children.text: nanvabhāvaviśiṣṭaṃ bhūtalaṃ sādhayiṣyāma', tacca pūrvavagatamiti taddharmo bhaviṣyatītyata āha--- yatreti /
children.translated_text: Objection: But we shall make the ground qualified by absence the [thesis] to be proved, and since that has been previously cognized, [the non-arising] will be its property — therefore he says — 'yatra' etc.

children.text: na hi bhūtale pratyakṣānutpatti', jñāyamānatvāt tasyeti ||50||
children.translated_text: For there is no non-arising of perception in the ground, since it is [itself] being cognized. // 50 //
Even because of not being a property of the thesis, the non-arising of perception and the like is not an inferential mark — thus he says — 'pramāṇānām' etc.

children.text:
ghaṭasya tarhi dharmo bhaviṣyati tadgocare pratyakṣādīnāmanutpatterata āha---yaiti /
satyam /
yatra pratyakṣādīni notpadyante taddharmatā kathañcid bhavedapi, na tvasāviha pramīyate /
dharmadharmitvayorabhāvāt /
na hi
children.translated_text: Then it will be a property of the pot, since there is non-arising of perception and the like in its domain — therefore he says — 'ya' etc. True — where perception and the like do not arise, the property-status [of non-arising] could somehow obtain. But that [the pot] is not what is being measured here, because of the absence of the property-bearer and property [relationship]. For indeed—
but the connection with absence would be through its being its object;

children.text: tajjñānād viṣaytavaṃ ca jñāne meyaṃ na vidyate // Msv_5,8.52 //
children.translated_text: and from the cognition of that, its being the object — [but] the knowable is not found in the cognition. // Msv_5,8.52 //
A connection of conjunction, inherence, and the like simply does not exist;

children.text: nāgṛhīte hi dharmatvaṃ gṛhīte siddhasādhanam // Msv_5,8.53 //
children.translated_text: when [absence is] not grasped, there is no property-status; when grasped, there is the fallacy of proving what is already proved. // Msv_5,8.53 //
It differs from [the non-arising of] perception and the like by being expressible by the word 'absence';
for the absence of <s>pramāṇas</s> is like the absence of the knowables. // Msv_5,8.54 //
Absence too is measured by a <s>pramāṇa</s> appropriate to itself;

children.text: prameyatvād yathā bhāvastasmād bhāvātmakāt pṛthak // Msv_5,8.55 //
children.translated_text: just as existence, because of being knowable — hence [absence is] separate from what has the nature of existence. // Msv_5,8.55 //

children.text: karmāṇi sarvāṇi phalai' samastai' sarvairyathāvacca yadaṅgakāraṇḍai' /
children.translated_text: All ritual actions, with all their fruits, and with all their subsidiary components (<s>aṅga</s>) as appropriate—

children.text: na saṅgatānīha parasparaṃ hi nāṅgaṃ tadetatprabhavaṃ kratūnām // Msv_5,8.56 //
children.translated_text: are not mutually connected here; this is not a subsidiary — this is the origin of the rites. // Msv_5,8.56 //
Having made that the property-bearer, the qualification by absence is to be proved, since it is not cognized.

children.text: nāpi tadviśiṣṭaṃ bhūtalādi, tadānīṃ tasya tatrābhāvāditi ||51||
children.translated_text: Nor is the ground and the like qualified by that [absence], since at that time it is absent there. // 51 //

children.text: abhāvasya tu sādharmo bhaviṣyati tadviṣayatvāt tasyā' /
children.translated_text: But [the non-arising] will be a property of absence, since that [non-arising] has absence as its object.

children.text: abhāve hi prameye sā liṅgaṃ bhavatyeva /
children.translated_text: For when absence is the knowable, that [non-arising] is indeed an inferential mark.

children.text: kintu nāsrañcetito bhāvo viṣayo bhaviṣyati, jñāte ca prameyābhāva ityāha---abhāveneti ||52||
children.translated_text: But the existence [of the object] will not be an object intended from here; and when the absence of the knowable is known — thus he says — 'abhāvena' etc. // 52 //

children.text: anyastu na kaścidabhāvenānutpatte' sambandhaprakāro vidyate, yena taddharmatāmanugamyānumānaṃ bhaviṣyatītyāha---saṃyogaiti /
children.translated_text: But there is no other kind of connection of non-arising with absence by which, having followed the property-status of that, inference could occur — thus he says — 'saṃyoga' etc.
And this is another [argument for] its not being a property of the thesis — thus he says — 'nāgṛhīte' etc.
For smoke is not cognized as a property of an ungrasped mountain.

children.text: atha tadvadabhāvo 'pi prāk pratīyata ityucyate, siddhaṃ tarhi sādhyata iti ||53||
children.translated_text: But if it is said: 'Like that, absence too is cognized beforehand' — then what is to be proved is already established. // 53 //

children.text: evaṃ pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ prasādhitaṃ bhedaṃ prayogeṇa darśayati---abhāvaśabdeti ||54||
children.translated_text: Having thus established the difference through perception and inference, he demonstrates it through a formal argument — 'abhāvaśabda' etc. // 54 //
He states another formal argument — 'abhāvo 'pi' etc. ending with 'bhāva.'
